Facilitator's Guide: Before You Begin

Choose what your students and your room need before the first instructional unit.

Week 0 is a menu

Nothing in this module is required as a first-week script. Use the pieces that help you introduce yourself, establish how your room works, get students into the course, or learn how this particular group works together. Change them, replace them, or skip them. Nobody signs a lab contract.

Choose the job you need Week 0 to do

  • Welcome students: introduce yourself and explain what Smart Solutions is. The optional About Me + What Is VILS Canva template includes the reusable course overview; replace Elisha's photos and personal details before presenting it. If you want a written handout too, personalize the optional syllabus Canva template.
  • Establish routines: use your own materials, adapt Elisha Lucero's classroom slides, or build a social contract with students.
  • Learn the group: choose one community builder. One is enough.
  • Handle accounts and devices: use the Chromebook option or the Xello check-in when students actually have their devices and logins.

What is in the module

  1. Teacher references: this guide, the Year at a Glance, and the Program Scope + Sequence. Keep teacher pages unpublished.
  2. Student orientation: Student's Guide: Getting Started has the English and Spanish Canvas videos.
  3. Optional classroom setup: Class Jobs and the Welcome Week menu.
  4. Optional community builders: About Me Smartphone, Moon Landing Teamwork Challenge, and Partner Draw.
  5. Optional device day: Chromebook Rules GimKit Day.
  6. Xello: Log in to Xello only when ClassLink and student access are ready.

Use Elisha's rules only if they fit your room

The course file Classroom Rules and the CREATE System contains Elisha Lucero's own expectations. It is an example and an editable starting point, not the Smart Solutions program's required rule system.

The CREATE reminder is: Care for others; Read the TVB; Equipment must be respected; Act safely and responsibly; Tidy your work area; Engage in your learning.

Before students open anything

  • Choose the pages you will actually use and publish only those pages.
  • Replace teacher-specific rules, images, contact details, and device procedures.
  • Confirm ClassLink, Xello, Canvas, and Chromebook access before assigning a login task.
  • Set dates in your own course calendar. The master template cannot know your school calendar.
  • Open Student View and follow the same path students will follow.

A note about Gimkit

Students need their own devices for a normal Gimkit game. Run it after device setup, or project it and answer as a whole class. A large question bank does not need to become one long game; use a timed mode and stop when the review has done its job.

Grading

The routines and community builders are ungraded. The Xello check-in is the only scored Week 0 item in the template. Check its points and submission settings before you publish it in your local copy.

The live module order for the 2027 Smart Solutions template.

Use Modules as the course table of contents. The order below matches the live course. Publish only the current student work and keep Facilitator's Guides unpublished.

Piskel Micro Animation stays between Comics and Graphic Design. Its superhero theme makes it a useful bridge from comic storytelling into visual-design work. Its current module title still labels it Enrichment, so teachers should decide whether to use it before the graphic-design unit.

Welcome Week: Syllabus + Lab Contract

Choose the expectations and routines your students actually need.

TEACHER OPTION · use it, change it, or lose it

  • English
  • Español

Week 0 is a menu. Use your own expectations, borrow Elisha's, build a social contract, or mix the pieces that fit. Nothing here is a course requirement.

👋 Optional teacher templates

  • About Me + What Is VILS: keep the Smart Solutions overview; replace Elisha's photos and personal details before presenting.
  • Syllabus template: personalize the policies, contact information, dates, and campus expectations, or skip it.

Both are teacher options. Students do not submit anything.

🧭 Classroom expectations menu

  1. Your own materials. Walk the syllabus and expectations you already use.
  2. Elisha's materials. Download Classroom Rules and the CREATE System. The deck includes TVB, CREATE, Chromebook rules, consequences, late work, media release, and pathway choices. These are Elisha's classroom expectations. Edit anything that does not fit your campus, or skip the deck.
  3. A class social contract. Use the social contract slides as a group activity, or use the bellringer form to collect words for a class word cloud. Both Google links open a copy for the teacher.

If you use Elisha's rules, Gimkit: VILS Rules 2026 is an optional check. The kit has 78 questions, so use a timed mode. Students need their own devices, or you can project it and play as a class.

🔧 Routine menu · pick what fits

TVB and movementPractise reading the Time, Voice, and Body settings. Add your restroom process, posted roles, or work zones if you use them.
EquipmentPractise assigned logins and devices, equipment checkout, approved sites, downloads, and returning gear to its labelled spot.
ChromebooksPractise carrying by the base, checking for damage, using the assigned device, and returning it to the correct cart slot plugged in.
SafetyPractise PPE, tied-back hair, clear cords and walkways, file clearance, and staying with machines during a job.
CleanupPractise the 7-minute reset: return tools, log off, wipe tables, push in chairs, and be seated when the area is clean.
Work and helpPractise the help queue, group roles or pair rules, and when collaboration or headphones are allowed.

✅ Practise it: How you teach it is your call. Whatever you choose, model the routine and let students practise it once.

🔌 Gimkit needs devices

The Gimkit needs one device per student. Save it until Chromebooks are assigned, or project it and play together.

resource.body:
OPTION · Moon Landing Teamwork Challenge

A consensus-building challenge that shows students a team can out-think any one person in it.

TEACHER OPTION — pick the openers that fit your class; you do not do them all.

  • English
  • Español

Teams rank survival gear after a crash landing on the moon, then find out how close they got to NASA.

🎒 What you need: The deck, the ranking chart and the answer key — all three are in the box below.

  1. Set the scene: your ship crash-landed on the lit side of the moon, roughly 200 miles from the rendezvous point.
  2. Every student ranks the survival items alone first. No talking yet — this is the number you will compare against later.
  3. Teams reach a consensus ranking. Rule: no voting and no averaging, you have to talk each other into it.
  4. Reveal NASA’s expert ranking. Score the gap for each individual sheet and for the team sheet, then compare.

💬 Ask this at the end: How does effective teamwork and communication improve decisions when the stakes are high?

✅ Wrap up: Almost every time, the team score beats the individual scores. Name that out loud — it is the whole point, and it earns you the rest of the year.

🌙 Everything for this activity

Print the ranking chart before class: one per student, plus one per team.

🖥️ Teacher slide deck — 14 slides with speaker notes, projects the whole activity (.pptx) 🖨️ Student ranking chart — the 15 items, blank ranking and scoring columns (PDF, 1 page) 🔑 Teacher answer key — NASA’s rankings and the score bands (PDF, 1 page)

Original source packet: Moon Landing (Grahame Knox).

Los equipos ordenan equipo de supervivencia tras un aterrizaje forzoso en la luna y luego ven qué tan cerca quedaron de la NASA.

🎒 Qué necesitas: La presentación, la hoja de clasificación y la clave — los tres están en el recuadro de abajo.

  1. Plantea la escena: su nave se estrelló en el lado iluminado de la luna, a unas 200 millas del punto de encuentro.
  2. Cada estudiante ordena los artículos solo primero. Todavía sin hablar — ese es el número que van a comparar después.
  3. Los equipos llegan a un orden por consenso. Regla: nada de votar ni de promediar, tienen que convencerse hablando.
  4. Revela el orden experto de la NASA. Calcula la diferencia de cada hoja individual y la del equipo, y compáralas.

💬 Pregunta esto al final: ¿Cómo mejoran las decisiones el trabajo en equipo y la comunicación cuando hay mucho en juego?

✅ Para cerrar: Casi siempre el puntaje del equipo le gana al individual. Dilo en voz alta — ese es todo el punto, y te gana el resto del año.

🌙 Todo lo que necesitas para esta actividad

Imprime la hoja de clasificación antes de la clase: una por estudiante y una por equipo.

🖥️ Presentación para el maestro — 14 diapositivas con notas, proyecta toda la actividad (.pptx) 🖨️ Hoja de clasificación del estudiante — los 15 artículos y las columnas de puntaje en blanco (PDF, 1 página) 🔑 Clave para el maestro — el orden de la NASA y las bandas de puntaje (PDF, 1 página)

Paquete original: Moon Landing (Grahame Knox). Los tres archivos están en inglés.

OPTION · Partner Draw

A ten-minute game: one partner describes a shape, the other draws it without looking.

TEACHER OPTION — pick the openers that fit your class; you do not do them all.

  • English
  • Español

Back to back, one student describes and one draws. Nobody gets to point, and that is the lesson.

🎒 What you need: The Partner Draw slide deck, blank paper, and pencils.

  1. Seat partners back to back. One is the describer, one is the drawer.
  2. Show the describer a shape from the deck. The drawer must not see the screen.
  3. Words only — no gestures, and the describer may not name the object. The drawer may ask questions.
  4. Compare the drawing to the original, then swap roles and run a second shape.
  5. Debrief: which words actually worked? Almost always it is the specific ones and the ones about position.

✅ Wrap up: Land it on the point: precise language is a technical skill, not a personality trait. You will call back to this all year.

⏱️ This one is short

Partner Draw started as a ten-minute bellringer, so it fits in front of a longer activity rather than filling a period.

Espalda con espalda, un estudiante describe y otro dibuja. Nadie puede señalar, y esa es la lección.

🎒 Qué necesitas: La presentación de Partner Draw, hojas en blanco y lápices.

  1. Sienta a las parejas espalda con espalda. Uno describe y el otro dibuja.
  2. Muéstrale una figura de la presentación a quien describe. Quien dibuja no debe ver la pantalla.
  3. Solo palabras — nada de gestos, y quien describe no puede decir el nombre del objeto. Quien dibuja sí puede preguntar.
  4. Comparen el dibujo con el original, luego cambien de papel y hagan una segunda figura.
  5. Comenten: ¿qué palabras sí funcionaron? Casi siempre son las específicas y las que hablan de posición.

✅ Para cerrar: Cierra con la idea clave: el lenguaje preciso es una habilidad técnica, no un rasgo de personalidad. Vas a retomar esto todo el año.

⏱️ Esta es corta

Partner Draw nació como actividad inicial de diez minutos, así que va bien antes de una actividad más larga en vez de llenar toda la clase.

OPTION · Chromebook Rules GimKit Day

Device numbers, Canvas logins, and the rules — closed out with a live Gimkit review.

TEACHER OPTION — pick the openers that fit your class; you do not do them all.

  • English
  • Español

The logistics day — cards, device numbers, logins — with a game at the end so it does not feel like paperwork.

🎒 What you need: VILS cards, the Chromebook cart, your Chromebook rules presentation, and Gimkit ready to launch.

  1. Bellringer: students find their VILS card as they walk in.
  2. Assign Chromebook numbers and record them. Students return to the same numbered machine every day.
  3. Walk the Chromebook rules and etiquette presentation — handling, charging, what not to install, and what to do about damage.
  4. Everyone logs into the VILS Canvas course. Expect password resets; budget more time than you think.
  5. Close with Gimkit — Chromebook and VILS Rules 2025 to lock the rules in. It is a 96-question kit, so cap the round.

✅ Wrap up: Before they leave, every student should know their Chromebook number and be able to reach the Canvas course without help.

🔢 Write the numbers down twice

The number a student gets today is the one they keep all year. Keep one copy in your gradebook and one on the cart — you will need it in March when a machine turns up damaged.

El día de logística — tarjetas, números de equipo, contraseñas — con un juego al final para que no se sienta trámite.

🎒 Qué necesitas: Las tarjetas VILS, el carrito de Chromebooks, tu presentación de reglas y Gimkit listo para abrir.

  1. Actividad inicial: los estudiantes buscan su tarjeta VILS al entrar.
  2. Asigna los números de Chromebook y anótalos. Cada estudiante regresa al mismo equipo numerado todos los días.
  3. Recorre la presentación de reglas y etiqueta de la Chromebook — cómo cargarla, cómo manejarla, qué no instalar y qué hacer si se daña.
  4. Todos entran al curso de Canvas de VILS. Habrá contraseñas que reiniciar; calcula más tiempo del que crees.
  5. Cierra con Gimkit — Chromebook and VILS Rules 2025 para afianzar las reglas. Son 96 preguntas, así que limita la ronda.

✅ Para cerrar: Antes de salir, cada estudiante debe saber su número de Chromebook y poder entrar al curso de Canvas sin ayuda.

🔢 Anota los números dos veces

El número que le toca hoy a cada estudiante es el que conserva todo el año. Guarda una copia en tu registro y otra en el carrito — la vas a necesitar en marzo cuando aparezca un equipo dañado.

⬡ Xello Check-in • College & Career Readiness ⬡

LOG IN TO XELLO

Ten minutes now. Everything else this year lands here.

⏱️ ~25 min
🛠️ Xello via ClassLink
💻 Your device
📤 Screenshot of dashboard
  • English
  • Español

📢 Before we build anything, you need somewhere to keep track of it. Xello is that place — your quizzes, saved careers, experiences, and plans all live in one profile that follows you into high school.

Today's words

dashboard • profile • About Me • after high school goal

1

Log in to Xello

Open ClassLink and click the Xello tile. Go through ClassLink, not a Google search — that is the only login that connects to your saved work.

2

Set your after high school goal

On About Me, find your after high school goal and pick one of three: Not sure yet, More school or training, or Alternate route. About 2 minutes.

This is the one that unlocks everything after it. Xello keeps Matchmaker locked until this goal is set, and Matchmaker is what Personality Style, the Skills lesson, and Explore career matches all build on.

You can change your answer any time. Not sure yet is a real choice, not a way out of choosing.

3

Check your profile, then screenshot it

Make sure your name and grade are right on About Me — if something is wrong, tell your teacher instead of fixing it yourself. Then go back to your Xello dashboard, the home screen with your name on it. Capture that screen.

• Chromebook: Ctrl + Show Windows

• Windows: Windows key + Shift + S

4

Upload the screenshot here

Attach the image to this assignment. Your work has to be readable in the picture — a blurry photo of your screen taken with a phone does not count.

💡 This one unlocks the rest

Every Xello check-in this year starts the same way: ClassLink, then the Xello tile. There are about a dozen of them between now and June, and the after high school goal is the gate on the first one.

Xello is not a class you pass. It is a profile that follows you into high school, so what goes in it should be true.

💬 Reflect

In the comments of your submission, finish this sentence:

"The after high school goal I picked was ______ because ______."

Word Bank

dashboard • profile • About Me • after high school goal

✅ Before you log off:

✓ Logged in through ClassLink

✓ After high school goal set on About Me

✓ Name and grade checked on About Me

✓ Screenshot of my dashboard uploaded

✓ Reflection sentence in the comments

📢 Antes de construir cualquier cosa, necesitas un lugar donde llevar la cuenta. Xello es ese lugar — tus exámenes, carreras guardadas, experiencias y planes viven en un solo perfil que te acompaña a la preparatoria.

Palabras de hoy

dashboard (tablero) • profile (perfil) • About Me (Sobre mí) • after high school goal (meta después de la preparatoria)

1

Entra a Xello

Abre ClassLink y haz clic en el cuadro de Xello. Entra por ClassLink, no por una búsqueda de Google — ese es el único acceso que se conecta con tu trabajo guardado.

2

Escoge tu meta después de la preparatoria

En About Me, busca your after high school goal y escoge una de tres: Not sure yet (todavía no sé), More school or training (más escuela o capacitación) o Alternate route (ruta alterna). Como 2 minutos.

Esta es la que desbloquea todo lo demás. Xello mantiene Matchmaker bloqueado hasta que escojas esta meta, y sobre Matchmaker se construyen Personality Style, la lección de Skills y Explore career matches.

Puedes cambiar tu respuesta cuando quieras. Not sure yet es una opción real, no una forma de no escoger.

3

Revisa tu perfil y toma captura

Asegúrate de que tu nombre y tu grado estén correctos en About Me — si algo está mal, avísale a tu maestro en vez de arreglarlo tú. Luego regresa a tu tablero de Xello, la pantalla de inicio que tiene tu nombre. Captura esa pantalla.

• Chromebook: Ctrl + Mostrar ventanas

• Windows: tecla Windows + Shift + S

4

Sube la captura aquí

Adjunta la imagen a esta tarea. Tu trabajo tiene que leerse bien en la imagen — una foto borrosa de tu pantalla tomada con el celular no cuenta.

💡 Esta desbloquea lo demás

Cada check-in de Xello este año empieza igual: ClassLink y luego el cuadro de Xello. Habrá como una docena de aquí a junio, y la meta después de la preparatoria es la puerta del primero.

Xello no es una clase que se pasa. Es un perfil que te acompaña a la preparatoria, así que lo que pongas ahí debe ser cierto.

💬 Reflexiona

En los comentarios de tu envío, completa esta oración:

(La meta después de la preparatoria que escogí fue ______ porque ______.)

"The after high school goal I picked was ______ because ______."

resource.body:
SW1 · WEEKS 1 AND 2 · TEACHER ONLY

Design Thinking + Superhero Comics

Week 1 gives students one fast pass through design thinking. Week 2 asks them to carry one hero through a cover, biography, smart gadget, logo, and final four-panel solution. The comic is graded once, at the end.

How the two weeks fit

WhenWhat students doWhat they learn
Week 1Run Ready, Set, Design live or through the interactive lesson. Use Five Chair as a second practice round or flex route. Complete the Xello check-in.Design starts with a person and a problem. A first idea is something to test, not something to defend forever.
Week 2Build one paper comic across five connected lessons.Visual choices, character choices, systems, and cause and effect all have to agree well enough for a reader to follow the hero without a spoken explanation.

Why Matchmaker is in Week 1

The S&S names Personality Style and Learning Style in Week 1. Xello lists Matchmaker as phase 1 and Personality Style as phase 2, so the Canvas check-in keeps Matchmaker, Personality Style, and Learning Style in that order. This is a product sequence. It is not a new learning pillar for the Comics project. Review Xello's current assessment sequence.

If students finish Matchmaker here, do not assign the same quiz again in Week 5. Use that later check-in to review results, save careers, or catch up students who were absent.

The comic has one job per page

LessonStudent workLearning piece
1. CoverTitle, hero, and purposeful colour choicesA cover gives a reader the first clues about identity, tone, and audience.
2. BiographyExperience, motivation, ability, challenge, and goalThe same power can lead to different choices. Motivation is what makes the difference visible.
3. GadgetA labelled smart gadget that solves a specific needNeed -> input -> process -> output. Students trace how the gadget receives information, follows a rule, and responds.
4. LogoThree small sketches, one final logo, and short design explanationsA useful logo is simple, recognisable at different sizes, and connected to the hero through meaningful symbols and colours.
5. Smart solutionChallenge, hero choice, gadget action, and visible resultA reader should be able to see the cause and effect. The last panel has to show what changed.

Teacher guides

Every teacher guide is unpublished and sits directly before the lesson it supports.

  • Ready, Set, Design teacher guide and materials
  • Comics Lesson 1 teacher guide
  • Comics Lesson 2 teacher guide
  • Comics Lesson 3 teacher guide
  • Comics Lesson 4 teacher guide
  • Comics Lesson 5 teacher guide

Materials and storage

  • Ready, Set, Design material bags for groups, or the self-paced interactive route.
  • Optional Five Chair materials for a second design round or flex route. The Ready, Set, Design guide has the real facilitator guide, deck, worksheet, checkpoint, and materials list.
  • Three sheets of paper per comic, plus pencils, erasers, and colouring supplies.
  • One teacher sample with the cover and Pages 1 through 4 labelled.
  • A storage plan. Collect the comics between classes so five days of work do not live loose in backpacks.

One grade at the end

Keep Lessons 1 through 4 as checks for progress. The completed comic is one 100-point Major grade: cover and visual identity (10), biography and motivation (15), gadget need/function/input/output (20), logo communication (20), final smart-solution sequence (25), and complete/readable submission (10). Drawing skill is not scored.

Optional video and Animation handoff

The Gabrielle Jordan Williams video is an optional entrepreneurship example. Lesson 4 works without it. Use the original TEDx video or copy the reusable Edpuzzle into their own account.

Animation is a separate, optional five-day to one-and-a-half-week unit after Comics. It may reuse the hero, one action, and the visual identity; Animation adds its own plot diagram, storyboard, production, feedback, and export work. Comics is complete after Lesson 5 whether the teacher runs Animation or moves directly to Graphic Design.

Optional portfolio setup

The Portfolio page after Lesson 5 is optional and unpublished. Use it during a flex or catch-up block, assign it in pieces, or save it for a later portfolio week. Move into Graphic Design after Lesson 5 unless you have deliberately added portfolio time.

Before publishing for students

  1. Open the Ready, Set, Design interactive lesson in Student View. Use the live presentation route if the SCORM launch is blocked. If you run Five Chair, test its four copy links from the teacher account that will use them.
  2. Test the Ready, Set, Design worksheet copy link and one sample PDF upload.
  3. Confirm students can reach Xello through the district login route. Then publish the Xello check-in when you assign it in Week 1.
  4. Open all five comic decks and leave each lesson's work-time slide projected during independent work.
  5. Test the final comic upload and six-part rubric in Student View.

TEACHER ONLY · WEEK 1

Ready, Set, Design

Teach the five steps of design thinking, then let students practice the full cycle in a fast group challenge. Teams work from a user need, sketch several ideas, build a small prototype, test it, and make one useful change.

Core lesson: teach it whole group

Use the complete lesson deck as the main route. Slides 1 through 12 teach what design thinking is, why designers begin with the user, and what happens during empathize, define, ideate, prototype, and test.

Slides 13 through 23 put those steps into practice. Teams receive a challenge card with a user need, generate several ideas, build with a limited materials bag, test the prototype, make one change, and share what they learned.

Choose the ending that fits your class. Slide 24 is an optional NASA/ClassVR extension; without headsets, project the linked video instead. Slide 25 is a longer exit ticket to use instead of the quick exit on slide 22.

Optional independent route

The Canvas Learn: Ready Set Design! item and student worksheet can support an absent student, a self-paced class period, or extra review. They are not the default lesson and do not replace the group build-and-test experience.

Video route: run the challenge without the deck

ASU published its own Ready, Set, Design! walkthrough (ASU Edson E & I Youth Entrepreneurship). Project it in place of slides 13 through 23 when you are short on time, covering for someone, or the deck will not open. Teach the five design-thinking steps first either way, from slides 1 through 12 or your own route.

At 1:41 the video states the materials rule on screen: one bag per group, and no glue, tape, or scissors. It also says one to two partners, while this guide plans groups of four. Set your own grouping and tell students to ignore that line.

Teacher copies

  • Facilitator guide: make a copy
  • Lucero complete lesson deck: download the PowerPoint or make a Google Slides copy. This is the default whole-group route. Slides 1 through 12 teach the design-thinking process with examples, and slides 13 through 23 guide the materials-bag challenge. Slide 24 is an optional NASA/ClassVR extension; slide 25 is an alternate longer exit ticket.
  • Student worksheet: make a copy
  • Checkpoint: make a copy

Five Chair Challenge: second round or flex route

The course map names Five Chair alongside Ready, Set, Design in Week 1. Both teach the same design cycle. Run Five Chair after the materials-bag challenge if students need a second practice round, or swap it in when a user-centred chair problem is a better fit. Do not require two full written packets unless your calendar has room.

  • Five Chair facilitator guide: make a copy
  • Five Chair presentation: make a copy
  • Five Chair student worksheet: make a copy
  • Five Chair checkpoint: make a copy

Five Chair asks partners to design for one specific user, build several chair prototypes with different materials, and revise after testing. Gather cardboard, paper, scissors, tape, clay or play-dough, and a small selection of pipe cleaners, straws, paper clips, toothpicks, or craft sticks.

Optional worksheet turn-in

The whole-group build does not require the worksheet. If you choose to use it, students open the copy link and upload the completed file to Canvas.

If you prefer Google Assignments, create a new External Tool assignment in your course, attach your copy, choose one copy per student, save, and test it in Student View.

A /copy link works only for people who can access the Google file. Test it with a student account before class. Google explains how file access and organisation rules affect shared files.

Teacher-led material bags

Plan groups of four. Each bag needs a small mix of fasteners, flat surfaces, and structural pieces. Include items such as pipe cleaners, rubber bands, paper clips, string, cardboard, paper, craft sticks, straws, and foil. The exact mix can vary. The constraint is part of the task.

  • Kit planner: Prototyping Bag Kit teacher template (PDF, 1 page). The three categories with a menu of items, blank boxes for your own counts, and one worked example. Print it, fill in what your closet actually has, and hand it to whoever assembles the bags.

Live flow

  1. Empathise: name the person in the challenge and what that person needs.
  2. Define: write one problem the group can act on.
  3. Ideate: sketch more than one possible response before choosing.
  4. Prototype: build a small model from the materials in the bag.
  5. Test: let another person try it, name one problem, and change the model.

What to listen for

  • Students name a person or user, not a vague audience.
  • The prototype responds to the written challenge.
  • The test produces a change. "They liked it" is not enough information to revise a design.

Language support

Keep the five verbs visible: empathise, define, ideate, prototype, test. Students may discuss and label in their stronger language before completing the English worksheet. Start with Our user needs ____ because ____. After the test, shift to We changed ____ because ____.

WEEK 1 · XELLO CHECK-IN · 5 POINTS

TEACHER ONLY · COMICS 1

Welcome to Smart Solutions + Comic Cover

Outcome: Students assemble the paper booklet they will use for all five Comics lessons and create a cover that uses title, image, color, size, and placement to give readers clear first clues about the hero.

Before class

  • Download the revised Lesson 1 slide deck. Image credits and teaching notes are in the speaker notes.
  • Make one sample folded comic from three sheets of paper. Number the inside pages 1 through 4.
  • Set out pencils, erasers, and coloring supplies. Decide where comics will be stored between classes.
  • Decide whether students will staple at their tables or bring folded booklets to a supervised stapling station.
  • The student Canvas page includes a student cover collage and the cover-layout guide. The deck uses the collage during analysis and the layout guide on the leave-up work slide.

One-period route

  1. 4 minutes: Superpower bellringer and a concrete Smart Solutions welcome.
  2. 10 minutes: Model stacking and aligning first, then folding and creasing, stapling, and the booklet check.
  3. 8 minutes: Analyze the Black Panther and Ms. Marvel covers using title, image, color, size, and placement as evidence.
  4. 4 minutes: Study the authentic student examples and preview the four cover requirements.
  5. 20 minutes: Students sketch three thumbnails, choose one, and build the cover. Leave the cover-outline work slide projected.
  6. 4 minutes: Partner quick read and exit sentence.

Check before students leave

Each cover needs a readable title, the hero's name, one central hero image, and colors or details that fit the hero. Students should be able to name one trait or idea and point to a visible design choice that communicates it. Drawing skill is not the target.

Support without lowering the thinking

  • Keep the three thumbnail frames visible before students commit to a final design.
  • Allow stick figures, traced shapes, labels, and collage.
  • Keep the trait word bank visible.
  • Use the stem: "My cover suggests my hero is ____ because I used ____."

Handoff to Lesson 2: The cover tells us how the hero looks from the outside. The biography explains why that hero makes particular choices.

metadata.title: Teacher Guide: Comics Lesson 1: Welcome and Comic Cover

items.title: Teacher Guide: Comics Lesson 1: Welcome and Comic Cover

resource.body:
COMICS · LESSON 1 OF 5

Welcome to Smart Solutions: Build Your Comic Cover

Build the book you will use all week, then design a cover that gives readers their first clues about your hero.

BIG QUESTION / GRAN PREGUNTA: How can a title and image tell us who a hero is before we read the story? / ¿Cómo pueden un título y una imagen decirnos quién es un héroe antes de leer la historia?
  • Time / Tiempo: one class period / un periodo de clase
  • You need / Necesitas: 3 sheets of paper, pencil, and coloring supplies / 3 hojas de papel, lápiz y materiales para colorear
  • Today you add / Hoy agregas: the comic cover / la portada del cómic
  • English
  • Español

What is Smart Solutions?

Smart Solutions is a class about making things that respond to real people and real problems. During the year, you will work with visual design, fabrication, code, circuits, artificial intelligence, and robotics. You do not need to know how to use all of those tools yet. That is the point of the class.

We begin on paper because the same folded book holds all five lessons. Each day adds one part of one short story: the cover, biography, gadget, logo, and final action.

One booklet. Five connected design challenges. Your drawing style can look different from everyone else's.

Learn: a cover gives the first clue

Before someone reads a comic, the cover gives the first clues about what is inside. Look at the title, image, color, size, and placement. What idea or trait do those choices suggest?

Words for today: cover · title · image · color · clue · communicate

Build your comic

  1. Stack 3 sheets of paper so the edges line up.
  2. Fold the stack in half. Press along the fold.
  3. Give the folded book to your teacher for stapling unless your teacher tells you to staple it yourself.
  4. Number the four inside work pages lightly in pencil: Page 1, Page 2, Page 3, Page 4.

Design the cover

Use this layout as a guide. Your design, lettering, colors, and hero should be your own.

Your cover needs:

  • a comic title;
  • your hero's name;
  • a drawing or collage that gives us a first look at the hero; and
  • two visual choices you can explain, such as color, size, lettering, pose, or placement.
If you get stuck: Write three words you want someone to think when they see your hero. Pick a title, color, and pose that fit those words. A clear stick figure is fine.

Before you put it away

  • Point to two choices on your cover.
  • Tell a partner what each choice communicates.
  • Put your name and class period somewhere your teacher can find them.

Exit sentence: "My cover suggests my hero is ____ because I used ____."

Word bank: adventurous · careful · funny · mysterious · powerful · hopeful · urgent · bold

¿Qué es Smart Solutions?

Smart Solutions es una clase donde creamos cosas que responden a personas y problemas reales. Durante el año trabajarás con diseño visual, fabricación, código, circuitos, inteligencia artificial y robótica. Todavía no tienes que saber usar todas esas herramientas. Para eso es la clase.

Comenzamos en papel porque el mismo libro doblado guarda las cinco lecciones. Cada día agregas una parte de una historia corta: la portada, la biografía, el gadget, el logo y la acción final.

Un libro. Cinco retos de diseño conectados. Tu estilo de dibujo puede ser diferente al de todos los demás.

Aprende: la portada da la primera pista

Antes de leer un cómic, la portada da las primeras pistas sobre lo que hay adentro. Observa el título, la imagen, el color, el tamaño y la posición. ¿Qué idea o rasgo sugieren esas decisiones?

Palabras de hoy: portada · título · imagen · color · pista · comunicar

Arma tu cómic

  1. Coloca 3 hojas de papel una encima de otra y alinea los bordes.
  2. Dobla las hojas por la mitad. Marca bien el doblez.
  3. Entrégale el libro doblado a tu docente para engraparlo, a menos que te diga que lo engrapes tú.
  4. Numera suavemente las cuatro páginas de trabajo: Página 1, Página 2, Página 3, Página 4.

Diseña la portada

Usa este diseño como guía. Tu dibujo, letras, colores y héroe deben ser tuyos.

Tu portada necesita:

  • un título para el cómic;
  • el nombre de tu héroe;
  • un dibujo o collage que nos dé la primera impresión del héroe; y
  • dos decisiones visuales que puedas explicar, como color, tamaño, letras, pose o posición.
Si te atoras: Escribe tres palabras que quieres que alguien piense al ver a tu héroe. Escoge un título, color y pose que combinen con esas palabras. Un monito de palitos claro funciona.

Antes de guardarlo

  • Señala dos decisiones en tu portada.
  • Explícale a un compañero qué comunica cada decisión.
  • Escribe tu nombre y periodo en un lugar donde tu docente pueda encontrarlos.

Oración de salida: "Mi portada sugiere que mi héroe es ____ porque usé ____."

Banco de palabras: aventurero · cuidadoso · chistoso · misterioso · poderoso · esperanzador · urgente · fuerte

TEACHER ONLY · COMICS 2

Biography, Motivation, and Choice

Outcome: Students build Page 1 so the hero's identity, abilities, facts, and goals give a reader enough evidence to predict one choice that hero would make.

Before class

  • Download the revised Lesson 2 slide deck. Image credits and teaching notes are included in the speaker notes.
  • Prepare one connected detail and one random detail from any familiar character. Students should hear why a fun fact, such as a favorite food, does not automatically explain a hero's choices.

Suggested one-period route

  1. Launch: Compare Superman and Icon. They have similar abilities but make different choices. Ask which life details could explain that difference.
  2. Teach: Build the chain: fact or experience → what matters → goal → likely choice. Keep power and motivation separate.
  3. Model: Use Jaime Reyes, then the completed VILBot biography page, to show how connected details support a prediction.
  4. Create: Leave the Page 1 work slide projected while students complete the biography page with words, labels, drawings, or a combination.
  5. Test: Partners predict one choice and point to the biography detail that supports it. Students revise one unclear connection before the exit ticket.

Check before students leave

Look for a readable identity, abilities, notes or facts, and goals. At least one fact should help explain why a goal matters. Ask: "What would this hero do if someone needed help, and what on the page makes you think that?"

Support without writing the hero for them

  • Offer the stems "My hero cares about ____ because ____" and "When ____, my hero usually ____."
  • Let students dictate to speech-to-text, then choose the words they want to keep.
  • Reduce decoration time before reducing the biography evidence.

Handoff to Lesson 3: The biography gives the hero a reason to act. The gadget gives the hero a designed way to respond to a need.

metadata.title: Teacher Guide: Comics Lesson 2: Biography and Motivation

items.title: Teacher Guide: Comics Lesson 2: Biography and Motivation

resource.body:
COMICS · LESSON 2 OF 5

Build Your Hero: Biography and Motivation

A list of powers tells us what a hero can do. Their motivation tells us what they will choose to do.

BIG QUESTION / GRAN PREGUNTA: Which details from a hero's life best predict what they will do next? / ¿Qué detalles de la vida de un héroe predicen mejor lo que hará después?
  • Time / Tiempo: one class period / un periodo de clase
  • You need / Necesitas: your comic and coloring supplies / tu cómic y materiales para colorear
  • Today you add / Hoy agregas: Page 1 / Página 1
  • English
  • Español

Learn: details shape decisions

Two heroes can have the same power and use it differently. One protects people because someone once protected them. Another avoids attention because using the power caused trouble before. Biography gives the power a direction.

Words for today: biography · motivation · goal · predict · evidence

Teacher model: Notice how labels make the stats, abilities, facts, and goals easy to find.

Your page can look different. Keep the required information easy to find.

Create Page 1

Open to Page 1. Include:

  • superhero name and secret identity;
  • a drawing of the hero;
  • two or three powers or abilities;
  • stats that fit the hero, such as strength, speed, creativity, or humor;
  • notes or facts that make the hero specific; and
  • one or more goals.
If you get stuck: Finish these two sentences first. "My hero cares about ____ because ____." "This means my hero would probably choose to ____." Build the rest of the page around that choice.

Partner prediction

  1. Show your partner Page 1.
  2. Your partner predicts one choice your hero would make during a problem.
  3. Your partner points to the biography detail that supports the prediction.
  4. If the prediction does not fit, add or revise one detail so the hero's motivation is clearer.

Exit sentence: "My hero is motivated by ____. We can see that when ____."

Word bank: protect · discover · repair · teach · defend · connect · prevent · guide · investigate · remember

Aprende: los detalles cambian las decisiones

Dos héroes pueden tener el mismo poder y usarlo de maneras diferentes. Uno protege a la gente porque alguien lo protegió antes. Otro evita llamar la atención porque su poder le causó problemas. La biografía le da dirección al poder.

Palabras de hoy: biografía · motivación · meta · predecir · evidencia

Modelo del docente: Fíjate cómo las etiquetas ayudan a encontrar las estadísticas, habilidades, datos y metas.

Tu página puede verse diferente. Haz que la información requerida sea fácil de encontrar.

Crea la Página 1

Abre tu cómic en la Página 1. Incluye:

  • el nombre del superhéroe y su identidad secreta;
  • un dibujo del héroe;
  • dos o tres poderes o habilidades;
  • estadísticas que correspondan con el héroe, como fuerza, velocidad, creatividad o humor;
  • notas o datos que hagan específico al héroe; y
  • una o más metas.
Si te atoras: Termina primero estas dos oraciones. "A mi héroe le importa ____ porque ____." "Por eso, mi héroe probablemente escogería ____." Construye el resto de la página alrededor de esa decisión.

Predicción con un compañero

  1. Muéstrale la Página 1 a tu compañero.
  2. Tu compañero predice una decisión que tomaría tu héroe durante un problema.
  3. Tu compañero señala el detalle de la biografía que apoya la predicción.
  4. Si la predicción no encaja, agrega o cambia un detalle para aclarar la motivación.

Oración de salida: "Mi héroe está motivado por ____. Podemos verlo cuando ____."

Banco de palabras: proteger · descubrir · reparar · enseñar · defender · conectar · prevenir · guiar · investigar · recordar

TEACHER ONLY · COMICS 3

Smart Gadget: Need, Input, Process, Output

Outcome: Students create Page 2 and explain a complete system: user need → input → process → output. The process is the rule the gadget follows.

Before class

  • Download the revised Lesson 3 slide deck. The exact image credits and teaching notes are in the speaker notes.
  • Preview the automatic hand dryer and motion-sensor light photographs. Students analyze those devices from their seats; there is no classroom technology walk.
  • Keep the Page 2 student exemplar visible when students begin work.

One-period route

  1. 5 minutes: Bellringer with the two real devices. Students name what each device notices and does.
  2. 8 minutes: Model input, rule, and output with the automatic hand dryer.
  3. 6 minutes: Partners trace the motion-sensor light system.
  4. 25 minutes: Students design and label Page 2.
  5. 5 minutes: A partner traces the chain using the drawing only.
  6. 1 minute: Exit sentence.

Check before students leave

The need belongs to a user. The input is information the gadget detects or receives. The process explains what the gadget does with that information, often through an if-then rule. The output is a response a person can observe.

Rubric focus: Gadget need, function, input, and output: 20 points.

Support and extension

  • Give four labeled boxes with arrows before asking for a full gadget drawing.
  • Let students point and explain orally while you or a partner adds labels.
  • Keep the word bank and sentence stems visible during work time.
  • Extension: add a second input or explain what happens when the sensor receives incorrect information.

Handoff to Lesson 4: The hero and gadget now have a clear purpose. The next lesson turns that purpose into a simple, recognizable logo message.

metadata.title: Teacher Guide: Comics Lesson 3: Hero Gadget Design

items.title: Teacher Guide: Comics Lesson 3: Hero Gadget Design

resource.body:
COMICS · LESSON 3 OF 5

Design a Smart Gadget: Need, Input, Process, Output

A gadget is not smart because it glows. It is smart when it receives information and does something useful with it.

BIG QUESTION / GRAN PREGUNTA: How can a gadget receive information and respond to a specific user need? / ¿Cómo puede un gadget recibir información y responder a una necesidad específica del usuario?
  • Time / Tiempo: one class period / un periodo de clase
  • You need / Necesitas: your comic, pencil, and coloring supplies / tu cómic, lápiz y materiales para colorear
  • Today you add / Hoy agregas: Page 2 / Página 2
  • English
  • Español

Learn: follow the information

A smart system has an input, a process, and an output. The process is the rule the gadget follows.

  • The input is the information or signal the gadget receives.
  • The process is what the gadget does with the input. It often follows an if-then rule.
  • The output is the action, sound, light, movement, or message the gadget produces.

Example: An automatic hand dryer detects hands nearby. If hands are detected, it turns on. Warm air is the output.

Words for today: user need · sensor · input · process · output

Student example: This page uses panels, labels, and arrows to show a gadget in action.

This older example does not label the full chain. Your Page 2 must label the user need, input, process, and output.

Choose the need before the gadget

Look back at Page 1. What problem matters to your hero? Choose one person or group affected by that problem. Your gadget should help that user do something they cannot do easily now.

Planning stem: "My user needs a way to ____ when ____."

Create Page 2

Include:

  • the gadget's name;
  • the user need or problem;
  • a labeled drawing;
  • at least one input;
  • a process, including an if-then rule when it fits; and
  • at least one output.
If you get stuck: Start with the signal. What could the gadget sense or receive: light, sound, movement, distance, temperature, a button press, or a message? Then decide what should happen next.

Trace the chain

Show your page to a partner. Your partner should be able to point through this chain:

user need -> input -> process -> output

Exit sentence: "My gadget receives ____, processes it by ____, and ____ so the user can ____."

Word bank: detects · measures · receives · compares · warns · displays · moves · opens · guides · sends

Aprende: sigue la información

Un sistema inteligente tiene una entrada, un proceso y una salida. El proceso es la regla que sigue el gadget.

  • La entrada es la información o señal que recibe el gadget.
  • El proceso es lo que el gadget hace con la entrada. Muchas veces sigue una regla si-entonces.
  • La salida es la acción, el sonido, la luz, el movimiento o el mensaje que produce el gadget.

Ejemplo: Un secador de manos automático detecta las manos cercanas. Si detecta manos, se enciende. El aire caliente es la salida.

Palabras de hoy: necesidad del usuario · sensor · entrada · proceso · salida

Ejemplo de estudiante: Esta página usa paneles, etiquetas y flechas para mostrar un gadget en acción.

Este ejemplo anterior no tiene etiquetas para toda la cadena. Tu Página 2 debe incluir la necesidad del usuario, la entrada, el proceso y la salida.

Escoge la necesidad antes del gadget

Regresa a la Página 1. ¿Qué problema le importa a tu héroe? Escoge una persona o grupo afectado por ese problema. Tu gadget debe ayudarle a hacer algo que ahora no puede hacer fácilmente.

Oración para planear: "Mi usuario necesita una manera de ____ cuando ____."

Crea la Página 2

Incluye:

  • el nombre del gadget;
  • la necesidad del usuario o el problema;
  • un dibujo con etiquetas;
  • por lo menos una entrada;
  • un proceso, incluyendo una regla si-entonces cuando corresponda; y
  • por lo menos una salida.
Si te atoras: Comienza con la señal. ¿Qué podría detectar o recibir el gadget: luz, sonido, movimiento, distancia, temperatura, un botón o un mensaje? Después decide qué debe pasar.

Sigue la cadena

Muéstrale la página a un compañero. Tu compañero debe poder señalar esta cadena:

necesidad del usuario -> entrada -> proceso -> salida

Oración de salida: "Mi gadget recibe ____, lo procesa al ____ y ____ para que el usuario pueda ____."

Banco de palabras: detecta · mide · recibe · compara · avisa · muestra · mueve · abre · guía · envía

TEACHER ONLY · COMICS 4

Hero Logo Design

Outcome: Students complete Page 3 with three thumbnail sketches, one final emblem, one to three purposeful colors, and short explanations of one symbol and one color choice.

Teaching focus: Keep students focused on the logo: What do its symbol and colors tell us about this hero? Students need three sketches, one final emblem, and short explanations. They do not need to write a separate brand-promise statement. If you teach the optional Animation unit, students will build on this work later.

Before class

  • Download the Hero Logo Design PowerPoint. Confirm the Page 3 teacher model appears on Slides 10 and 16. Image sources and reuse notes are recorded in the speaker notes.
  • Have student comics, pencils, erasers, and coloring supplies ready.
  • The Gabrielle Jordan video and Edpuzzle are optional enrichment. This lesson does not depend on either one.

Optional entrepreneurship video

Lesson 4 works without this video. If you want an entrepreneurship example, use the original Gabrielle Jordan Williams TEDx video.

For embedded questions or Live Mode, copy the reusable Edpuzzle to My Content. Then create a new Canvas assignment, choose External Tool, select Edpuzzle, choose the copied video, save, and test it in Student View. Edpuzzle does not support reusing, cloning, or importing a previous Canvas-linked class or assignment.

Use Edpuzzle's current Canvas setup steps. If you want to project the questions while students answer on their own devices, use Live Mode after you assign the copied lesson to your class.

One-period route

  1. 5 minutes: Bellringer. Students use the trait bank and evidence stem to read familiar logos.
  2. 10 minutes: Teach symbol + color = one quick message. Compare familiar hero emblems.
  3. 7 minutes: Model simple, readable, and meaningful. Show the authentic Page 3 exemplar.
  4. 20 to 25 minutes: Students sketch three ideas, run the one-inch and five-second tests, then complete the final logo and explanations.
  5. 5 minutes: Lightning share or exit ticket.

Leave this up during work time

Slide 16 is the independent-work screen. It keeps the task, success criteria, rubric focus, sentence stem, next step, and authentic exemplar visible without prescribing a timer, voice level, or movement routine.

What to look for

  • Simplicity: a viewer can quickly understand what the mark shows.
  • Versatility: the mark stays recognizable when it is small or large.
  • Relevance: the symbol and one to three meaningful colors connect to the hero's trait, purpose, power, gadget, or user need.

Do not grade drawing skill. Score whether students made and explained clear design decisions.

Language support

Keep the visible banks and stems available. Ask partners to name the message before the designer explains it: “I see _____ because the logo uses _____.” Students may discuss ideas in their stronger language before writing the short explanation.

metadata.title: Teacher Guide: Comics Lesson 4: Hero Logo Design

items.title: Teacher Guide: Comics Lesson 4: Hero Logo Design

resource.body:
COMICS · LESSON 4 OF 5

Design Your Hero Logo

Create a simple mark that tells readers something important about your hero at a glance.

BIG QUESTION / GRAN PREGUNTA: How can a simple symbol and color communicate an idea about a hero? / ¿Cómo pueden un símbolo simple y un color comunicar una idea sobre un héroe?
  • Time / Tiempo: one class period / un periodo de clase
  • You need / Necesitas: your comic, pencil, and coloring supplies / tu cómic, lápiz y materiales para colorear
  • Today you add / Hoy agregas: Page 3 / Página 3
  • English
  • Español

One mark, one quick message

A logo cannot tell your hero's whole story. It can give readers one strong clue. Your symbol and colors should communicate one trait, purpose, or idea connected to the hero you already created.

Words for today: logo · emblem · symbol · trait · audience

Teacher model: Study the V symbol and the written explanation that connects it to the hero.

This older model does not show the three required sketches. Sketch three ideas first. Use one to three purposeful colors in the final logo. A detailed background is not required.

Build Page 3

  1. Choose one idea or trait your logo should communicate.
  2. Sketch three small logo ideas.
  3. Test your strongest idea at a small size and with a partner.
  4. Draw one final logo using one to three purposeful colors.
  5. Explain one symbol choice and one color choice.
Trait bank: brave · clever · helpful · protective · creative · calm · fast · strong · curious · fair

Sentence stems:

  • My _____ represents _____ because _____.
  • I used _____ to make the hero feel _____.

Partner read

  1. Show the logo without explaining it.
  2. Your partner looks for five seconds and says: “I see _____ because the logo uses _____.”
  3. Keep or revise one design choice after listening.
Success check: The logo is easy to understand, recognizable when it is small or large, connected to the hero, and uses one to three meaningful colors. Drawing skill is not the goal. Clear design decisions are.

Un símbolo, un mensaje rápido

Un logo no puede contar toda la historia de tu héroe. Puede darles una pista fuerte a los lectores. Tu símbolo y tus colores deben comunicar un rasgo, propósito o idea conectado con el héroe que ya creaste.

Palabras de hoy: logo · emblema · símbolo · rasgo · audiencia

Modelo del docente: Estudia el símbolo V y la explicación escrita que lo conecta con el héroe.

Este modelo anterior no muestra los tres bocetos requeridos. Dibuja tres ideas primero. Usa de uno a tres colores escogidos con intención en el logo final. No necesitas un fondo detallado.

Construye la Página 3

  1. Escoge una idea o un rasgo que debe comunicar tu logo.
  2. Dibuja tres ideas pequeñas para el logo.
  3. Prueba tu mejor idea a un tamaño pequeño y con un compañero.
  4. Dibuja un logo final con uno a tres colores escogidos con intención.
  5. Explica una decisión sobre el símbolo y una sobre el color.
Banco de rasgos: valiente · inteligente · servicial · protector · creativo · tranquilo · rápido · fuerte · curioso · justo

Oraciones de apoyo:

  • Mi _____ representa _____ porque _____.
  • Usé _____ para que el héroe se sienta _____.

Prueba con un compañero

  1. Muestra el logo sin explicarlo.
  2. Tu compañero mira por cinco segundos y dice: “Veo _____ porque el logo usa _____.”
  3. Conserva o cambia una decisión de diseño después de escuchar.
Revisión de éxito: El logo es fácil de entender, se reconoce cuando es pequeño o grande, se conecta con el héroe y usa de uno a tres colores con significado. La meta no es dibujar perfectamente. La meta es tomar decisiones claras de diseño.

metadata.title: Lesson 4: Hero Logo Design (Create Your Superhero's Logo)

items.title: Lesson 4: Hero Logo Design (Create Your Superhero's Logo)

resource.body:
TEACHER ONLY · COMICS LESSON 5

Smart Solution in Action + Final Comic Submission

Lesson outcome: Students complete Page 4 as a readable sequence showing a challenge, the hero's choice, the gadget in action, and a visible result. They then submit the cover and Pages 1 through 4 as the 100-point unit assessment.

Projection deck: Open Smart Solutions Lesson 5: Smart Solution in Action. The Canvas assignment is the accessible student and absence route.

Before class

  • Open the final assignment and confirm the revised 100-point whole-comic rubric is attached.
  • Set out the comics, pencils, and coloring supplies. Students continue with the same hero, gadget, and visual identity from Pages 1 through 3.
  • Decide whether students will use one of the three provided sustainability prompts or choose another teacher-approved access, safety, communication, or community problem.
  • Choose a submission route: separate photos of the cover and four pages, or one slow, readable video when separate photos create an access barrier.
  • Test the assignment preview with a student account before class.

Teaching sequence

  1. Bellringer and vocabulary: Students study the three real problem images, name what they notice, and identify who or what is affected.
  2. Challenge and solution: Define a challenge as a problem or condition that affects a person, group, place, or resource. Define a solution as an idea or action that improves at least part of the situation.
  3. Sustainability choice: Introduce water, energy, and shared spaces as possible contexts for this lesson. Sustainability is not a required focus for the rest of the course.
  4. Teacher model: Read the VilBot example from first panel to last. Point to the challenge, hero's choice, gadget action, and visible result.
  5. Plan: Students write one short note for each of the four parts before drawing. Check the order and result before they add details.
  6. Build and partner test: The partner reads first while the creator stays quiet. If the reader cannot point to one of the four parts, the creator adds a visual, label, caption, arrow, or speech bubble.
  7. Submit: Students photograph or record the whole comic, open every preview, and submit.

Pacing choices

One-period route: Move from the challenge choices to the VilBot model, plan four panels, work, run a short partner check, and photograph at the end. Use this only when students already have complete Pages 1 through 3.

Two-period route: On Day 1, teach through planning and begin the page. On Day 2, reopen with the four-part trace, finish and partner-test the sequence, then complete the whole-comic submission.

What to look for while students work

  • The challenge affects someone or something specific.
  • The hero makes a choice that fits the motivation developed on Page 1.
  • The gadget action still uses the input, process or rule, and output established on Page 2.
  • The hero and gadget still carry the visual identity developed on Page 3.
  • The final panel is visibly different from the first. A paragraph should not be needed to explain what changed.

Language and access support

  • Keep the work-time slide projected. It includes the exact rubric focus, bilingual word bank, and complete English and Spanish sentence stems.
  • Let students plan with short notes, sketches, labels, arrows, or speech bubbles. Drawing skill and coloring are not scored.
  • For students who freeze at a blank page, start with the result panel and work backward: What caused this result? What did the hero notice? What challenge started the scene?
  • Allow oral rehearsal before writing and accept the final exit response orally when that preserves the same evidence.

Whole-comic rubric

  • Cover and visual identity: 10 points
  • Biography and motivation: 15 points
  • Gadget need, function, input, and output: 20 points
  • Logo communication: 20 points
  • Final smart-solution sequence: 25 points
  • Complete and readable submission: 10 points

Optional Animation handoff

The comic is complete after Lesson 5. If you choose the optional Animation unit, students carry forward the hero, one action from Page 4, and the visual identity they already built. Animation then runs as its own five-day to one-and-a-half-week design cycle. If you move directly to Graphic Design, nothing is missing from the comic unit.

Teacher source copies

  • Identifying Challenges in Your Communities facilitator guide
  • Identifying Challenges in Your Communities presentation
  • Mapping Sustainability facilitator guide
  • Mapping Sustainability presentation

metadata.title: Teacher Guide: Comics Lesson 5: Smart Solution in Action

items.title: Teacher Guide: Comics Lesson 5: Smart Solution in Action

resource.body:
COMICS · LESSON 5 OF 5

Smart Solution in Action: Create Your Final Comic Page

Show the challenge, your hero's choice, the gadget working, and what changes.

BIG QUESTION / GRAN PREGUNTA: How can readers tell that a solution actually changed the problem? / ¿Cómo pueden los lectores saber que una solución cambió el problema?
  • Time / Tiempo: one or two class periods / uno o dos periodos de clase
  • You need / Necesitas: your comic, pencil, and coloring supplies / tu cómic, lápiz y materiales para colorear
  • Turn in / Entrega: clear photos or one slow video showing the cover and Pages 1 through 4 / fotos claras o un video lento que muestre la portada y las Páginas 1 a 4
  • English
  • Español

What Page 4 needs to show

Your last comic page is a cause-and-effect sequence. A reader should be able to find all four parts without hearing your explanation:

  1. Challenge: Show what is happening and who or what is affected.
  2. Hero's choice: Show what your hero notices and decides to do.
  3. Gadget action: Show the input, process, and output in the scene.
  4. Visible result: Show what is different because of the action.

Words for today: challenge · affected · cause · effect · process · result

Teacher model: Read from the first panel to the last. Point to the challenge, hero's choice, gadget action, and visible result.

Your panel layout can look different. Keep the four parts in a clear reading order, and make the gadget's input, process, and output understandable in the scene.

Choose a challenge that fits

Choose a problem that gives your existing hero and Page 2 gadget a clear job. You may use:

  • De-Hydrator: she is draining the lake a desert town depends on;
  • Amper the Energy Drainer: he is pulling electricity from a community;
  • The Big Bad Litter Bug: a party is covering a shared park in trash;
  • a problem involving access, safety, communication, or community; or
  • another challenge approved by your teacher.
Test the fit: I choose ____ because my hero can ____ and my gadget can ____.

Plan before you draw

  1. Write one short note for each part: challenge, choice, action, result.
  2. Check Page 1. Does the choice fit what your hero cares about?
  3. Check Page 2. Can the gadget receive the needed input, follow a process or rule, and create the output shown?
  4. Check Page 3. Does the hero and gadget still look like the same visual identity?

challenge -> hero's choice -> gadget action -> visible result

Create and test Page 4

  1. Lay out panels in a reading order another person can follow.
  2. Draw the gadget changing the situation.
  3. Add short captions, labels, arrows, or speech bubbles where needed.
  4. Make the last panel visibly different from the first.
  5. Give the comic to a partner. Stay quiet while they point to the challenge, choice, action, and result.
  6. Revise one place that confused your reader.

Reader stem: I understand ____. I need more information about ____.

Creator stem: I will clarify ____ by ____.

Submit the whole comic

  1. Photograph the cover and Pages 1 through 4 in bright, even light. You may record one slow, readable video if separate photos create an access barrier.
  2. Make sure every page is included, the text is readable, and no fingers cover the work.
  3. Select Start Assignment, upload your files, and open each preview before submitting.

How the 100 points are scored

  • Cover and visual identity: 10 points
  • Biography and motivation: 15 points
  • Gadget need, function, input, and output: 20 points
  • Logo communication: 20 points
  • Final smart-solution sequence: 25 points
  • Complete and readable submission: 10 points

Drawing skill and coloring are not scored. Clear ideas, useful labels, and a sequence another person can follow are what count.

Exit sentence: My hero responds to ____ by ____. As a result, ____.

Word bank: detects · redirects · filters · alerts · protects · restores · changes · result

Lo que debe mostrar la Página 4

Tu última página es una secuencia de causa y efecto. Un lector debe poder encontrar las cuatro partes sin escuchar tu explicación:

  1. Reto: Muestra qué está pasando y quién o qué resulta afectado.
  2. Decisión del héroe: Muestra qué nota y qué decide hacer tu héroe.
  3. Acción del gadget: Muestra la entrada, el proceso y la salida en la escena.
  4. Resultado visible: Muestra qué es diferente por la acción.

Palabras de hoy: reto · afectado · causa · efecto · proceso · resultado

Modelo del docente: Lee desde el primer panel hasta el último. Señala el reto, la decisión del héroe, la acción del gadget y el resultado visible.

Tus paneles pueden tener otra organización. Mantén las cuatro partes en un orden claro y haz que la entrada, el proceso y la salida del gadget se entiendan en la escena.

Escoge un reto que encaje

Escoge un problema que les dé un trabajo claro a tu héroe y al gadget de la Página 2. Puedes usar:

  • De-Hydrator: está vaciando el lago que necesita un pueblo en el desierto;
  • Amper the Energy Drainer: está sacando la electricidad de una comunidad;
  • The Big Bad Litter Bug: una fiesta está cubriendo un parque compartido de basura;
  • un problema de acceso, seguridad, comunicación o comunidad; o
  • otro reto aprobado por tu docente.
Prueba si encaja: Escojo ____ porque mi héroe puede ____ y mi gadget puede ____.

Planea antes de dibujar

  1. Escribe una nota corta para cada parte: reto, decisión, acción y resultado.
  2. Revisa la Página 1. ¿La decisión encaja con lo que le importa a tu héroe?
  3. Revisa la Página 2. ¿Puede el gadget recibir la entrada necesaria, seguir un proceso o regla y crear la salida que muestras?
  4. Revisa la Página 3. ¿El héroe y el gadget todavía tienen la misma identidad visual?

reto -> decisión del héroe -> acción del gadget -> resultado visible

Crea y prueba la Página 4

  1. Organiza los paneles en un orden que otra persona pueda seguir.
  2. Dibuja el gadget cambiando la situación.
  3. Agrega leyendas cortas, etiquetas, flechas o globos de diálogo cuando sean necesarios.
  4. Haz que el último panel sea visiblemente diferente del primero.
  5. Dale el cómic a un compañero. Quédate en silencio mientras señala el reto, la decisión, la acción y el resultado.
  6. Revisa un lugar que confundió a tu lector.

Oración del lector: Entiendo ____. Necesito más información sobre ____.

Oración del creador: Voy a aclarar ____ al ____.

Entrega el cómic completo

  1. Fotografía la portada y las Páginas 1 a 4 con luz clara y pareja. Puedes grabar un video lento y legible si tomar fotos separadas crea una barrera de acceso.
  2. Confirma que cada página esté incluida, que el texto sea legible y que ningún dedo cubra el trabajo.
  3. Selecciona Start Assignment, sube tus archivos y abre cada vista previa antes de entregar.

Cómo se califican los 100 puntos

  • Portada e identidad visual: 10 puntos
  • Biografía y motivación: 15 puntos
  • Necesidad, función, entrada y salida del gadget: 20 puntos
  • Comunicación del logo: 20 puntos
  • Secuencia final de solución inteligente: 25 puntos
  • Entrega completa y legible: 10 puntos

No se califican la habilidad para dibujar ni el coloreado. Lo que cuenta son las ideas claras, las etiquetas útiles y una secuencia que otra persona pueda seguir.

Oración de salida: Mi héroe responde a ____ al ____. Como resultado, ____.

Banco de palabras: detecta · redirige · filtra · avisa · protege · restaura · cambia · resultado

Drawing skill is not scored. / La portada tiene un título, el nombre del héroe y dos decisiones visuales intencionales que el estudiante puede explicar. No se califica la habilidad para dibujar.

ratings.long_description: All required evidence is present, and the two visual choices clearly communicate the hero's identity. / Toda la evidencia está presente y las dos decisiones visuales comunican claramente la identidad del héroe.
The cover is mostly complete, but one visual choice or explanation needs clarification. / La portada está casi completa, pero una decisión visual o explicación necesita más claridad.
The cover has some required parts, but the visual identity is difficult to explain. / La portada tiene algunas partes requeridas, pero es difícil explicar la identidad visual.
The cover is missing or does not contain enough evidence to score. / Falta la portada o no contiene suficiente evidencia para calificar.

rubric.long_description: Page 1 connects the hero's identity, abilities, motivation, goal, and challenge. / La Página 1 conecta la identidad, habilidades, motivación, meta y reto del héroe.

ratings.long_description: All five parts are present, and biography details help explain a choice the hero would make. / Las cinco partes están presentes y los detalles de la biografía ayudan a explicar una decisión del héroe.
Most parts are present, but one connection between motivation, goal, challenge, or choice needs clarification. / La mayoría de las partes están presentes, pero una conexión necesita más claridad.
Several biography details are present, but they do not yet explain the hero's choices. / Hay varios detalles, pero todavía no explican las decisiones del héroe.

rubric.description: Gadget: Need, Function, Input, Output / Gadget: necesidad, función, entrada y salida
rubric.long_description: Page 2 shows a user need, the gadget's function, at least one input, and at least one output in a workable chain. / La Página 2 muestra una necesidad del usuario, la función del gadget, por lo menos una entrada y una salida en una cadena que funciona.

ratings.long_description: The need, function, input, and output are all clear and connect to each other. / La necesidad, función, entrada y salida son claras y se conectan entre sí.
All parts appear, but one link in the chain needs clarification. / Todas las partes aparecen, pero una conexión necesita más claridad.
The gadget is shown, but two or more parts of the need-input-output chain are missing or unclear. / Se muestra el gadget, pero faltan o no están claras dos o más partes de la cadena.
Page 2 is missing or does not contain enough evidence to score. / Falta la Página 2 o no contiene suficiente evidencia para calificar.

rubric.long_description: Page 3 has a finished logo and explains how at least one symbol or color communicates one clear idea or trait about the hero. / La Página 3 tiene un logo terminado y explica cómo por lo menos un símbolo o color comunica una idea o característica clara del héroe.

ratings.long_description: The logo is simple, readable at different sizes, and meaningful. The explanation clearly connects a symbol or color to the hero. / El logo es sencillo, legible en diferentes tamaños y significativo. La explicación conecta claramente un símbolo o color con el héroe.

The logo and explanation are present, but one visual connection or design choice needs clarification. / El logo y la explicación están presentes, pero una conexión visual o decisión de diseño necesita más claridad.
The logo is difficult to read, is incomplete, or does not yet communicate a clear idea or trait. / El logo es difícil de leer, está incompleto o todavía no comunica una idea o característica clara.
Page 3 is missing or does not contain enough evidence to score. / Falta la Página 3 o no contiene suficiente evidencia para calificar.

rubric.description: Final Smart-Solution Sequence / Secuencia final de solución inteligente
rubric.long_description: Page 4 shows a challenge, who or what is affected, the hero's choice, the gadget action, and a visible result. The action fits the hero and gadget developed on Pages 1 through 3. / La Página 4 muestra un reto, quién o qué resulta afectado, la decisión del héroe, la acción del gadget y un resultado visible. La acción encaja con el héroe y el gadget desarrollados en las Páginas 1 a 3.

ratings.long_description: The sequence is easy to follow, the gadget system makes sense, and the final panel clearly shows what changed. / La secuencia es fácil de seguir, el sistema del gadget tiene sentido y el último panel muestra claramente qué cambió.

The sequence is mostly clear, but one part of the challenge, choice, action, or result needs clarification. / La secuencia está casi clara, pero una parte del reto, decisión, acción o resultado necesita más claridad.

The page shows a problem and action, but two or more parts are missing, difficult to follow, or disconnected from the earlier pages. / La página muestra un problema y una acción, pero faltan dos o más partes, son difíciles de seguir o no se conectan con las páginas anteriores.
Page 4 is missing or does not contain enough evidence to score. / Falta la Página 4 o no contiene suficiente evidencia para calificar.

rubric.description: Complete and Readable Submission / Entrega completa y legible
rubric.long_description: The cover and Pages 1-4 are complete enough to read, and the uploaded photos or video show every page. Drawing skill and coloring are not scored. / La portada y las Páginas 1-4 están suficientemente completas y legibles, y las fotos o el video muestran cada página. No se califican la habilidad para dibujar ni el coloreado.

ratings.long_description: Every page is visible, readable, and included in the submission. / Cada página está visible, legible e incluida en la entrega.
Every page is included, but one page or image is difficult to read. / Cada página está incluida, pero una página o imagen es difícil de leer.
One or more pages are missing, unfinished, or difficult to see. / Falta una o más páginas, no están terminadas o son difíciles de ver.
No usable comic submission is available to score. / No hay una entrega del cómic que se pueda calificar.
