resource.body:
OPTIONAL/FLEX · XELLO PORTFOLIO

Start Your Portfolio

If your teacher assigns this page, create the sections you will use all year, then add the Xello results and comic you already finished.

  • English
  • Español
Optional/flex pacing: Your teacher may give you up to two class periods, assign this in smaller pieces during flex time, or save it for later.

1. Open Xello and follow the setup video

Open ClassLink, select Xello, and keep Xello open in another tab while you watch.

2. Create the nine sections

  1. About Me
  2. Graphic Design
  3. 3D Modelling + Branching Stories
  4. Circuits, Code + Game Design
  5. AI + Machine Learning
  6. Robotics
  7. AR/VR + Capstone
  8. My Career Path
  9. CTSO, if you participate in TSA or another organisation

Most sections will be empty today. You are building the folders before the work arrives.

3. Add what you already have

  • Add your Matchmaker, Personality Style, and Learning Style results to About Me.
  • Add clear photos of your completed superhero comic to Graphic Design.
  • Give the comic a short title and one sentence explaining what the project shows.

Word bank: project · design choice · process · skill · result · revise

Description stem: This project shows how I used ____ to ____.

4. Check the public view

Open your portfolio's public link. Confirm that the title, comic images, and description appear in the right section. Use this portfolio example only to check the structure; your words and projects should be your own.

Stop when: all nine section titles exist, About Me has the three results, and Graphic Design has the comic plus its description.
Horario opcional/flexible: Tu maestro puede darte hasta dos periodos de clase, asignar este trabajo en partes durante tiempo flexible o guardarlo para más adelante.

1. Abre Xello y sigue el video de configuración

Abre ClassLink, selecciona Xello y deja Xello abierto en otra pestaña mientras miras el video.

2. Crea las nueve secciones

  1. Sobre Mí
  2. Diseño Gráfico
  3. Modelado 3D + Historias Ramificadas
  4. Circuitos, Código + Diseño de Videojuegos
  5. IA + Aprendizaje Automático
  6. Robótica
  7. RA/RV + Proyecto Final
  8. Mi Camino Profesional
  9. CTSO, si participas en TSA u otra organización

La mayoría de las secciones estarán vacías hoy. Estás creando las carpetas antes de que llegue el trabajo.

3. Agrega lo que ya tienes

  • Agrega tus resultados de Matchmaker, Personality Style y Learning Style a Sobre Mí.
  • Agrega fotos claras de tu cómic de superhéroe terminado a Diseño Gráfico.
  • Escribe un título corto y una oración que explique qué muestra el proyecto.

Banco de palabras: proyecto · decisión de diseño · proceso · habilidad · resultado · revisar

Oración para la descripción: Este proyecto muestra cómo usé ____ para ____.

4. Revisa la vista pública

Abre el enlace público de tu portafolio. Confirma que el título, las imágenes del cómic y la descripción aparezcan en la sección correcta. Usa este ejemplo de portafolio solamente para revisar la estructura; las palabras y los proyectos deben ser tuyos.

Detente cuando: existan los nueve títulos, Sobre Mí tenga los tres resultados y Diseño Gráfico tenga el cómic con su descripción.

Animation Unit | Facilitator Guide

Teacher option: Use this as a complete five-day unit after Superhero Comics, add one or two flex days, or skip it. The comic is already complete, and Graphic Design does not depend on Animation.

What students learn

Students take one moment from a finished comic and rebuild it with motion. They learn how key poses, duplicated frames, frame holds, in-betweens, layers, timing, and loops change what an audience can understand. The final animation needs to show what people can count on the hero to do through a visible action.

What students make

  • a promise-in-action statement and five-part micro plot;
  • a six-panel storyboard, or an approved four-panel support storyboard;
  • a 1 to 2 second Piskel practice loop;
  • a first pass and work-in-progress checkpoint; and
  • a final animated GIF, saved source file, and short reflection.

Production targets

Standard route: 10 seconds at 12 fps, about 120 displayed frames. Students use duplicated frames and frame holds; they do not draw 120 different pictures.

Support route: 5 to 8 seconds at 8 to 12 fps, a four-panel storyboard, and one clear motion with frame holds. Students still communicate the promise, test the work, revise one choice, save the source, and submit a working GIF. The support route uses the same rubric.

Before Day 1

  • Open Piskel for Kids on the same Chromebook model students use. Confirm that the district filter allows the editor and downloads.
  • Choose a district-approved storage location for editable .piskel files.
  • Make sure students can open the visual Plot Diagram copy.
  • Choose the default YouTube tutorial or set up the optional Edpuzzle route below.
  • Preview the final rubric and decide which students need the approved support route.

Five-day route

  1. Day 1, Adapt: Reopen the hero's promise, choose one visible action, and complete the micro plot.
  2. Day 2, Plan and practice: Storyboard the motion, learn the Piskel controls, create a short practice loop, and save the editable source.
  3. Day 3, Prototype: Build the starting pose, main action, result, and first complete pass.
  4. Day 4, Refine: Adjust timing, add holds or in-betweens, test the work in progress, and make one specific revision.
  5. Day 5, Finish: Test without explaining, make the last revision, export the GIF, verify playback, submit, and reflect.

Whole-group deck map

  • Day 1: slides 1 to 14. Leave slide 14 up during Plot Diagram work.
  • Day 2: slides 15 to 30. Leave slide 28 up for practice work or slide 30 up for the Practice Wall.
  • Day 3: slides 31 to 39. Leave slides 38 and 39 up for production and the save routine.
  • Day 4: slides 40 to 45. Leave slide 44 up for partner feedback and slide 45 up for the WIP checkpoint. The six-slide Day 4 loop can rotate during work time; pause it on loop slide 4 for feedback and loop slide 5 for the checkpoint.
  • Day 5: slides 46 to 56. Leave slides 49 and 50 up during the gallery walk or slide 54 up for submission.

Plot Diagram setup

Default: Students open the Drawing copy link, complete their own copy, download it as a PDF, and upload the PDF to Canvas. This route continues to work after a course copy and does not depend on a roster connection.

Optional Google Assignments route: Make a teacher-owned copy of the Drawing. In the receiving Canvas course, link your school Google account, attach the Drawing, and choose the option that gives every student a copy. Test the student turn-in and return flow before publishing the assignment. Google's current setup instructions explain the course-linking step.

Piskel tutorial options

Default: The student page embeds the original Piskel tutorial. Students pause to try each control, then show what they learned in the Practice Wall.

Optional individual Edpuzzle: Open the reusable Piskel Edpuzzle and copy it to My Content. In Canvas, edit Day 2: Learn Piskel | Watch and Try, choose External Tool, select Edpuzzle, and attach the copied lesson. Save the assignment while it is still unpublished, then test the launch in Student View. The default YouTube version stays on the student page unless you intentionally replace it with this option.

Optional Live Mode: Assign the copied Edpuzzle to the class, open its assignment screen, and select Live Mode. Wait for every student to join before selecting Start; students cannot join after the session begins. Edpuzzle's Live Mode guide has the current limits and steps.

Edpuzzle states that previous Canvas classes and assignments cannot be reused, cloned, or imported as working course connections. Follow Edpuzzle's Canvas setup guide when you choose this route.

Portable WIP checkpoint

Default: students show the exported WIP to a partner or teacher, name the action the viewer saw, record one next step, and save the updated source file. No outside account or personal board is required.

Teacher option: if you want an online WIP board, create one in a district-approved tool, add your own link, and test student posting before you publish the module.

Source-file routine

Piskel keeps periodic recovery sessions in the browser, but that recovery stays with the browser and device. At the end of Days 2, 3, and 4, students download the editable .piskel file and move it to district-approved storage. They save the source again before the final export on Day 5. The GIF is the viewing copy; students cannot use it to continue editing the project.

What to watch while students work

  • A long animation with no visible action is not stronger than a short, readable one. Move students to the support route before they fall behind.
  • Students often change too much between frames. Model one small change, preview it, then decide whether another in-between is needed.
  • When motion looks too fast, duplicate frames at the pose the audience needs time to read.
  • Ask students to play the animation without explaining it. The viewer's first description is the clearest check on whether the promise can be seen.
  • Do not wait until Day 5 to check source files. A working GIF does not replace an editable project.

Assessment

The Promise, Plot Diagram, Storyboard, tutorial, and Practice Wall are formative checks and do not change the final grade. The final animation is one 100-point Major grade:

  • Promise communicated through action: 25
  • Motion, timing, and ending control: 25
  • Visual clarity and connection to the hero: 20
  • Planning, feedback, and revision: 20
  • File management, export, and reflection: 10

Teacher slide decks

Full five-day lesson deck

Download the 56-slide PowerPoint. It follows the complete sequence from adapting the comic through exporting and reflecting. Speaker notes include teacher moves and source credits. The Canvas student pages remain the accessible route for students who need to work independently or catch up after an absence.

Day 4 projection loop

Download the six-slide Day 4 loop. Open it in PowerPoint Slide Show mode during work time. It is configured to advance every 18 seconds and repeat. Use the Slide Show controls to pause or resume automatic timings; use the arrow keys to move manually.

Before publishing the module

  1. Keep the module itself unpublished until you decide to teach it.
  2. Test Piskel, the Plot Diagram copy link, tutorial playback, GIF discussion posts, final GIF upload, and submission comments in Student View.
  3. If you choose Google Assignments or Edpuzzle, reconnect and test that course-specific integration before students see it.
  4. Confirm that every student-facing item you plan to use is published. Teacher guides remain unpublished.

Superhero Micro-Animation Hub

Your mission: turn one moment from your finished comic into a 10-second looping pixel GIF in Piskel. Keep the same hero and problem. Show what people can count on your hero to do through one visible action. Design flow: Define → Ideate → Prototype → Test & Share.

  • 🧭 Overview
  • 🛡️ Define
  • 🧠 Ideate
  • 🎞️ Learn Piskel
  • 🎬 Prototype
  • 🗣️ Test & Share
  • 📚 Resources

Week at a Glance

Day 1
Define: Reopen the comic promise, choose one visible action, and finish the Plot Diagram.
Objective Keep the same hero and problem. Make no more than one clarity change.
Day 2
Plan + Practice: Finish 6 storyboard panels, or an approved 4-panel route, watch the tutorial, and post the practice loop.
Objective Plan key poses and learn the controls before building the final scene.
Day 3
Prototype: Build the first complete pass across the whole scene and save the editable source.
Objective Use key poses, duplicated frames, layers, onion skin, and holds to make the action readable.
Day 4
Test: Finish a WIP, get feedback, make one specific revision, and save again.
Objective Use feedback to improve timing or clarity.
Day 5
Share: Test the final animation, export the GIF, submit it, and complete both reflections.
Objective Deliver a working animation and explain one revision.
Progress Tracker
✅ Comic promise reopened 📝 Plot diagram submitted 🎞️ Storyboard submitted 🎓 Tutorial watched + tools tried 🔁 50% WIP checked 🏁 Final GIF submitted

Define • Comic Promise + Plot Diagram

Bring your comic forward. Reopen the promise you already made. Keep the same hero and the same problem. You may make one clarity change. Then name the action the audience will actually see.
Sentence stem: People can count on my hero to _____ when _____.
BAM!
  1. Plot Diagram: Exposition, Rising Action, Climax, Falling Action, Resolution for one tight moment.
  2. Constraints: 10 seconds • 12 fps • about 120 displayed frames • one shot or two simple cuts. Duplicate poses and hold frames; do not draw 120 different pictures.
  3. Deliverables: Reopen your comic promise, name one visible action, and upload your Plot Diagram.
🟢 Reopen Promise + Choose the Action

Ideate • Plot → Storyboard

Step 1: Finalize Plot Diagram

  • Pick a before → choice → after moment that proves your promise.
  • Note timing beats where the loop returns to frame 1.
⬆️ Submit Plot Diagram
WHOOSH!

Step 2: Storyboard (6 panels or an approved 4-panel route)

  • Include motion arrows, timing notes, layer plan, and a loop idea.
  • Keep drawings simple. Notes matter more than perfect art.
⬆️ Submit Storyboard

Learn Piskel

  1. Default: Watch the embedded YouTube tutorial, pause it, and try each tool in Piskel.
  2. Teacher option: Your teacher may connect the Edpuzzle version for embedded questions or Live Mode.
  3. Practice: Draw 3 to 5 unique poses. Duplicate or hold them to reach 12 to 24 displayed frames, post the 1 to 2 second loop, and leave two specific peer replies.
🎓 Piskel Tutorial • Watch and Try ▶️ Tips Playlist 🟢 Practice Wall
💡 Power-Up Tips: Hotkeys & Loop Tricks
  • Hotkeys: Ctrl/⌘+Z undo • Ctrl/⌘+D duplicate • hold Shift to select.
  • Onion skin: keep on while roughing; toggle off to check stutter.
  • Loop hack: animate to the apex, then duplicate frames in reverse.
  • Specs: 128×128 or 192×192 • 12 fps • Name: Lastname-Firstname-HeroName-Piskel.

Prototype • Animate your scene

Support
  • 5 to 8 seconds at 8 to 12 fps
  • One clear action with a visible result
  • The same feedback, file, and reflection expectations
Standard
  • 10 seconds at 12 fps
  • A recognizable connection to the same hero
  • One clear action, visible result, and intentional timing
Extension
  • Keep the duration target your teacher approved
  • Add one advanced technique only after the action reads clearly
  • Polish timing, effects, or the loop instead of adding more story
🔁 Days 3 and 4 • Build + Revise 📤 Export Guide
Example
Checklist
  • Separate layers for bg / character
  • Onion skin on for smooth motion
  • Loop tested at 12 fps
  • The action shows what people can count on the hero to do
Milestones
  • Rough pass complete
  • In-betweens added
  • Loop closes cleanly
Troubleshoot
  • Stutter? Duplicate frames evenly
  • Smear frames for fast moves
  • Reduce colors for clarity
Tip: If a video won’t load in Canvas, open on YouTube.

Test & Share • Gallery Walk

  1. Open the final GIF and let it loop. Keep device sound off unless your teacher says the animation uses audio.
  2. Visit two classmates. Leave one specific reply for each:
    • I like… something specific that works
    • I wonder… a curious question or suggestion
  3. Revise timing or frames, then export your final GIF.
Reminder: Kind • Specific • Helpful.
⬆️ Submit Final GIF

Resources & Help

  • Save the editable source: Piskel does not autosave to the cloud. Download the .piskel file before closing the tab or changing devices, then move it to the storage location your teacher gives you.
  • Keyboard tips: Ctrl/⌘+Z undo • Ctrl/⌘+D duplicate • Onion skin for in-betweens.
  • Export: File → Export → GIF • 12 fps • check repeat.
  • Hero Promise Idea Bank: Protect • Include • Repair • Encourage • Inform • Clean • Empower.
⚡ Open Piskel 🟢 Practice Wall 🔁 Days 3 and 4 🏁 Submit Final GIF 📚 Resources ⬆ Back to Top
Specs: 128×128 or 192×192 • 12 fps • Name files Lastname-Firstname-HeroName-Piskel

Tip: If a link doesn’t open inside Canvas, right-click → Open in new tab.

🔦 DEFINE PHASE

Bring Your Comic Promise Forward

Your task: reopen the promise from your comic and choose one action the audience can see. Keep the same hero and the same problem. You may make one clarity change, but you are not starting over.

⚡ Goal: reuse your comic 🧭 Clear purpose 🎯 Audience ready
✍️

Reopen the Promise + Make It Visible

Copy the promise from your comic. Use the stem only if one clarity change will make it easier to understand:

People can count on [hero] to _____ when _____.

🛡️
Example 1

“People can count on Signal to guide lost people when phones stop working.”

💡
Example 2

“People can count on Harbor to warn neighbors before floodwater reaches the street.”

Promise refresher: it tells the audience what they can count on your hero to do. The animation will show one moment when the hero follows through. Word bank: protect • guide • repair • warn • connect • rescue
In Canvas, enter the promise from your comic and the visible action:
Promise: People can count on _____ to _____ when _____.
Visible action: The audience will see this when _____.
📣

Exit Check: Connect Promise to Action

Submit the promise and visible action before you start the Plot Diagram.

CHECKLIST
  • ✅ The promise from your comic
  • ✅ One visible action that proves it
  • ✅ Your name and your hero’s name
Check: same hero, same problem, and no more than one clarity change.

The audience will see the promise when _____.

🏅 Hero Badge Unlocked: Story Purpose 🧩 Back to Hub
If a link won’t open inside Canvas, right-click → open in new tab.

Plot Diagram

Day 1: Complete the visual plot diagram

Open the visual Plot Diagram. Select Make a copy, rename it with your name, and fill in the five sections. Keep the visual diagram; do not replace it with a paragraph in Canvas.

  1. Exposition: Show the setting and what looks normal at first.
  2. Rising action: Show the problem that forces the hero to make a choice.
  3. Climax: Show the single visible action that proves the promise.
  4. Falling action: Show what changes immediately after the action.
  5. Resolution: Show how the audience knows the action mattered. If you plan a loop, note how the ending can return to the opening.

Before you submit

  • Every section of the visual diagram is complete.
  • The scene has one setting and one main problem.
  • The climax is an action the audience can see.
  • The scene fits the standard target or your teacher-approved support target.

Turn it in: In the Drawing, select File > Download > PDF Document. Upload that PDF here. If your teacher connected Google Assignments, use its Turn in button instead.

Sentence stems: We first see... The problem begins when... My hero chooses to... Right after... In the end...

Word bank: exposition · rising action · climax · falling action · resolution · setting · choice · result · loop

Storyboard Your Micro-Animation

Create a 6-panel storyboard (or a teacher-approved 4-panel storyboard) that shows your hero’s promise through action. Keep it simple and clear. Upload a photo of your storyboard at the end.

DEFINE IDEATE · we are here PROTOTYPE TEST & SHARE

What Your Storyboard Should Show

  • 6 panels that match your plot diagram, or 4 panels if your teacher approved that route.
  • Clear beginning, middle, climax, and resolution.
  • Simple drawings with short captions.
  • The hero's promise shown through one visible action and result.
Planning example: simple drawings + short captions make motion easier to animate. Use the current 6-panel route or your approved 4-panel route.

⏱️ Work Time: Plan Before You Animate

  • Big, readable shapes; consistent character.
  • Short captions only when needed.
  • Plan a clean loop (ending echoes the start).
Sentence stems: First, _____. Then, _____. The action shows _____ because _____.
Word bank: pose • frame • motion • timing • layer • loop

🚀 Exit Check: Upload Storyboard Photo

  1. Return to this Canvas assignment.
  2. Take a clear photo of your sheet with name + hero visible.
  3. Submit through the camera option.
🛡️ Hero Badge: Story Purpose Back to Hub If a link won’t open inside Canvas, right-click → open in new tab.

Learn Piskel

Day 2: Watch and try the tools

Watch the tutorial before the Practice Wall. Keep Piskel open in another tab so you can pause the video and try each tool. If your teacher connected Edpuzzle, follow the Edpuzzle directions instead.

Open the tutorial in a new tab if the embedded player does not load.

  1. Play the full tutorial. Pause when you need time to try a tool.
  2. Find the canvas, pen, eraser, frame list, duplicate-frame control, onion skin, preview, and fps control.
  3. Replay a section or turn on captions when you need to see a step again.
  4. No separate upload is required here. Your practice loop is the tool check.

Tool check: I can add a frame, duplicate a frame, preview the animation, change fps, and find the save/export controls.

Next: Use those controls to make the 1 to 2 second Practice Wall loop, then save the editable .piskel source before leaving class.

Word bank: canvas · frame · duplicate · onion skin · preview · fps · import · export

PROTOTYPE PHASE
Practice check • redo allowed

Practice GIF: Post in the Discussion

Build one small, readable motion in Piskel. Save the editable source, export a GIF, and post it below.

✏️

Quick Steps

  1. Draw 3 to 5 unique poses for one small motion.
  2. Duplicate or hold poses until the loop has 12 to 24 displayed frames at 12 fps.
  3. Preview the loop. Fix one jump, pause, or unclear pose.
  4. Download Last-First-Practice.piskel and move it to your class storage location.
  5. Export a repeating GIF, post it below, and check that it plays.
Exit ticket: Leave two peer replies using these stems:
  • I like how __________ because __________.
  • I wonder if you could __________ to __________.
Example: I noticed the glow becomes brighter one step at a time. I wonder if two duplicated frames at the brightest point would make it easier to see.
Word bank: frame • pose • duplicate • onion skin • loop • timing • source file
⬇️

Post your GIF in the discussion below

No special filename needed.

⚙️ Export at 12 FPS (Loop ON)
🎥

Try this 3-frame arm-raise demo

Example
  • Use onion skin to line up poses.
  • Duplicate frames to hold a pose long enough to read.
  • Keep one motion simple, readable, and high contrast.
✅ Goal: one smooth motion
💬 Leave 2 peer comments
🕒 Done this period

Days 3 and 4: Animate the Promise

Day 3: Build across the whole scene

  1. Make the key poses first.
  2. Duplicate frames to create holds.
  3. Add only the in-betweens needed to read the action.
  4. Preview at full speed after each section.
  5. Download the editable .piskel source before leaving.

Day 4: Test, revise, and save again

  1. Show the WIP to a partner or teacher.
  2. Ask what action they saw and what the result was.
  3. Make one specific revision to timing, motion, or visual clarity.
  4. Export a WIP GIF for the checkpoint.
  5. Download the updated editable source.

Targets

Standard: 10 seconds at 12 fps, one clear action with a visible result, intentional timing, and a clean loop or complete ending.

Approved support: 5 to 8 seconds at 8 to 12 fps, one clear motion, and a clean loop or complete ending.

Feedback language

I saw the hero _____, and the result was _____.

The clearest moment was _____ because _____.

Try changing _____ so the audience can see _____.

Word bank: key pose · frame hold · in-between · timing · layer · loop · feedback · revise · source file · WIP

Ready for Day 5?

  • The full action can be watched from beginning to end.
  • The audience can tell what people can count on the hero to do.
  • The loop or ending works.
  • You can name the revision you made after feedback.
  • The latest editable source is stored where your teacher told you.
Open Piskel for Kids WIP check: show a partner or teacher Back to Hub Day 5 Export + Submit

Final Export and Turn-In

Day 5: Test, revise, and submit

1. Test without explaining

Play the GIF for another person. Ask what the hero is doing, what people can count on the hero to do, and where the motion is too fast, too slow, or hard to follow.

2. Make one specific revision

Use the test result. Change one part of the timing, frame holds, in-betweens, silhouette, color, or loop transition. Do not restart the project today.

3. Save both files

  • Download Lastname-Firstname-HeroName-Piskel.piskel and move it to your class storage location.
  • Export Lastname-Firstname-HeroName-Piskel.gif.
  • Open the downloaded GIF. Check that it plays and the ending looks complete or returns cleanly to the beginning.

4. Upload and reflect

  1. Select Start Assignment, upload the final GIF, and check that the preview opens.
  2. Add both reflections in one submission comment:
    The choice that communicates my hero's promise best is _____ because _____.
    After feedback, I changed _____. This made the animation _____.
  3. Submit and confirm that Canvas shows the file.
Final check: The action shows what people can count on the hero to do • timing is intentional • the loop closes cleanly or the ending looks complete • the source file is saved • the GIF name is correct • both reflections are included.
Word bank: frame hold • key pose • in-between • timing • silhouette • feedback • revise • source file • export

rubric.long_description: The audience can understand what people can count on the hero to do by watching the visible action.

ratings.long_description: The promise is immediately clear through a specific action and result without explanatory text.
The action and result communicate the hero's promise clearly.
The promise is present, but the action or result needs explanation to be understood.
The animation does not yet show a clear promise through action.

rubric.long_description: Frames, duplicated frames, holds, and transitions create readable motion and a clean loop or deliberate completed ending.

ratings.long_description: Timing choices make the motion easy to read, and the loop or ending is deliberate and controlled.
Motion is readable, timing is intentional, and the loop or ending works.
Some motion is readable, but timing or the ending makes part of the action unclear.
The animation is incomplete or the motion cannot yet be followed.

rubric.description: Visual clarity and connection to the hero
rubric.long_description: The character, setting, color, emblem, or another visual choice connects the animation to the planned hero and keeps the action readable.

ratings.long_description: Purposeful visual choices make the hero recognizable and keep every stage of the action clear.
The hero is recognizable and the main action is visually clear.
The hero or action is partly recognizable, but important visual information is hard to read.
The visual connection to the hero or the main action is missing or unreadable.

rubric.long_description: The plot and storyboard connect to the final scene, and the student uses feedback to make one specific revision.

ratings.long_description: The final animation follows the plan, and feedback leads to a specific revision that improves communication or timing.
The animation follows the plan and includes a specific revision made after feedback.
Planning or feedback is present, but its connection to the final animation is incomplete.
Planning evidence, feedback, or a specific revision is missing.

rubric.long_description: The source is saved, the GIF opens after upload, the filename is correct, and both reflection answers name a motion or timing choice and a revision.

ratings.long_description: All files work and follow the naming routine, and both reflections use specific evidence from the animation.
The GIF works, the source and filename are handled correctly, and both reflections are complete.
The submission opens, but one file-management or reflection requirement is incomplete.
The GIF does not open or multiple file-management and reflection requirements are missing.

BEFORE YOU TEACH | TEST THE PORTABLE ROUTES

Google copies are convenient; Canvas files are the backup

  • Lesson 2 worksheet: make a Google copy or use the Word download on the student page.
  • Emoji Define form: make a Google copy or use the Word download on the student page.
  • Default Canvas turn-in: students submit a shared Google link or upload the completed Word file.

If your district uses Google Assignments: you may edit either assignment, choose External Tool, select your district Google Assignments integration, attach your own copy, save, and test it in Student View. This setup belongs to the teacher's current Canvas course.

Optional Edpuzzle check

Students can watch The Universal Arts of Graphic Design directly in Canvas. If you want Edpuzzle questions or Live Mode, copy the public Edpuzzle lesson to My Content, reconnect this assignment through the Edpuzzle External Tool, and test it in Student View.

Open Edpuzzle's Canvas setup guide

FACILITATOR'S GUIDE

GRAPHIC DESIGN WITH THE 1960s

Everything you need to run this unit.

⏱ ~13 CLASS PERIODS🎯 MAKE: ORIGINAL EMOJI + PORTFOLIO📱 CANVA VIA CLASSLINK · EDPUZZLE · XELLO

THE UNIT AT A GLANCE

Module itemWhat happens~Time
GRAPHIC DESIGN FOUNDATIONS — run these in order; each one feeds the next
Lesson 1: Pop Art of the 60'sUnplugged. Pop-Art name tag on paper with markers, then a photo and a sentence-starter reflection.1 period
Lesson 2: Graphic Design with CanvaFirst Canva day. Two graphics from a word bank: one lines-only and one circles-only. Students add both PNGs to the Google or Word worksheet, reflect, then submit a link or file.1 period
EdPuzzle | The Universal Arts of Graphic DesignVideo check on what graphic design actually is. The YouTube video is ready in Canvas; Edpuzzle questions or Live Mode are optional.20–30 min
Lesson 3: Paths, Shapes, and ColorsPop-Art t-shirt in Canva: repeating background, text, border, extra shapes. Upload PNG.1 period
Lesson 4: Pictographs — Communicating through ShapesTwo pictographs using the six Gestalt principles. No words allowed in the design.1 period
Lesson 5: Advanced Shapes and ColorsBand logo using the Combo app (union, subtract, intersect, exclude) plus a gradient. This is the skill the emoji project runs on.1 period
EMOJI PROJECT — one six-day design-thinking cycle
Facilitator's Guide: Emoji Project OverviewTeacher page. The four-step build day by day, what to have ready, and the peer review sheet to print before Day 5. Students work from the Emoji Hub below, not from this page.—
Emoji HubStudent roadmap page. Open it together once, then send them back to it each day.10 min
Step 1: DefineEmoji history and the Unicode Consortium, then each student researches a gap and submits a concept for your approval.Day 1
Step 2: IdeateTwo thumbnail sketches, pick one, write the pitch sentence. You demo shapes-only building in Canva.Day 2
Step 3: PrototypeBuild the emoji in Canva from shapes, use at least one Combo operation, export a transparent PNG, start the showcase slide.Days 3–4
Step 4: ShowcaseSplit gallery walk. Day 5 group A presents while group B scores as Unicode reviewers; day 6 they swap. Ends with the approval vote.Days 5–6
CAPSTONE
Portfolio Part 2: Graphic DesignStudents add a Graphic Design section to the Xello portfolio they started in Week 0, upload their two best pieces, and write a reflection for each.1 period

SLIDES

Optional. Every lesson here runs off the student pages without slides. Use these if you would rather teach live from the front of the room. They are in course Files under teacher materials > graphic design.

  • Lesson 1 deck: Graphic Design L1 — Pop Art of the 60's (Lucero)
  • Lesson 2 deck: Graphic Design L2 — Graphic Design with Canva (Lucero), or the shorter 2026 live-teach revision.
  • Lesson 3 deck: Paths, Shapes and Colors (Verizon VILS U1C2L2)
  • Lesson 4 deck: Pictographs (Verizon VILS U1C2L3), bilingual.
  • Lesson 5: no deck in course Files.
  • Emoji Step 1: Define deck: History of Emoji (Lucero)
  • Emoji Step 4: Showcase deck: You Are the Unicode Consortium (Lucero)
  • Emoji Steps 2 and 3: no deck in course Files.

MATERIALS + PREP

  • Lesson 1 only: paper, pencils, and markers, crayons or colored pencils. It is the one unplugged day — pull supplies the day before.
  • Canva through ClassLink for every student, working, before Lesson 2.
  • No Edpuzzle prep is required. Set up Edpuzzle only if you want to use the optional questions or Live Mode.
  • Emoji project: the Define form, sketch worksheet, and showcase slide template are linked from the student pages. Test the Google copy links with your district account; the Define page also includes a Word backup. The peer review runs on paper: print the Peer Review Sheet (PDF linked in the Emoji Project guide, or in course Files under print materials).
  • Showcase days: enough station space for half the class to present at once.
  • Portfolio day: Xello logins confirmed.

WATCH-FORS

  • Lesson 1 says “take a webcam photo,” but the assignment is set to file upload. Tell students to take the photo, save it, then click Start Assignment and upload the file. Otherwise you will get a line of students stuck at the submit screen.
  • Do not skip Lesson 5. The Combo app is a prerequisite for the emoji prototype; students who miss it cannot meet the shapes-only rule.
  • Hold the shapes-only rule from day one. No stickers, icons, templates or clipart in Canva. If you let it slide during Ideate you will not get it back during Prototype.
  • Showcase is a two-day split, not one big day. Half present, half review, then swap. Print one Peer Review Sheet per student before day 5 (two pages, eight station boxes) and set out a ballot box — finished sheets go in it, and the YES/NO circles are the vote.

GRADING

Step 4: Showcase is the module’s Major grade, at 100 points — the finished emoji is what carries the unit. Lessons 1–5 are Minor grades at 5 points each (25 points total), each graded on the upload plus the reflection, which puts the module at 125 points. The EdPuzzle and Emoji Steps 1–3 are set to 0 points; they feed Step 4 rather than standing on their own. Portfolio Part 2 is a page, so it is not graded in Canvas; check it in Xello.

Graphic Design with the 1960s • Lesson 1

GRAPHIC DESIGN OF THE '60s

🕰️ Time Travel to the 1960s!

📋 AT A GLANCE
⏱️ TIME
1 class period
🎯 MAKE
Pop-Art Name Tag
📱 TOOLS
Paper + Colors
📤 SUBMIT
Photo + Reflection
  • English
  • Español
🎯 LEARNING GOALS

By the end of this lesson, you will:

✅ Describe how Design Thinking is used in art and graphic design

✅ Create a '60s style Pop-Art name tag

💥 WHAT IS POP-ART?

In the 1950s and 1960s, artists realized there was a new group of customers: young people. They wanted bright, bold, and affordable art. Through prototyping and testing, artists found a solution: Pop-Art. That is Design Thinking: try an idea, test it, then improve it.

📖 VOCAB: Pop-Art = an artistic movement in the 1950s and '60s to make art more vibrant and accessible for a younger audience.
🎥 WATCH: Pop-Art History

Learn how Pop-Art began to meet the needs of young customers in the '50s and '60s.

✏️ YOUR MISSION: Pop-Art Name Tag
✅ GOAL: Create Your Name
✍️ Write your name in a Pop-Art font (big, bold, comic style)
🎨 Use Pop-Art colors (bright opposites that stand out)
⭐ STRETCH GOAL: Add a Background
🌟 Create a Pop-Art background behind your name (dots, patterns, shapes, or bold colors)

🎨 MATERIALS: Paper, pencil, and something to color with (markers, crayons, colored pencils)

🌟 EXAMPLES

💥 POW! SUBMIT YOUR POP-ART! 💥

📸 Take a webcam photo of your name tag

💬 Answer in the comments:

"I made my name tag look like Pop Art by using ______, which makes it feel ______."

STYLE CHOICES:

bright colors • bold outlines • comic font • opposite colors • Ben-Day dots • patterns • thick letters

FEELINGS:

bold • exciting • fun • energetic • eye-catching • vibrant • retro • loud • playful

🎯 METAS DE APRENDIZAJE

Al final de esta lección, podrás:

✅ Describir cómo se usa Design Thinking en el arte y diseño gráfico

✅ Crear una etiqueta de nombre estilo Pop-Art de los años '60

💥 ¿QUÉ ES EL POP-ART?

En los años 1950 y 1960, los artistas se dieron cuenta de que había un nuevo grupo de clientes: los jóvenes. Querían arte brillante, llamativo y económico. A través de prototipos y pruebas, los artistas encontraron una solución: Pop-Art. Eso es Design Thinking: propones una idea, la pruebas y la mejoras.

📖 VOCABULARIO: Pop-Art = un movimiento artístico en los años '50 y '60 para hacer el arte más vibrante y accesible para un público joven.
🎥 MIRA: Historia del Pop-Art

Aprende cómo comenzó el Pop-Art para satisfacer las necesidades de los jóvenes en los años '50 y '60.

✏️ TU MISIÓN: Etiqueta Pop-Art
✅ META: Crea Tu Nombre
✍️ Escribe tu nombre en una fuente Pop-Art (grande, llamativa, estilo cómic)
🎨 Usa colores Pop-Art (opuestos brillantes que resalten)
⭐ META EXTRA: Agrega un Fondo
🌟 Crea un fondo Pop-Art detrás de tu nombre (puntos, patrones, formas o colores llamativos)

🎨 MATERIALES: Papel, lápiz y algo para colorear (marcadores, crayones, lápices de colores)

🌟 EJEMPLOS

💥 ¡ZAS! ¡ENVÍA TU POP-ART! 💥

📸 Toma una foto con la cámara web de tu etiqueta

💬 Responde en los comentarios:

"Hice que mi etiqueta se vea como Pop Art usando ______, lo cual la hace sentir ______."

OPCIONES DE ESTILO:

colores brillantes • contornos gruesos • fuente cómic • colores opuestos • puntos Ben-Day • patrones • letras gruesas

SENTIMIENTOS:

llamativa • emocionante • divertida • energética • vibrante • retro • audaz • juguetona

Graphic Design with the 1960s • Lesson 2

GRAPHIC DESIGN WITH CANVA

Visual Communication Using Shape Constraints

🤔 BIG QUESTION: How can simple design choices make an idea clear without using words?

📋 AT A GLANCE
⏱️ TIME
1 class period

Canva

🎯 LEARNING GOAL

🎥 VIDEO TUTORIAL

Watch this video to learn how to use Canva for this activity:

🚀 OPEN CLASSLINK → CANVA
✏️ YOUR MISSION

Choose 2 words. Create 2 designs.

⭕

Rapid Relaxed Complicated Organized Labyrinth

📤 HOW TO EXPORT

💥 POW! SUBMIT YOUR DESIGNS! 💥

Use the Google copy when it opens for your school account. If it does not, download the Word copy instead.

GOOGLE COPYDOWNLOAD

4. In Canvas, submit either the share link to your Google Doc or your completed Word file.

Q1: What did you try to show in your lines-only design?

Q2: How did using only circles change your design compared to using lines?

WORD BANK:

For Q2: easier • harder • different • similar • limiting • creative • challenging • fun

🎯 META DE APRENDIZAJE

HACER COPIA
DE GOOGLEDESCARGAR COPIA

Q1: What did you try to show in your lines-only design?

(¿Qué trataste de mostrar con solo líneas?)

"I chose the word ______. I used lines to show this by ______."

Q2: How did using only circles change your design compared to using lines?

(¿Cómo cambió tu diseño usando solo círculos vs líneas?)

"Using circles was ______ because ______."

WORD BANK / BANCO DE PALABRAS:

Q1: spacing (espacio) • direction (dirección) • thickness (grosor) • overlapping (superposición) • repeating (repetición) • angles (ángulos) • curves (curvas)

Q2: easier (más fácil) • harder (más difícil) • different (diferente) • similar (parecido) • limiting (limitante) • creative (creativo) • challenging (desafiante) • fun (divertido)

Graphic Design with the 1960s • Video Check

WHAT IS GRAPHIC DESIGN?

Why Design Rules the World (And You Didn't Even Notice)

  • English
  • Español

👀 LOOK AROUND YOU RIGHT NOW

📱 Your phone screen 🪧 Signs in the hall 🍫 Food packaging 👕 Your clothes 🛑 Street signs

ALL of that is graphic design!

🧠 3 BIG IDEAS TO WATCH FOR

1. Design = Communication 💬

Graphic design isn't just about making things pretty — it tells you something or makes you feel something. Every color, shape, and font choice has a reason.

2. Design is Everywhere 🌍

You use it to cross streets, pick food, scroll your phone. Good design makes your life easier — and you don't even notice it's working.

3. Designers Think Like You 🧑‍🎨

They ask: "What would make someone feel something?" The best designs create a moment you remember and understand instantly.

🎬 WHILE YOU WATCH

Notice the examples they show — matchbooks, hotel signs, buildings, book covers.

Ask yourself: "What is this design trying to make me think or feel?"

💥 READY? LET'S GO! 💥

Watch the video below. Pause after each section and use the prompts above to name the design decisions you notice.

Open the video in a new tab

👀 MIRA A TU ALREDEDOR AHORA MISMO

📱 La pantalla de tu teléfono 🪧 Letreros en el pasillo 🍫 Empaques de comida 👕 Tu ropa 🛑 Señales de tráfico

¡TODO eso es diseño gráfico!

🧠 3 GRANDES IDEAS PARA OBSERVAR

1. Diseño = Comunicación 💬

El diseño gráfico no solo hace las cosas bonitas — te dice algo o te hace sentir algo. Cada color, figura y tipo de letra tiene una razón.

2. El Diseño Está en Todas Partes 🌍

Lo usas para cruzar calles, elegir comida, navegar en tu teléfono. El buen diseño te hace la vida más fácil — y ni te das cuenta de que está funcionando.

3. Los Diseñadores Piensan Como Tú 🧑‍🎨

Se preguntan: "¿Qué haría que alguien sienta algo?" Los mejores diseños crean un momento que recuerdas y entiendes al instante.

🎬 MIENTRAS VES EL VIDEO

Observa los ejemplos que muestran — cajas de cerillos, letreros de hoteles, edificios, portadas de libros.

Pregúntate: "¿Qué quiere este diseño que yo piense o sienta?"

💥 ¿LISTO? ¡VAMOS! 💥

Mira el video de abajo. Haz una pausa después de cada sección y usa las preguntas de arriba para nombrar las decisiones de diseño que notas.

Abrir el video en una pestaña nueva

Graphic Design with the 1960s • Lesson 3

PATHS, SHAPES & COLORS

Design a Pop Art T-Shirt in Canva

🤔 BIG QUESTION: How can simple shapes and bright colors communicate bold ideas?

📋 AT A GLANCE
⏱️ TIME
1 class period
🎯 MAKE
Pop Art T-Shirt
📱 TOOL
Canva
📤 SUBMIT
PNG + Reflection
  • English
  • Español
🎯 LEARNING GOAL

✅ Use digital design tools to create bold, eye-catching Pop Art using shapes, patterns, and color

🎨 POP ART FEATURES

Pop Art uses these 3 features:

🌈

Bright Colors

+ strong borders

🔵🔵🔵

Repeating Patterns

dots, lines, images

📺

Mass Media Vibes

comics, magazines, movies

📖 VOCAB: Path = lines you draw by hand; closing them makes a shape • Border = the edge around a shape • Font = style of text
🎥 VIDEO TUTORIAL

Watch to learn how to use elements, copy/paste shapes, apply colors, and add text:

🚀 OPEN CLASSLINK → CANVA
✏️ YOUR MISSION

Design a Pop Art T-Shirt!

Your design MUST include:

🔵🔴🟡

Repetitive Background

dots, stripes, or patterns

✍️

Text

a word or your name (fun font!)

⬜

Border

around shape or text

⭐

Extra Shapes

add whatever you want!

💡 Stuck? Try creating a simple Pop Art nametag first!

⭐ LEVEL UP: Make 4 copies of your design and change the color scheme on each one — like Warhol's famous repeating portraits! Submit all 4 as a panel.

📤 HOW TO EXPORT

1. Click Share (top right corner)

2. Click Download

3. Select PNG as file type

4. Click Download again to save

💥 POW! SUBMIT YOUR WORK! 💥

1. Click Start Assignment on this page

2. Upload your PNG file

3. Answer the reflection question in the Comments box

💬 REFLECTION: How did you use shapes, colors, and patterns to make your design look like Pop Art?

"My design looks like Pop Art because I used ______ to create ______."

WORD BANK:

bright colors • repeating dots • strong borders • patterns • circles • lines • bold text • repetition

🎯 META DE APRENDIZAJE

✅ Usar herramientas de diseño digital para crear Arte Pop llamativo usando formas, patrones y color

🎨 CARACTERÍSTICAS DEL ARTE POP

El Arte Pop usa estas 3 características:

🌈

Colores Brillantes

+ bordes fuertes

🔵🔵🔵

Patrones Repetitivos

puntos, líneas, imágenes

📺

cómics, revistas, películas

📖 VOCABULARIO: Path/Trazado = líneas dibujadas a mano; cerrarlas forma una figura • Border/Borde = el contorno de una forma • Font/Fuente = estilo del texto
🎥 VIDEO TUTORIAL

Mira para aprender a usar elementos, copiar/pegar formas, aplicar colores y agregar texto:

🚀 ABRIR CLASSLINK → CANVA

¡Diseña una Camiseta de Arte Pop!

Tu diseño DEBE incluir:

🔵🔴🟡

Fondo Repetitivo

puntos, rayas o patrones

✍️

Texto

una palabra o tu nombre (¡fuente divertida!)

⬜

Borde

alrededor de forma o texto

⭐

Formas Extra

¡agrega lo que quieras!

💡 ¿Atascado/a? ¡Intenta crear una etiqueta de nombre Arte Pop primero!

⭐ SUBE DE NIVEL: Haz 4 copias de tu diseño y cambia los colores en cada una — ¡como los famosos retratos repetidos de Warhol! Envía las 4 como un panel.

📤 CÓMO EXPORTAR

1. Haz clic en Share/Compartir (esquina superior derecha)

2. Haz clic en Download/Descargar

💥 ¡ZAS! ¡ENVÍA TU TRABAJO! 💥

1. Haz clic en Start Assignment en esta página

2. Sube tu archivo PNG

💬 REFLECTION: How did you use shapes, colors, and patterns to make your design look like Pop Art?

(¿Cómo usaste formas, colores y patrones para que tu diseño se vea como Arte Pop?)

"My design looks like Pop Art because I used ______ to create ______."

WORD BANK / BANCO DE PALABRAS:

bright colors (colores brillantes) • repeating dots (puntos repetidos) • strong borders (bordes fuertes) • patterns (patrones) • circles (círculos) • lines (líneas) • bold text (texto en negrita) • repetition (repetición)

Graphic Design with the 1960s • Lesson 4

COMMUNICATION THROUGH SHAPES

Pictographs — Shapes That Speak Without Words

🤔 BIG QUESTION: How can simple shapes communicate a message without using any words?

📋 AT A GLANCE
⏱️ TIME
1 class period
🎯 MAKE
2 Pictographs
📱 TOOL
Canva
📤 SUBMIT
PNG + Reflection
  • English
  • Español
🎯 LEARNING GOAL

✅ Communicate a message or idea using only shapes — no words needed

🎨 KEY CONCEPTS

Today you'll learn about 3 big ideas:

🪨

Pictographs

Pictures that represent words — from cave art to modern icons

🧠

Gestalt Principles

Rules for how our eyes group shapes into meaning

💬

Visual Communication

Using shapes to send a clear message without text

📖 VOCAB: Petroglyph = an image carved into rock (carving)
📖 VOCAB: Pictograph = a drawing or painting that represents a word or phrase — the earliest form of writing. On computers we call them icons
📖 VOCAB: Gestalt Principles = rules that describe how our eyes see and group visual elements. Gestalt is German for "configuration"
🧠 THE 6 GESTALT PRINCIPLES

These are rules for how our eyes make sense of shapes. Use at least one in your pictograph!

1. Similarity

We group things that look alike (same color, shape, or size)

2. Continuation

Our eyes follow the smoothest path or line

3. Closure

Our brain fills in missing parts to see a whole shape

4. Proximity

Things placed close together look like they belong together

5. Figure/Ground

We separate a shape (figure) from its background

6. Symmetry & Order

Our brain prefers balanced, simple arrangements

🎥 VIDEO TUTORIAL

Watch this video about pictographs, Gestalt principles, and how to create your own in Canva:

🚀 OPEN CLASSLINK → CANVA
✏️ YOUR MISSION

Create 2 pictographs in Canva! Each design MUST include:

🔵

At Least 1 Shape

Circles, squares, triangles, etc.

🧠

1 Gestalt Principle

Use at least one principle per design

💬

Clear Message

Each pictograph represents a word, idea, or action

🚫

No Words

Your shapes do the talking — no text on the design!

🧠 LOS 6 PRINCIPIOS GESTALT

Estas son reglas sobre cómo nuestros ojos interpretan las figuras. ¡Usa al menos uno en tu pictografía!

1. Similitud

Agrupamos cosas que se ven parecidas (mismo color, forma o tamaño)

2. Continuación

Nuestros ojos siguen el camino más suave o la línea

3. Cierre

Nuestro cerebro completa las partes que faltan para ver una figura completa

4. Proximidad

Las cosas que están cerca se ven como si pertenecieran juntas

5. Figura/Fondo

Separamos una figura de su fondo

6. Simetría y Orden

Nuestro cerebro prefiere arreglos equilibrados y simples

📖 VOCAB: Compound Shape = two or more shapes combined to form one new shape

🔷 THE 4 COMPOUND SHAPE OPERATIONS

These are the 4 ways to combine shapes using the Combo App in Canva:

1. Union ➕

Merges shapes together into one big shape. Like gluing two pieces of paper together.

2. Subtract ➖

Cuts the top shape out of the bottom shape. Like a cookie cutter!

3. Intersect ✂️

Keeps only the part where shapes overlap. Everything else disappears.

4. Exclude / Difference 🔄

Removes the overlapping part and keeps everything else. Opposite of intersect!

🛠️ HOW TO USE THE COMBO APP

1. Add 2 or more shapes to your Canva design

2. Move them so they overlap

3. Select both shapes (hold Shift + click each one)

4. Click Apps in the left sidebar → search "Combo"

5. Choose your operation: Union, Subtract, Intersect, or Exclude

🌈 GRADIENT TYPES

In Canva, click on any shape's color → choose Gradient instead of solid color:

Linear ↔️

Colors blend in a straight line (left to right, top to bottom)

Radial 🎯

Colors blend outward from the center like a target

Angular 🔄

Colors blend in a circle, like a color wheel

🔷 LAS 4 OPERACIONES DE FIGURAS COMPUESTAS

Estas son las 4 formas de combinar figuras usando la App Combo en Canva:

Solo mantiene la parte donde las figuras se superponen. Todo lo demás desaparece.

TWO THINGS TO WATCH

💥 KEEP IDEATE WIDE

Day 2 is for quantity, not commitment. Students who lock onto their first sketch reach Prototype with one fragile idea and no fallback. Ask for a page of rough options before anyone picks, and hold the choosing until the end of the period.

One Peer Review Sheet per student — two pages, eight station boxes. Each box scores one emoji (1–4) and circles YES or NO on adding it to Unicode: Peer Review Sheet (PDF). Also in course Files under print materials.

🏛️ Who Decides Which Emoji Exist?

The Unicode Consortium is a group of tech companies (Apple, Google, Microsoft) that votes on which emoji get added to every phone in the world. A new emoji takes 1–2 years to get approved.

So I have to convince them my emoji should exist? 😮

Yep. That's YOUR job in this project. 📝

👍👎 What Makes an Emoji Get Approved?

👍 Gets a YES

It's popular — people already search for it online

It's missing — there's a gap in an emoji family it would fill

It's unique — you can't express it by combining existing emoji

👎 Gets a NO

Too specific — only a tiny group of people would use it

Already exists — a similar emoji is already out there

Brand/logo — no Nike swoosh, no Mickey Mouse, no TikTok logo

SMART SOLUTIONS · WEEK 5

Laser Cutting | Facilitator Guide

Students learn how cut, score, and engrave operations come from a file, then solve a small identification problem with a laser-ready tag.

Core route: five class periods. The whole-group deck teaches each concept and provides a daily leave-up screen. Canvas holds the accessible directions, absence route, submission requirements, and rubric.

Teacher deck
Download the Laser Cutting teacher deck
First Look worksheet
Printable PDF · Editable Word version
Sample tile
Download the Cut, Score, Engrave SVG
Assessment
First Look 5 points · Identity Tag 100 points · Xello 5 points.

What makes this a design project

User and need
A student or classroom needs to identify, return, or sort an item.
Privacy constraint
The tag cannot expose a full legal name, student ID, phone number, or private account information.
Fabrication constraints
2 to 3 inches, one closed cut silhouette, readable surface information, and a file that survives a real-size test.

Five-day run sheet

DayTeachStudents doDeck
1Pixels vs. paths; cut, score, engrave; room and material safety.Inspect a physical sample or sourced photo and complete the First Look worksheet.Slides 1–11. Leave slide 11 up.
2Define the identification need. Model privacy-safe information, three thumbnails, and laser-ready geometry.Choose an item and user, sketch three ideas, build the first vector file, and submit it for a file check.Slides 12–18. Leave slide 18 up.
3Real-size testing, partner trace, purpose check, and revision.Test the tag at real size, find one problem, revise, and resubmit.Slides 19–21. Leave slide 21 up.
4Run the trained-operator machine queue and model safe finishing.Finish, photograph, and document the revision while waiting.Slides 22–23. Leave slide 23 up.
5Critique purpose, privacy, and fabrication decisions separately.Submit evidence, reflect, and connect one Matchmaker career result to fabrication work.Slides 24–27. Leave slide 26 up during submission.

Before students arrive

  1. Make physical evidence available. Cut the sample tile SVG from your approved classroom material, or prepare several existing objects that clearly show cut, score, and engrave. Number the samples so pairs can record which one they inspected.
  2. Print the worksheet. One per student is easiest. The editable Word version is available if your class completes it digitally.
  3. Test your exact machine route. Import the sample, assign operations, run one piece, and confirm that the score and engrave remain visibly different.
  4. Prepare the queue. Create one folder by class period. Use Period-Lastname-Firstname-FindableTag.svg.
  5. Prepare low-cost testing. Students need a real-size print, trace, or paper cutout before their file enters the machine queue.
  6. Set up work stations. Students should have meaningful test, revision, finishing, photo, and Xello work while the trained operator runs the machine.

Trained operator boundary

Use only documented laser-compatible material approved for the exact machine. Follow the manufacturer’s current manual, ventilation or filtration requirements, supervision rules, fire response procedure, and required training. Students do not change settings, bypass an enclosure or interlock, load unknown material, or start a job unless your local safety procedure explicitly allows trained student operators.

Common concepts, different software

Teach the physical result first: a through-cut, a thin surface line, and a filled surface area. Then show how your classroom software assigns those results.

Glowforge App
  • Upload SVG or PDF for vector cut and engrave information.
  • Strokes import as cuts; the operator can change a stroke to score.
  • Filled vector areas and raster images engrave.
  • JPG and PNG are engraving-only routes.

Glowforge file guidance

xTool Creative Space
  • Import the SVG and select the vector elements.
  • Convert the identifier text to paths or outlines before export. XCS does not display live text inside an SVG.
  • Assign an outline path to Cut or Score.
  • Assign a filled vector area or raster image to Engrave.
  • Use SVG for this project. PDF is not an xTool Creative Space import route.
  • Use the safety training and settings for your exact xTool model.

xTool file and text guidance · xTool Cut, Score, and Engrave comparison · xTool safety training

First Look routine

  1. Show the sourced three-heart comparison so students can see one operation at a time.
  2. Give each pair a physical sample. Do not name its operations yet.
  3. Students sketch, mark Found or Not used, and cite visible evidence on the worksheet.
  4. Pairs compare answers. Reveal the operation map or sample file only after they commit to evidence.
  5. Collect the worksheet scan or photo plus the sentence: The laser used ______ to ______. I know because ______.

Day 2 model

The Gulf Coast Marine Rescue image shows how one visual identity can move onto a small object. It is not the student brief. Model the actual brief aloud: choose an item, name the user, protect private information, sketch three silhouettes, then choose the idea that stays readable and structurally strong.

Define stem: ______ needs a tag that helps ______ without showing ______.
Critique stem: I think this tag is for ______ because I notice ______.
Word bank: identify · return · sort · purpose · privacy · silhouette · readable · closed path · cut · score · engrave

Queue plan

  1. Students submit only after the Day 3 real-size and partner checks.
  2. The trained operator confirms material, size, placement, cut/score/engrave assignments, and ventilation or filtration.
  3. Students wait at the finishing, documentation, or revision station, not around the machine.
  4. If a file fails, return it with one specific note. The student revises before rejoining the queue.

Exact project rubric

  • Purpose and privacy: 20
  • Laser-ready geometry and file: 25
  • Cut, score, and engrave plan: 20
  • Testing and revision: 20
  • Documentation and reflection: 15

Xello on Day 5

Students who completed Matchmaker in Week 1 reopen their results, choose one related career, and explain which part of the week’s work connects to it. Students who missed Matchmaker finish it first.

Optional extended challenge

A Taste of Texas remains available as a longer competition or CTSO route. It asks for three logo applications and a full visual portfolio, so it is not the default five-day project. Use it only when your calendar and machine queue can support it.

Download the complete A Taste of Texas challenge.

Publication boundary: keep this facilitator guide unpublished. Publish the three student assignments only after you have tested your file route, sample, material, safety routine, and machine queue.

DAY 1 · FIRST LOOK

Read a Finished Laser-Cut Sample

Before you build a file, learn to recognize what the machine did to the material.

Objective
Use visible evidence to identify cut, score, and engrave operations.
You need
A finished sample or the projected photo, plus the First Look worksheet.
Turn in

Print or type
Open the printable PDF
Open the editable Word version
File view | Open when directed
Open the Cut, Score, Engrave sample tile SVG
Commit to your visible evidence before you inspect the file.

Operation comparison from xTool Support, “What is the Difference between Engrave, Score, and Cut?”

What the operations leave behind

Cut
The line travels through the material and separates a piece.
Score
A thin line stays on the surface.
Engrave
A filled or shaded area is removed from the surface.

How the file connects

  • Vector path or stroke: a line the software can assign to cut or score.
  • Filled vector shape or raster image: an area the software can assign to engrave.
  • Important: your file does not choose safe settings. The trained operator checks the material, size, placement, and operation settings before the machine runs.

Machine boundary

Stay outside the machine work zone unless directed. Never bring material from home for the laser. If the material is not approved for the exact machine, it does not go in.

Complete the First Look worksheet

  1. Sketch and label the finished sample or projected photo.
  2. For each operation, mark Found or Not used.
  3. Point to visible evidence: an opening, outside edge, thin surface line, or filled surface area.
  4. Connect one visible result to the file element that probably made it.
  5. Upload a clear scan or photo of the worksheet. Add the sentence below in the submission comment.
Sentence stem: The laser used ______ to ______. I know because ______.

MAJOR PROJECT · 100 POINTS

Make It Findable | Laser-Ready Identity Tag

Design a small tag that helps someone identify, return, or sort a real school or lab item without showing private information.

Study how the central symbol stays recognizable when the graphic moves onto a small object. Your project follows the specific brief below.

Design brief: School and lab items get lost, mixed up, or returned to the wrong place. Make one 2-to-3-inch identity tag for a backpack, lanyard, pencil pouch, toolbox, device case, or shared supply bin. It should tell someone who the item belongs to or what the item is for, but it cannot show a full legal name, student ID, phone number, or other private information.

Day 2 | Define the need and sketch three ideas

  1. Choose one item and one user. You may design for yourself, a partner, or a shared class tool.
  2. Finish the statement: ______ needs a tag that helps ______ without showing ______.
  3. Sketch three different silhouettes. Do not draw the same idea three times.
  4. Each sketch must include a short privacy-safe identifier: initials, a short nickname, a role, or one word.
  5. Circle the idea that is easiest to recognize and strongest enough to become a physical object.
Purpose
Someone can identify, return, or sort the item.
Privacy
No full legal name, ID number, phone number, or private account information.
Size
The finished object is 2 to 3 inches and readable at arm’s length.

Build the first laser-ready file

  1. Build one closed outer path for the cut.
  2. Add one bold icon and the short identifier inside the outline.
  3. Use the class operation plan to assign surface details to score or engrave.
  4. Keep important details away from the outside cut line and any keychain hole.
  5. For the xTool route, convert the identifier text to paths or outlines, then export SVG. XCS does not display live SVG text.
  6. For the Glowforge route, export SVG or the approved PDF. PDF is not the xTool route.
Cut silhouette
One closed outside shape. No accidental loose pieces.
Surface information
One icon plus initials, a short nickname, a role, or one word.
Optional hole
A closed circle with enough material around it to stay strong.
Filename: Period-Lastname-Firstname-FindableTag.svg
Submit the file only after it passes the file check.

Day 3 | Test what the screen hides

  1. Print or trace the design at its real 2-to-3-inch size.
  2. Ask a partner to trace the outside cut path and point to each surface operation.
  3. Check whether the user can tell what the tag is for without seeing private information.
  4. Circle tiny details, weak bridges, loose pieces, doubled lines, or text that is hard to read.
  5. Make at least one useful revision and export the new file.
Partner stem: I think this tag is for ______ because I notice ______. I can follow the cut path around ______.
Designer stem: I changed ______ because the test showed ______.
Word bank: purpose · privacy · silhouette · closed path · bridge · loose piece · readable · scale · cut · score · engrave

Day 4 | Fabricate, finish, document

  • Work at the assigned station while your file moves through the fabrication queue.
  • Stay outside the machine work zone unless directed.
  • Finish the piece only after it is released to you.
  • Photograph the front of the object in clear light.
  • Save one screenshot of the final vector file.

Day 5 | Turn in

  1. Upload the final SVG. If your class used the approved Glowforge PDF route, upload the PDF instead.
  2. Upload the finished-object photo. If your class could not fabricate every file, upload the real-size test and final file instead.
  3. Upload the real-size test or a before-and-after screenshot that shows your revision.
  4. In the submission comment, answer both reflection prompts.
Reflection 1: The tag helps ______ identify, return, or sort ______ because ______.
Reflection 2: I changed ______ after the test because ______.

Rubric

CriterionWhat countsPoints
Purpose and privacyThe tag clearly helps someone identify, return, or sort the chosen item without exposing private information.20
Laser-ready geometry and fileThe file has a closed outside path, correct size, usable vector structure, and no accidental loose or doubled paths.25
Cut, score, and engrave planThe operation choices match the silhouette, surface information, and approved class material plan.20
Testing and revisionEvidence shows a real-size or file test, a specific problem, and a useful revision.20
Documentation and reflectionThe required files and images are clear, and both reflections explain the purpose and revision.15

The file is usable after one small correction to a path, fill, size, or filename.
Two or more file-prep problems keep the design from entering the machine queue.

rubric.long_description: The operation choices match the silhouette, surface information, and approved class material plan.

Most operation choices make sense, but one path, fill, or material connection needs clarification.
Operation roles are unclear or do not match the intended physical result.
Operation and material evidence is missing.

rubric.long_description: Evidence shows a real-size or file test, a specific problem, and a useful revision.

ratings.long_description: The test reveals a concrete issue and the revision directly addresses it.
A test and revision are present, but the connection between them needs clarification.
The test is incomplete, not real size, or does not lead to a visible revision.
Testing or revision evidence is missing.

rubric.long_description: The required files and images are clear, and both reflections explain the purpose and revision.

The evidence is complete, but one explanation needs more specific support.
One or more required files, images, or reflections are unclear or incomplete.

DAY 5 · XELLO CHECK-IN · 5 POINTS

Connect Your Matchmaker Results to Fabrication Work

You already completed Matchmaker in Week 1. Reopen the results and look for a career that uses at least one skill from this project.

Missed Matchmaker? Complete Matchmaker first, then return to this page. Do not repeat it if you already have results.

Open Xello

  2. Open your saved Matchmaker results.
  3. Choose one career that connects to something you did this week.
  4. Take a screenshot showing the career title.
  5. Upload the screenshot and complete the two stems in the submission comment.
Design

Technical work

Production

Stem 1: One Matchmaker career that connects to this project is ______.
Stem 2: The connection is ______ because both require ______.
Word bank: graphic design · engineering · manufacturing · fabrication · quality control · drafting · technician · safety · testing · revision

Success check

  • The screenshot shows the career title.
  • The response names one real task from the laser project.
  • The connection explains a shared skill, not only “it looks interesting.”

✂ The Workshop · Teacher Guide

HOLIDAY ORNAMENT LASER EXTENSION

A short seasonal application after students learn the core laser workflow.

Where this fits

Use this as an optional 2 to 3 day extension after the CNC/Laser Cutting module. Students should already know cut, score, engrave, SVG, real-size testing, and the class file queue. This project applies those skills to a smaller seasonal object. It does not replace the core laser lesson.

Time
2 to 3 class periods
Product
One 4 by 4 inch ornament
Tools
Canva, SVG, Glowforge
Grade
5-point Minor check

Teacher materials

Laser Cutting Teacher Deck. Reuse slides 4 to 10 for pixels, paths, cut, score, engrave, and safety. Reuse slides 15 to 23 for file setup, real-size testing, partner trace, the teacher-run queue, and documentation.

  • Project the teacher model already embedded in the student activity. It shows the digital plan and the finished wood ornament.
  • Prepare teacher-approved wood, string or ribbon, safety equipment, and a labeled drying or pickup area.
  • Create the class queue folder before students export. The exact filename is Period-Lastname-Firstname-Ornament.svg.
  • Test both videos, Canva access, and one sample SVG before class.

Run sheet

DayTeachStudents doEvidence
1Use the Define video and CNC deck slides 4 to 10. Make the distinction explicit: paths and fills describe geometry; the teacher confirms the machine operation.Sketch three genuinely different ornament ideas. Select one using the size, hanging-hole, and readability constraints.Three sketches plus one reasoned choice.
2Use slides 15 to 20. Model the closed outer path, hanging hole, engraved or scored detail, filename, and paper test.Build the SVG in Canva, print or trace it at real size, and revise after a partner traces the expected operations.Laser-ready SVG that passes the partner trace.
3Use slides 21 to 23. Check material, scale, placement, and operations. You run the Glowforge.Finish the ornament, photograph it, and explain one design decision and one revision.SVG, finished-object evidence, and reflection.

Default video route

The student Define item embeds Holiday Ornaments: Define. That portable route works when the course is copied.

If you want questions, accountability, or Live Mode, copy the Edpuzzle lesson into your own account and reconnect it as an External Tool in your course. Test the new assignment in Student View before publishing. Do not rely on an imported Edpuzzle launch from another Canvas class.

Machine and material boundary

  • The teacher operates the Glowforge. Students hand off a checked file through the class queue.
  • Run the required exhaust and filtration. Never leave an active laser unattended.
  • Use only material you can identify and approve. Do not guess about unknown plastics or coatings.
  • Do not bypass the lid, interlocks, or other safety systems.

Important correction to the old lesson

Color can help a class organize a file, but color is not the machine instruction by itself. A closed stroke or path can be assigned to cut or score. A filled shape or raster image can be assigned to engrave. The teacher must inspect the imported file and confirm each operation before running the job.

The student page now teaches the simpler chain: geometry → operation → material result.

Five-point check

  1. Closed outer cut path
  2. Hanging hole placed safely inside the edge
  3. One readable engraved or scored detail
  4. Real-size test, revision, and correct filename
  5. Submitted evidence plus a specific reflection

Keep the module, guide, and both student items unpublished until you choose this extension and test the queue in Student View.

✂ Holiday Ornament · Learn

WHAT WILL THE LASER DO?

Watch the short video, then read one design like the machine will.

Topic
Cut, score, engrave
Objective
Predict the result of a path or fill
Evidence

Open the video on YouTube

Watch for three actions

Cut

The beam travels through the material so a piece can separate.

Score

The beam draws a shallow line on the surface.

Engrave

The beam removes or darkens a filled area on the surface.

Stop and jot

Look at the real examples in the next activity. Identify:

  • one path that should cut all the way through
  • one mark or area that should stay on the surface

Sentence stem: The laser should ______ the ______ because ______.

✂ Holiday Ornament · Laser Extension

DESIGN AN ORNAMENT THAT CAN BE MADE

Your file must tell the teacher where the object ends and which marks stay on the surface.

Product
One 4 by 4 inch ornament
File
One teacher-checked SVG
Evidence
Model, revision, photo, reflection

Read two real examples

These are two different designs. Use them to compare a digital file with a finished material result. The teacher still confirms each machine operation before fabrication.

The file-to-material chain

1 · Geometry
Path, outline, fill, or image
2 · Operation
Cut, score, or engrave
3 · Result
Separate, mark, or darken

Color may help organize layers, but color alone does not run the laser. The teacher checks the imported geometry, operation, material, and settings.

Day 1 · Ideate and choose

  1. Sketch three different ornament ideas. Changing only the text or color does not make a new idea.
  2. Give every idea a closed outer shape, a hanging hole, and one readable surface detail.
  3. Circle the strongest idea. Complete: I chose ______ because it will remain readable at 4 inches and ______.

Word bank: outline · path · hanging hole · detail · readable · simple · contrast

Day 2 · Build, trace, revise

  1. Create a 4 by 4 inch page in Canva or the vector tool your teacher names.
  2. Build one closed outer path. Add a closed hanging hole with enough wood around it to stay strong.
  3. Add one or more simple details that can be scored or engraved. Avoid tiny text, hairline gaps, crowded shapes, and loose pieces.
  4. Export one SVG named Period-Lastname-Firstname-Ornament.svg.
  5. Print or trace the design at real size. Cut the paper outline and check the hole, edge strength, and readability.
  6. Give the paper test to a partner. Your partner traces the expected cut and surface marks. Revise anything they cannot predict.

Machine boundary

You submit the checked file. Your teacher runs the Glowforge. Do not upload to the Glowforge App, place material, change settings, or start a job unless your teacher is directing that exact step beside you.

Day 3 · Watch, finish, document

Open the print-run video on YouTube

  1. Hand off the SVG through the class queue.
  2. When your ornament is ready, add any teacher-approved finish and attach the string or ribbon.
  3. Photograph the finished object from directly above in good light.

Leave this screen up during work time

Today’s task

  • Finish the SVG
  • Test it at real size
  • Complete the partner trace
  • Revise and submit

Success criteria

  • Closed outer path
  • Strong hanging hole
  • Readable surface detail
  • Correct size and filename

Partner stem: I predict the machine will ______ this path and ______ this area.

Submit

  • Your Period-Lastname-Firstname-Ornament.svg
  • A photo of the finished ornament. If the class queue is still running, submit the real-size paper test and add the finished photo when your teacher returns the object.

Text entry: My design changed from ______ to ______ after ______. The finished ornament communicates ______ because ______.

Word bank: revised · simplified · strengthened · readable · contrast · cut · score · engrave

Five-point check

  1. Closed outer cut path
  2. Hanging hole placed safely inside the edge
  3. Readable scored or engraved detail
  4. Real-size test, revision, and correct filename
  5. Submitted evidence plus a specific reflection

3D MODELING • TEACHER OVERVIEW

The Complete CAD Ladder: Draw, Model, Print, Decompose, Scale

Students draw a symbol, model it, design for a real body, break a familiar object into shapes, and finish by building a room to scale. This is the complete sequence. Teachers make calendar cuts locally.

The route at a glance

Week 1: CAD basics

Paper currency, then a 3D coin. Students learn the workplane, move, rotate, resize, align, Group, and Hole.

Week 2: Design for printing

Measure and build a ring. Teach flat bases, overhangs, slicing, and why a digital model may need revision before it prints.

Lesson 4: Shape decomposition

Favorite Toy teaches students to find the boxes, cylinders, spheres, and cutouts inside a complex object before they build it.

Capstone: Build to scale

Dream Room adds measurement, conversion, consistent scale, testing, and revision. It uses the prior CAD moves in one larger model.

Before students open Tinkercad

  1. Create your own Tinkercad Classroom. Use only the classroom links and codes generated for your class.
  2. Choose the district-approved join route. Tinkercad supports a teacher nickname plus class code and existing student accounts plus a class code. Test the route your students will use.
  3. Create Activities inside your class. Add Coin, Ring, Favorite Toy, and Dream Room. Attach a starting design only when the lesson calls for one.
  4. Open Student View before class. Make sure every Canvas file, video, assignment button, and Tinkercad direction works without your teacher permissions.

Official Guide to Tinkercad Classrooms

Grading and publication

  • Lessons 1 to 3 are 5-point Minor skill checks.
  • Favorite Toy and Dream Room are separate 100-point Major projects. Favorite Toy assesses shape decomposition and grouped construction. Dream Room assesses measurement, scale, and a larger finished model.
  • The full route uses both. If your calendar forces a cut, make that decision for your class. If you skip Favorite Toy, model shape decomposition with one real object before students begin Dream Room.
  • Dream Room Day 1 and Day 2 are formative and do not change the final grade.
  • Xello Add Skills is unpublished. Test district access, then publish it when assigning the check-in.

Dream Room teacher resources

Dream Room Scale Deck
Whole-group PowerPoint Conversion Worksheet PDF
Print one per student Editable Worksheet
Teacher copy Dream Room Lesson Guide
Lesson notes and examples

3D MODELING • TEACHER GUIDE

Weeks 1 and 2: CAD Skill Ladder

The first three lessons deliberately reuse the same moves. Students draw a design, model it, then make a model that has to survive the rules of 3D printing.

Lesson 1: Design Your Own Currency

Learning piece: visual symbols, front/back communication, and the difference between a flat drawing and a 3D object.

Teacher move: project two real bills or coins. Ask what makes the value and identity readable before students draw. Leave the checklist on screen while they work.

Lesson 2: Intro to 3D Modeling

Learning piece: CAD represents width, depth, and height. The same design can be built up with solids or carved with Holes.

Teacher move: model one coin live. Stop after cylinder, resize, align, and Group. Students open the Coin Activity you created in your class or start a new 3D design.

Lesson 3: Intro to 3D Printing

Learning piece: a printer builds in layers. Flat bases, supported geometry, accurate diameter, and iteration determine whether the digital ring becomes a physical ring.

Teacher move: calculate one ring diameter with the class before opening Tinkercad. Show a failed print if you have one. A failure gives students something concrete to diagnose.

Queue boundary: students submit a PNG. They leave the model in your Tinkercad class for slicing. Do not promise a same-day print.

Point-of-use language support

Word bank: workplane, rotate, resize, align, Group, Hole, diameter, layer, overhang, slice, iterate

Complete stems: “I used ___ to change ___.” “My model may not print correctly because ___.” “The first change I would test is ___ because ___.”
