⬡ 3D Modeling • Lesson 3 ⬡

💍 3D PRINT A CUSTOM RING

Design it. Print it. Wear it.

⏱️ 1–2 periods
💻 Laptop
📏 Paper + Ruler (cm)
🖨️ 3D Printer

🧠 Vocab / Vocabulario

3D Printing – Turning a digital model into a real object by stacking layers of melted plastic / Convertir un modelo digital en un objeto real apilando capas de plástico derretido

Slice – Telling the printer how to build your object layer by layer / Indicarle a la impresora cómo construir tu objeto capa por capa

  • English
  • Español

📣 You built a 3D coin. Now design a custom ring in TinkerCAD – and 3D print it for real.

1

Watch: What is 3D Printing?

2

Watch: 3D Printing Best Practices

🚨 3 Rules for a Successful Print:

1️⃣ Flat base – your design needs a flat bottom

2️⃣ No overhangs – plastic can't float in mid-air!

3️⃣ Iterate – every failed print teaches you something

3

📏 Measure Your Finger

✂️ Cut a strip of paper. Wrap it around your finger. Mark where it meets.

📏 Measure the paper to the mark in centimeters (cm).

🔄 Multiply by 10 to convert to millimeters (mm). (Ex: 4.93 cm × 10 = 49.3 mm)

➗ Divide by 3.14 = your ring diameter. (Ex: 49.3 ÷ 3.14 = 15.7 mm)

4

Practice Ring Designs

👉 Log in: tinkercad.com/joinclass — ask your teacher for the class code.

📚 Open the "Ring" activity in our class, or go to Learn → "3D Print Your Own Ring" → complete all 3 lessons (basic, diamond, heart)

💡 After each practice ring: Ctrl+C to copy it before starting the next practice ring so you don't lose it.

5

💍 Design Your Custom Ring

Build your own ring from scratch. Follow these steps:

A. Drag a cylinder → make it a Hole → set width to your finger diameter

B. Add another cylinder for the outside → make it 4 mm larger than the hole

C. Select both → set depth to 4 mm

D. Click Group to combine them → now customize. Add shapes, text, patterns.

💡 Remember the 3 rules: flat base, no overhangs, and iterate.

6

📤 Export & Submit

PNG → "Send To" → Export as PNG → upload to this Canvas assignment

STL → Leave your design in TinkerCAD – your teacher will access it from the class dashboard to slice & print.

📣 Construiste una moneda 3D. Ahora diseña un anillo personalizado en TinkerCAD – y imprímelo en 3D de verdad.

1

Mira: ¿Qué es la impresión 3D?

2

Mira: Mejores prácticas para impresión 3D

🚨 3 Reglas para una impresión exitosa:

1️⃣ Base plana – tu diseño necesita un fondo plano

2️⃣ Sin voladizos – ¡el plástico no flota en el aire!

3️⃣ Itera – cada impresión fallida te enseña algo

3

📏 Mide tu dedo

✂️ Corta una tira de papel. Enróllala en tu dedo. Marca donde se junta.

📏 Mide el papel hasta la marca en centímetros (cm).

🔄 Multiplica por 10 para convertir a milímetros (mm). (Ej: 4.93 cm × 10 = 49.3 mm)

➗ Divide entre 3.14 = diámetro de tu anillo. (Ej: 49.3 ÷ 3.14 = 15.7 mm)

4

Practica diseños de anillos

👉 Inicia sesión: tinkercad.com/joinclass — pregúntale a tu maestro/a por el código de la clase.

📚 Abre la actividad "Ring" en nuestra clase, o ve a Learn → "3D Print Your Own Ring" → completa las 3 lecciones (básico, diamante, corazón)

💡 Después de cada anillo de práctica: Ctrl+C para copiarlo antes de empezar el siguiente anillo de práctica, para que no lo pierdas.

5

💍 Diseña tu anillo personalizado

Construye tu propio anillo desde cero. Sigue estos pasos:

A. Arrastra un cilindro → hazlo Hole → pon el ancho al diámetro de tu dedo

B. Agrega otro cilindro para el exterior → hazlo 4 mm más grande

C. Selecciona ambos → pon la profundidad en 4 mm

D. Haz clic en Group para combinarlos → ahora personaliza. Agrega formas, texto, patrones.

💡 Recuerda las 3 reglas: base plana, sin voladizos, e itera.

6

📤 Exporta y envía

PNG → "Send To" → Export as PNG → sube a esta tarea en Canvas

STL → Deja tu diseño en TinkerCAD – tu maestro/a lo verá desde el panel de la clase para cortarlo e imprimirlo.

7

💬 Reflexión

En los comentarios de tu envío, completa esta oración en 2-3 oraciones:

"Si mi anillo no se imprimiera correctamente, lo primero que revisaría es ___ porque..."

Banco de Palabras / Word Bank

base plana • voladizo • tamaño • capas • diámetro • soporte • iterar • cortar

⬆️ Sube de Nivel

¿Terminaste? Diseña un dije para collar. Sigue el tutorial "Create a Fancy Necklace".

✅ ¿Listo?

PNG subido + reflexión en comentarios = completo

3D MODELING • LESSON 4 TEACHER GUIDE

Favorite Toy: Break a Complex Object into Shapes

Run this after the ring and before Dream Room. The lesson gives students a controlled place to practice shape decomposition before they manage measurement, scale, and room construction at the same time.

What students learn

Construction means seeing a complex object as smaller forms. Students identify the boxes, cylinders, spheres, tubes, and cutouts inside a familiar toy, then rebuild and revise it in Tinkercad.

Two-period teacher flow

  1. Decompose and plan. Model one object with a photo. Trace or name the simple forms before touching Tinkercad.
  2. Build the silhouette. Students block in the largest forms first. Details wait.
  3. Partner check. Can a partner identify the object? Which form looks wrong or is missing?
  4. Revise and submit. Students improve one part, export a PNG, and name the change in their reflection.

Canvas setup

Create a Favorite Toy Activity inside your own Tinkercad class and test the student join route before class. The Canvas assignment is a 100-point Major project. Keep Dream Room after it: the two projects assess different skills. If you must cut Favorite Toy, model the decomposition step with one real object before students plan their rooms.

resource.body:
3D MODELING • TEACHER GUIDE

Dream Room: Five-Day Capstone

Students plan from real references, convert measurements, build at a consistent scale, test the model with another person, revise, and submit evidence from Tinkercad.

Five-day flow

  1. Day 1: Plan. Choose a room, collect five reference items, and record real dimensions.
  2. Day 2: Scale. Work one conversion row together. Students convert the room and three items by hand before using the calculator.
  3. Day 3: Build the room shell. Floor, walls, door, window, and the first large object.
  4. Day 4: Build and test. Add at least three recognizable items. A partner checks scale, navigation space, and whether the room reads as intended.
  5. Day 5: Revise and submit. Fix one issue from feedback, inspect print-readiness, export the PNG, and explain the revision in submission comments.

Teach scale before the worksheet

Use the scale deck for the whole-group mini-lesson. The arithmetic is not the point by itself. Students need to understand that every object must use the same scale or the room stops making visual sense.

Leave-up screen: use the deck's final Convert + Build slide while students work.

Teacher resources

Dream Room Scale Deck
Whole-group PowerPoint Conversion Worksheet PDF
Print one per student Editable Worksheet
Teacher copy Dream Room Lesson Guide
Lesson notes and examples

Success criteria for the 100-point Major grade

  • Plan and documentation: 15
  • Proportional models: 20
  • Conversion accuracy: 15
  • Consistent and appropriate scale: 15

Convert real-world measurements for TinkerCAD

  • English

📣 TinkerCAD uses millimeters, not feet or inches. Today you'll learn how to convert your real-world measurements so everything fits to scale.

1

Watch: How to Scale Your Room

2

The Conversion Process

3 steps to go from real life to TinkerCAD:

Step A: Feet → Meters

Multiply feet × 0.305

Ex: 31 ft × 0.305 = 9.5 m

Step B: Meters → Millimeters

Multiply meters × 1,000

Ex: 9.5 m × 1,000 = 9,500 mm

Step C: Scale down to 1:100

Divide mm ÷ 100

Ex: 9,500 mm ÷ 100 = 95 mm in TinkerCAD

👀 Full example: Room 31ft × 21ft × 8ft

Dimension × 0.305 × 1,000 ÷ 100 TinkerCAD
31 ft 9.5 m 9,500 mm 95 mm 95 mm
21 ft 6.4 m 6,400 mm 64 mm 64 mm
8 ft 2.4 m 2,400 mm 24 mm 24 mm

📋 Quick Reference

1 ft = 0.305 m   |   1 in = 0.0254 m   |   1 m = 1,000 mm   |   Scale: ÷ 100

items.title: Dream Room Days 3–5: Build, Test, Revise

resource.body:
THINGLINK | FACILITATOR GUIDE

Interactive Places and Branching Choices

One tool, two clear ideas: tags guide an audience through a place, and choices change the path through a story.

The two-week route

Week 4: Make a place interactive

Day 1 analyze and plan. Day 2 build the 2D map. Day 3 compare flat and 360 media. Days 4 and 5 build, test, and revise a 360 guide.

Week 5: Choices change the route

Day 1 Two-Door practice. Day 2 story map. Days 3 and 4 build. Day 5 test every path, revise, and publish.

Before students sign in

  1. Create a ThingLink group for this class. Share the group invite code or use the district single sign-on route. Do not ask students to make unmanaged personal accounts.
  2. Test the student sign-in on a student device. Keep every scene for this unit in the same student account.
  3. Confirm that your ThingLink license can share Scenario Builder projects. K-12 sharing requires an Enhanced or Staff Training license. Essential and Individual Teacher accounts cannot share scenarios. If sharing is unavailable, use the linked-scene fallback in the Branching Narratives guide.
  4. Choose the 360 media route: ThingLink library, teacher-provided 360 JPEGs, or small groups using a charged 360 camera. Do not promise a camera route until file transfer has been tested.

Teacher resources

Interactive Place Map

Use the lesson guide and optional whole-group deck for the 2D map days. The student assignment remains the accessible and absence route.

360 Guide

Use the lesson guide for media preparation, 360 specifications, camera/library choices, and the partner accessibility check.

Branching Narratives

Use the lesson guide for Two-Door, the story-map gate, Scenario Builder, the linked-scene fallback, and the final rubric.

Current platform checks

  • 360 image: JPEG, 2:1 aspect ratio, and no larger than 8192 by 4096 pixels.
  • Accessible tags: descriptive titles, meaningful alt text, captions or transcripts for media, high-contrast icons, and a logical tag sequence.
  • Sharing: test the exact audience link in a signed-out or Student View window before students submit.
  • Edpuzzle: optional teacher-connected route only. The student page defaults to the original YouTube video.

Grading map

Minor

Interactive Place Map: 5 points
360 Guide: 5 points

Formative

VR overview, Two-Door, and Story Map: 0 points and omitted from the final grade

Major

Branching Narrative: 100 points with an attached Canvas rubric

Optional swap-ins

Planet Planning, the earlier Storyboard, and Planet Branching are available in Enrichment · Parked Alternates. Use one only if you want to replace the Week 5 project with a longer planning route.

Official setup and accessibility

ThingLink groupsAdd users with invite codes360 upload specificationsCreate accessible contentScenario Builder overview

WEEK 4 | LESSON GUIDE

Welcome Mission

Teach how background images and purposeful tags guide an audience, then have students build and test one interactive map for a first-time visitor.

Lesson at a glance

Students choose one first-time visitor and guide that person through three stops: arrive, find, and get help or continue. The map begins as a flat image, then gains tags that reveal information when the visitor needs it.

Day 1
Analyze real maps, choose a mission, and plan the background plus three tags.
Day 2
Build in ThingLink, test with a fresh viewer, revise one moment, and submit the link.
Suggested grade
5-point Minor check for a complete, working, audience-tested link.

Before students open ThingLink

  1. Confirm that students can create inside the district ThingLink group or class. Opening a public example does not prove that student creation access is ready.
  2. Choose the sharing route students will use. Test it in Student View or in a browser where you are not signed in as the creator.
  3. Open the teacher deck, class example, tutorial, and one new blank image project.
  4. Prepare approved background options for students who should not photograph or map a real space.
  5. Set the privacy boundary before students collect media. Use public, composite, fictional, or teacher-approved places.

Do not ask students to create personal teacher classes. Use the access route supplied by your school or district.

Day 1: Teach, analyze, plan

  1. Start with the visitor. Ask students to remember a first visit when they did not know where to go. What information would have helped?
  2. Compare real maps. Use the park, museum, and transit maps in the deck. Name each audience and the job each map performs.
  3. Teach background plus tag. The background gives the big picture. A tag supplies one detail, choice, source, or next step at the point where the visitor needs it.
  4. Open the class example. Let students predict what a tag will reveal from its placement and title before opening it.
  5. Assign the mission constraint. One visitor, one mission, and three stops: arrive, find, and get help or continue.
  6. Conference on purpose. Approve the visitor and mission before students collect media or build tags.

Teacher model: A fictional new maker enters a composite lab, finds the tool area, and locates cleanup or help. Use no real door codes, schedules, or restricted-room details.

Day 2: Model, build, test

  1. Model one tag from start to preview. Narrate the design decision: placement, title, information format, source credit, and accessibility.
  2. Keep the production target small. One readable background and at least three purposeful tags are enough for this first build.
  3. Check accessibility at the point of use. Students add background alt text, alt text for meaningful images, captions or a transcript for audio and video, concise titles, and a logical tag order.
  4. Use a no-coaching viewer test. The partner tries to arrive, find the destination, and get help or continue. The creator watches without explaining.
  5. Require one revision. Students fix one hesitation, unclear title, blocked path, broken link, or missing source.
  6. Submit the audience link. Students use the share setting you assigned, test the link, and submit it in Canvas.

What to look for

  • The same named visitor and mission guide every design choice.
  • The map includes arrive, find, and get help or continue.
  • Tag titles tell the visitor what they found. “Click here” does not count as a descriptive title.
  • Text, media, or links add useful information instead of repeating the background.
  • Sources and accessible alternatives are present.
  • The final link opens for the intended viewer, not only for the creator.

Suggested 5-point Minor check:

  1. Visitor and mission are clear.
  2. Background and all three stops guide the route.
  3. Tags are useful, credited, and accessible.
  4. Partner testing leads to one revision.
  5. The submitted viewer link works.

If creation access is not ready

Do not send students to make unsupported personal accounts. Keep the learning target and run the planning and viewer-test work while you resolve access.

  • Students finish the background and three-tag plan.
  • Build one class scene together and let teams propose tag placement, titles, media, and next steps.
  • Use the completed plan as the bridge into the individual build when access is restored.

Teacher resources

The deck teaches the whole sequence for projection. The student Canvas page is the independent and absence route.

Download the teacher deck Open the class example ThingLink image guide ThingLink accessibility guide K-12 access FAQ

WEEK 4 | DAYS 1 AND 2

Welcome Mission

Build an interactive map that helps a first-time visitor arrive, find what they came for, and know what to do next.

Your mission

Choose one visitor and one mission. Your map should guide that visitor through three required stops.

1. ARRIVE

Where does the visitor begin? What do they need to notice first?

2. FIND

What did the visitor come to find, use, or understand?

3. GET HELP OR CONTINUE

Where can the visitor ask for help, finish the task, or take the next step?

Choose a mission card

New maker

Help someone check in, find a tool or material, and locate cleanup or help.

New teammate

Help someone find the meeting spot, shared resource, and place to ask or submit.

First-time visitor

Help someone enter a public place, reach one destination, and find help or the exit.

Teacher-approved mission

Choose another place with a clear first-time visitor and a useful three-stop route.

Day 1: Plan the visit

  1. Name the visitor and what they came to do.
  2. Sketch or choose a safe, teacher-approved background image.
  3. Mark the three required stops: arrive, find, and get help or continue.
  4. Plan a short tag title and useful information for each stop.
  5. List the source for any photo, video, audio, or outside information you plan to use.

Planning stem: My map helps a first-time ___ complete ___.

Word bank: visitor · audience · arrive · destination · landmark · route · help · next step

Day 2: Build, test, revise

  1. Open ThingLink through the group or class route your teacher gives you.
  2. Upload your background image. Add at least three purposeful tags.
  3. Use descriptive tag titles. Name the stop or action instead of writing “Click here.”
  4. Add useful text, media, or a link. Credit media and information you did not create.
  5. Ask a partner to complete the visit without coaching. Revise one confusing moment.
  6. Use the share setting your teacher assigns. Test the viewer link, then submit it in Canvas.

Feedback stem: I expected to ___, but I got stuck when ___.

Revision stem: I changed ___ so the visitor can ___.

Privacy boundary

Use a public, composite, fictional, or teacher-approved place. Leave out information that should not be shared.

  • No door codes, private schedules, restricted areas, or security details
  • No identifiable student photos, video, or audio without documented permission
  • Do not make the project public unless your teacher tells you to use a public share setting

Success criteria

  • One named first-time visitor and one mission
  • Three required stops: arrive, find, and get help or continue
  • A readable background and at least three purposeful tags
  • Descriptive tag titles, working media or links, and source credit
  • Alt text for the background and meaningful images, plus captions or a transcript for audio and video
  • One revision based on a partner test
  • A working viewer link submitted in Canvas

Open the tools

Use your teacher’s group or class route when you are ready to create.

Open ThingLink Explore a class example

Video not loading? Open the official ThingLink tutorial on YouTube.

WEEK 4 | DAY 3

From Flat Map to 360 Preview

A flat image controls the frame. A 360 image lets the viewer choose where to look. Today you decide when that extra control actually helps.

Watch and notice

Video not loading? Open the original video.

Flat photo or 360 scene?

Flat photo

The creator chooses the frame. The viewer sees one direction.

360 scene

The viewer looks around the full environment and chooses where to focus.

Connect it to your Welcome Mission

Reopen your flat map. Choose one stop where a first-time visitor would understand more if they could look around the space. That stop becomes your 360 preview.

Sentence stem: A 360 preview would help my visitor ___ at ___ because ___ is outside the flat frame.

Word bank: arrive · find · notice · understand · avoid · access · surroundings

WEEK 4 | TEACHER GUIDE

Preview the Unfamiliar Stop

Move from looking at a place to looking around one important stop. The same first-time visitor still comes first.

What students learn

A flat image controls what the viewer sees. A 360 image lets the viewer choose where to look. Students use that difference on purpose: they reopen their Welcome Mission and build a closer preview of one stop where a first-time visitor needs to look around.

Day 3: Learn and choose media

  1. Use the embedded Mashable video. Edpuzzle is an optional teacher-connected alternative.
  2. Compare a flat photo with a 360 scene. Ask what the viewer can see or control in each.
  3. Students reopen their Welcome Mission and choose one unfamiliar or important stop that deserves a closer look.
  4. Students select a ThingLink library image, a teacher-provided image, or a teacher-approved camera route. If the class skipped Welcome Mission, assign a shared visitor and place first.

Optional Edpuzzle setup

The Canvas assignment defaults to the embedded Mashable video so it works after a course copy. If you want questions, grading, or Live Mode, reconnect Edpuzzle in your own course:

  1. Open the reusable Edpuzzle lesson and copy it to My Content.
  2. In Canvas, edit the Day 3 assignment. Change Submission Type to External Tool, choose Find, select Edpuzzle, and pick your copied lesson.
  3. Save the assignment unpublished, then test it in Student View before assigning it.
Open reusable Edpuzzle lessonCanvas setup guide

Days 4 and 5: Build, test, revise

  1. Students build six tag jobs: Arrive, Find, Know, Do, Help, and Access or Avoid. Each tag needs a descriptive title and useful content.
  2. Require alt text for images and captions or a short transcript for audio/video.
  3. Partners test tag order, contrast, labels, and the audience share link.
  4. Students revise one weak tag or navigation choice and name that revision in the Canvas comment.

360 media preflight

Format

JPEG with a 2:1 aspect ratio

Dimensions

Up to 8192 by 4096 pixels

Fallback

ThingLink library or teacher-provided files if cameras or transfers fail

Projection support

Teach Slides 1 through 12. Slides 1 through 5 teach when a 360 image helps. Slides 6 through 10 reconnect the Welcome Mission, define the visitor need, teach the six tag jobs, and model the 360 file and tag requirements. Slides 11 and 12 move students into building and partner testing. Leave Slide 13 projected during work time on Days 4 and 5. The Canvas assignment remains the accessible and absence route.

Download teacher deck

WEEK 4 | DAYS 4 AND 5

Preview the Unfamiliar Stop

Help the same first-time visitor look around one important stop and know what to do next.

Choose the stop to preview

Continue Welcome Mission

Use the same place and first-time visitor. Choose one stop that is important, unfamiliar, or easy to misunderstand.

Camera route

Use a teacher-approved 360 camera and location. Get permission before photographing people or spaces.

Library route

Use the ThingLink 360 library or an image your teacher provides. The visitor goal stays the same.

Build

  1. Open ThingLink through your class route and choose or upload one 360 JPEG.
  2. Name the visitor, the stop, and what the visitor needs there.
  3. Add six purposeful tag jobs: Arrive, Find, Know, Do, Help, and Access or Avoid. Give each tag a descriptive title.
  4. Add alt text to images. Add captions or a short transcript when a tag uses audio or video.
  5. Put the tags in a logical sequence and choose icons that stand out against the background.

Sentence stem: This tag helps ___ understand ___ by ___.

Word bank: audience · label · describe · navigate · notice · image · audio · video

Partner test and revision

  1. Send the audience link to a partner.
  2. Your partner checks: labels, contrast, tag order, media access, and whether the guide makes sense without you explaining it.
  3. Revise at least one weak tag or navigation choice.
  4. Submit the working ThingLink link. In a Canvas comment, write what you changed after testing.

Success criteria

  • The same named visitor and purpose from Welcome Mission
  • One working 360 scene
  • Six tag jobs: Arrive, Find, Know, Do, Help, and Access or Avoid
  • Alt text and captions or transcripts where needed
  • A logical tag sequence and readable icon contrast
  • One partner-tested revision
  • A working audience share link plus revision comment

Tool help

Open ThingLink 360 library

Video not loading? Open it on YouTube.

WEEK 5 | TEACHER GUIDE

Visitor Decisions

Students should feel the cause and effect: a visitor's choice changes the route, and the route changes the outcome.

The five-day route

  1. Day 1: Two-Door Challenge. Build one start, two choices, and two different outcomes.
  2. Day 2: Story Map. Approve the full route before students build.
  3. Days 3 and 4: Build at least four scenes, two decision points, and two endings.
  4. Day 5: A partner tests every route. The creator repairs one broken or confusing point, then publishes.

Project choices

Default: Visitor Decisions

The same first-time visitor makes orientation, safety, access, or service choices inside the place. Each choice changes the next step or outcome.

Optional creative route

An escape room or another teacher-approved scenario may use the same four-scene, two-decision structure.

Scenario Builder and fallback

Scenario Builder uses branching blocks to send viewers down different paths. If your license cannot share scenarios, students can meet the same target with four regular ThingLink scenes. Scene 1 is the start and first decision. One choice goes to Scene 2, a second decision; the other goes to Scene 4, an ending. Scene 2 sends viewers to Scene 3 or Scene 4, the two endings. Grade the same plan, choices, navigation, audience access, and revision.

Branching block guide

Leave-up checks

Story map

Every box has a title, what happens, choices, and arrows to the next scene.

Build

Start + 2 decision points + 2 endings. No dead ends unless the dead end is an intentional ending.

Test

Open every path. Record one confusing or broken point. Revise it before submitting.

Projection support

Teach Slides 14 through 23. Slides 14 through 16 teach cause, choice, and consequence. Slide 17 runs the Two-Door practice. Slide 18 models a complete visitor route. Slide 19 is the story-map approval screen. Slides 20 and 21 establish the default project and the Scenario Builder or linked-scene fallback. Slides 22 and 23 guide building and testing. Leave Slide 24 projected during build time. Use Slide 25 before submission and Slide 26 for the exit check.

Download teacher deck

WEEK 5 | DAY 1 | FORMATIVE

Two-Door Challenge

Build the smallest possible branching story, then prove that both choices work.

The learning piece

Cause: the viewer chooses a door. Effect: that choice sends the viewer to a different outcome. If both doors lead to the same result, the choice is not meaningful.

Build three scenes

1. Start

A locked room with Door A and Door B. Each door links somewhere different.

2. Outcome A

Show what happens after Door A. Make the result clear.

3. Outcome B

Show a different result after Door B.

Build and test

  1. Create the three images or scenes.
  2. Add two choices to the start scene.
  3. Link Door A to Outcome A and Door B to Outcome B.
  4. Open the viewer and test both paths.
  5. Submit the share links or screenshots your teacher requests.

Sentence stem: Door ___ changes the outcome because ___.

Word bank: choice · cause · effect · route · outcome · link · test

Success criteria

  • One start scene and two different outcome scenes
  • Two clearly labeled choices
  • Each choice opens the correct outcome
  • Both routes tested
  • One cause-and-effect reflection

WEEK 5 | DAY 2 | PLANNING GATE

Map the Visitor's Choices

A branching project is easier to repair on paper than after every scene has been built.

Choose the decisions

Default: Visitor Decisions

Continue the same place and visitor. Build orientation, safety, access, or service choices that change the visitor's next step or outcome.

Optional creative route

An escape room or another teacher-approved scenario may use the same required structure.

Map before you build

Draw every scene as a box. Draw every choice as an arrow. Your teacher should be able to trace both endings without guessing.

Inside every box

Scene title
What happens
Media you need

Beside every arrow

Choice label
Where it leads
Why the outcome changes

Required route

  • At least four scenes
  • At least two decision points
  • At least two different endings
  • One planned 360 scene
  • No accidental dead ends

Sentence stem: If the viewer chooses ___, then ___ happens because ___.

Word bank: start · choice · branch · scene · ending · cause · effect

Submit for approval

  1. Upload a clear photo or screenshot of the complete story map.
  2. In a Canvas comment, answer: Which choice changes the experience the most, and why?
  3. Wait for teacher approval before building the final project.

WEEK 5 | DAYS 3 TO 5 | MAJOR

Build the Visitor's Decision Path

Your visitor should feel that every choice matters and every route works.

Build from your approved map

  1. Create the start scene, decision points, and both endings.
  2. Add at least one 360 scene.
  3. Use clear choice labels that tell the viewer what they are deciding.
  4. Connect every branch. Intentional endings are fine; accidental dead ends are not.
  5. Add alt text, captions or transcripts, and a logical navigation order.

Minimum project route

Structure

4+ scenes · 2+ decision points · 2 endings

Media

At least one 360 scene and readable interactive content

Audience

Working share link that opens for the intended viewer

Test every path

  1. Give the audience link to a partner.
  2. Your partner follows every branch and records one broken, confusing, or inaccessible point.
  3. Repair at least one point and test the route again.
  4. Publish and submit the working ThingLink link.
  5. In a Canvas comment, answer both reflection questions below.

Sentence stem: One choice changes the experience by ___. After feedback, I changed ___ because ___.

Word bank: branch · consequence · route · ending · label · navigation · accessible · revise

100-point rubric

Plan and story structure · 20

The finished route matches the approved map and reaches two endings.

Choice and consequence · 20

Choices lead to meaningfully different outcomes.

Technical navigation · 20

Links work, the 360 scene opens, and there are no accidental dead ends.

Audience and accessibility · 20

Labels, contrast, alt text, captions, and sharing work for the intended audience.

Testing and revision · 20

A partner tested every route and the creator documented one revision.

Need help?

Video not loading? Open it on YouTube.

rubric.long_description: The finished project follows the approved story map with at least four scenes, two decision points, two endings, and one planned 360 scene.

ratings.long_description: The approved plan is fully visible in a complete route with every required scene, decision point, ending, and the planned 360 scene.
The route follows the plan, but one required structural part needs a small correction or clearer connection.
Several required scenes, decisions, endings, or the planned 360 scene are missing or disconnected from the plan.
There is not enough plan or story structure evidence to score.

rubric.long_description: Each decision changes what the audience sees or what happens next.

ratings.long_description: Every decision leads to a meaningfully different consequence that the audience can recognize.
The choices lead to different routes, but one consequence needs to feel more distinct or clear.
Multiple choices lead to nearly the same result or do not clearly change the experience.
There is not enough choice-and-consequence evidence to score.

rubric.long_description: All links work, the 360 scene opens, and there are no accidental dead ends.

ratings.long_description: Every branch works, the 360 scene opens, and all endings are intentional.
The full route mostly works, but one link, scene, or ending needs a small repair.
Several links fail, the 360 scene is missing, or accidental dead ends interrupt the route.
There is not enough working navigation evidence to score.

rubric.long_description: Choice labels are clear, contrast is readable, alt text or captions are present where needed, and the share link opens for the intended audience.

ratings.long_description: Labels, contrast, media access, navigation order, and the audience link all support the intended viewer.
The project is usable, but one accessibility or audience-access detail needs correction.
Multiple labels, contrast choices, media descriptions, or sharing settings block the intended audience.
There is not enough audience or accessibility evidence to score.

rubric.long_description: A partner tests every route and the creator documents one specific repair or revision.

ratings.long_description: A partner tested every route and the creator clearly documented and completed a useful revision.
Testing and a revision are present, but the evidence or explanation needs one small clarification.
Testing is incomplete, or the documented revision does not address the partner feedback.
There is not enough testing or revision evidence to score.

• Planet Design & Examples
  • Materials & Instructions
  • Submission Guidelines

Planet Design & Examples 🌌

Design your home planet. Below are some examples.


Your planet can be anything from a water world to a desert oasis. Remember, the sky's not the limit here!

Materials & Instructions 🎨

Materials Needed:
- A piece of paper 📄
- A pen or pencil ✏️
- A laptop or tablet 💻
- Your imagination! 🧠

 

You can draw your planet on paper, create a 2D design in Vectr or Canva, or make a 3D model in TinkerCAD

Steps to Create Your Home Planet:
1. Name Your Planet: Think of a creative name for your planet, like 'Vilta', 'Waterworld', or 'SandLand'.
2. Describe Your Planet: Imagine the landscapes and environments. Are there towering mountains, vast oceans, bustling cities, or mysterious forests? Write these details down.
3. Describe the Inhabitants: Who lives on your planet? What do they look like? How do they spend their days? Think about their appearance, behaviors, diet, and hobbies.
4. Create a Visual Representation: Draw or digitally design your planet. Show the features you described. Use colors and symbols that fit your planet's atmosphere and culture.

Submission Guidelines 📤

How to turn it in:
- If you've created your planet digitally, export it as a JPG and submit it here.
- If you've drawn on paper, snap a clear photo with your webcam and upload it.
- Make sure your artwork is clearly visible.
- Keep your design handy. You will map its story in Activity 2.

• Storyboard Planning
  • Branching Story & Example
  • Submission

🌌 Storyboard Planning 🌌

You designed a planet in Activity 1. Now plan its story on paper: map the journey and every choice your readers will make.

🗺 Creating a Story Map 🗺

A story map shows every choice a reader can make. Here are two examples:

You need to plan out at least two sets of choices for your reader to make. 

📖 What is a Branching Story? 📖

In a branching story, the reader's choices change what happens next.

🌐 Example from Filos's Planet 🌐

Read our mascot Filos's story on Inklewriter and watch how each choice changes it.

Read Filos's Story

📤 Submission Guidelines 📤

After completing your storyboard, submit it here. Share a photo or a digital copy. Make sure the writing is easy to read. Keep it handy. You will build this story in ThingLink Scenario Builder in Activity 3.

🌌 Design Your Home Planet Story 🌌

Interactive Narrative Project Using ThingLink

  • English
  • Español

Activity Overview

Imagine you are an alien from another planet visiting Earth for the first time! Create an interactive story using ThingLink Scenario Builder to describe your home planet, its landscape, and its inhabitants.

Build from the planet you designed in Activity 1 and the story map you drew in Activity 2.

🚀 Getting Started

Watch the tutorial video to learn how to build your interactive story in ThingLink Scenario Builder.

📚 Review Example Story:

Look at this example before you plan your own.

🎥 Tutorial Video:

Learn how to create your story using ThingLink Scenario Builder

💡 Tip: Sign in to ThingLink with your school Google account, the same way you did in Lesson 2. Save your work as you go.

📜 Creating Your Story

Now build the story of your home planet in ThingLink Scenario Builder. The requirements are below.

Story Requirements:
  • ✓ Give your home planet a creative name
  • ✓ Describe your planet's landscape (terrain, climate, features)
  • ✓ Describe the planet's inhabitants (appearance, culture, lifestyle)
  • ✓ Include at least 2 images or 360° scenes
  • ✓ Create at least 2 decision points where readers make choices
  • ✓ Each choice should lead to a different outcome or scene
💭 Story Ideas:

• A tour of your planet's most important locations
• Meeting different types of inhabitants
• Exploring dangerous vs. safe areas
• Discovering your planet's unique resources
• Experiencing a typical day on your planet

📤 Submission Guidelines

When your ThingLink story is complete, submit the share link through Canvas.

How to Get Your ThingLink Share Link:
  1. Open your completed ThingLink project
  2. Click the "Share" button in the top right
  3. Copy the public share link
  4. Paste the link into the Canvas submission box
🎬 Need Help Submitting?

Watch this tutorial on how to submit assignments in Canvas:

🌟 Be creative and have fun designing your alien home planet. 🌟

Descripción de la Actividad

¡Imagina que eres un extraterrestre de otro planeta visitando la Tierra por primera vez! Crea una historia interactiva usando ThingLink Scenario Builder para describir tu planeta natal, su paisaje y sus habitantes.

Parte del planeta que diseñaste en la Actividad 1 y del mapa de historia que dibujaste en la Actividad 2.

🚀 Comenzando

Mira el video tutorial para aprender a crear tu historia interactiva en ThingLink Scenario Builder.

📚 Revisa el Ejemplo de Historia:

Mira este ejemplo antes de planear la tuya.

🎥 Video Tutorial:

Aprende a crear tu historia usando ThingLink Scenario Builder

💡 Consejo: Inicia sesión en ThingLink con tu cuenta de Google escolar, igual que en la Lección 2. Guarda tu trabajo mientras avanzas.

📜 Creando Tu Historia

Ahora construye la historia de tu planeta natal en ThingLink Scenario Builder. Los requisitos están abajo.

Requisitos de la Historia:
  • ✓ Dale a tu planeta natal un nombre creativo
  • ✓ Describe el paisaje de tu planeta (terreno, clima, características)
  • ✓ Describe los habitantes del planeta (apariencia, cultura, estilo de vida)
  • ✓ Incluye al menos 2 imágenes o escenas 360°
  • ✓ Crea al menos 2 puntos de decisión donde los lectores tomen decisiones
  • ✓ Cada elección debe llevar a un resultado o escena diferente
💭 Ideas para la Historia:

• Un recorrido por los lugares más importantes de tu planeta
• Conocer diferentes tipos de habitantes
• Explorar áreas peligrosas vs. seguras
• Descubrir los recursos únicos de tu planeta
• Experimentar un día típico en tu planeta

📤 Pautas de Entrega

Cuando tu historia de ThingLink esté completa, envía el enlace para compartir a través de Canvas.

Cómo Obtener Tu Enlace de ThingLink:
  1. Abre tu proyecto ThingLink completado
  2. Haz clic en el botón "Compartir" en la parte superior derecha
  3. Copia el enlace público para compartir
  4. Pega el enlace en el cuadro de envío de Canvas
🎬 ¿Necesitas Ayuda para Enviar?

Mira este tutorial sobre cómo enviar tareas en Canvas:

🌟 Sé creativo y diviértete diseñando tu planeta natal alienígena. 🌟

Teacher-only guide. Keep this page unpublished and hidden from students.
Teacher guide · Optional/Flex

Career + Communication Flex Menu

Choose the communication or career project that solves a real scheduling or classroom need.

How this module works: Choose the piece that fills a real gap in your calendar or classroom. Email Etiquette and Vision Board each stand alone. Career Fair is the full project route. You do not need to assign all three.

Three ways to use this module

Option 1 · Email Etiquette

1 to 2 periods.
Teach how a useful school email works, repair weak messages together, then have students draft or send one email for a real school need.

Option 2 · Vision Board

1 to 2 periods.
Students connect who they are now to one direction they want to explore. The privacy boundary is part of the lesson: students choose what they are comfortable sharing.

Extended option · Career Fair

7 to 10 periods, plus the Expo.
Students research one career, build a public information page, design a booth system, and explain the work to real visitors.

Option 1 · Email Etiquette

Students learn: how subject, greeting, context, request, tone, closing, and recipient checks make an email easier to answer.

Demonstration of learning: students repair four weak messages and write one useful email connected to an actual school need.

Whole-group route
  1. Use slides 1 through 28 of the Lucero deck to teach the six parts, read the room, and model one repair.
  2. Students complete the practice sheet. Stop after the first two repairs and compare what changed.
  3. Decide whether students will send the final email or submit a draft. Do not make students send a message to a real person without naming the approved recipient first.

Deck note: Slides 29 through 31 contain the older favorite-activity assignment. Skip those slides and use the current Canvas task and practice sheet instead. Slide 32 is an optional final review.

Open teacher deck Practice PDF Editable DOCX

Watch for: a subject line that says only “Hello,” requests that cannot be answered, all-caps urgency, missing context, and students sending before checking the recipient or attachment.

Option 2 · Vision Board

Students learn: how words, images, color, and layout can make a connection between a present identity and a future direction visible.

Demonstration of learning: a paper or digital board with three words, three images, one present-to-future connection, and a short explanation of one choice.

Whole-group route
  1. Play the short Lucero introduction and talk through one example of an image carrying meaning.
  2. Students plan before collecting images. The brainstorm sheet prevents “random collage” from becoming the entire task.
  3. Use paper, Google Slides, or Canva. Students leave out private contact information, passwords, and anything they do not want displayed.
Brainstorm PDF Editable DOCX

Extended option · Career Fair

The project has one audience and one job: help a visitor understand what a career is actually like and whether it may be worth exploring. The five steps are meant to stay together. If you remove a deliverable, revise the points and rubric before students begin.

1 · Choose

Shortlist three careers, use a fit check, and commit to one. 10 points.

2 · Research

Collect current evidence about tasks, work setting, training, pay, outlook, and one honest challenge. 10 points.

3 · Explain

Build one public information page that a visitor can understand without the presenter standing beside it. 10 points.

4 · Invite

Design a readable poster and matching take-away handout for the booth. 10 points.

5 · Present

Run the booth, give the pitch, answer questions, and participate as a visitor. 60 points.

Career Fair teacher guide

Setup before you publish

  • Email: test student email access and decide the approved recipient and send-or-draft rule.
  • Vision Board: choose paper or digital formats, test the video, and establish the privacy boundary before students collect images.
  • Career Fair: test Xello if you plan to use it, check Google Sites and Canva sharing, arrange printing, reserve booth space, and decide who the visitors will be.
  • Before using an integration: reconnect the Edpuzzle or Google activity in your course, then test it in Student View.

Additional options

To College or Not To College, Defining College and Career Readiness, and the older CCR survey are available as unpublished options. Use one when it fits your class. For the video activity, connect the public Edpuzzle lesson or play the original video without the integration.

Option · Communication practice

Email Etiquette

Make the message easy to understand, easy to answer, and respectful of the reader's time.

Objective: Write an email that gives the reader enough context and one request they can answer.
Demonstration of learning: Repair four messages, then draft or send one useful school email.

What makes an email useful?

A teacher should not have to guess who you are, what happened, or what you need. A useful school email has six parts:

1 · Subject

Names the topic.

2 · Greeting

Names the reader.

3 · Context

Explains what happened.

4 · Request

Asks for an answerable next step.

5 · Thanks

Closes respectfully.

6 · Your name

Tells the reader who sent it.

Your task

  1. Download the practice sheet.
  2. Repair all four weak messages. Keep the real problem; change the wording that makes the message hard to answer.
  3. Choose one real school need: ask for help, explain an absence, follow up on missing work, or thank someone.
  4. Draft the email. Your teacher will tell you the approved recipient and whether you are sending it or submitting the draft.

Download practice PDFOpen editable DOCX

Before you send: Check the recipient, subject, attachment, and tone. Do not include a password or private information the reader does not need.

Success check

  • The subject names the topic.
  • The first sentence gives enough context.
  • The request can be answered.
  • The tone is respectful and sounds like you.
  • You checked the recipient and attachment before sending.
Sentence support: I am writing because _____. Could you please _____? Thank you for _____.

Option · Self-reflection

Vision Board

Plan the ideas first. Then choose the words and images that make those ideas visible.

Objective: Use words, images, color, and layout to connect who you are now to one direction you want to explore.
Demonstration of learning: Create a board with three words, three images, one present-to-future connection, and a short explanation of one choice.

Open the Vision Board video in a new tab

Plan before you collect images

  1. Use the brainstorm sheet to name interests, strengths, values, a proud moment, a learning goal, and one skill you want to grow.
  2. Choose three words and three images that carry those ideas. Do not collect images merely because they look good together.
  3. Build on paper, poster board, Google Slides, or Canva, using the format your teacher approves.
  4. Write the reflection: One choice that matters on my board is _____ because _____.

Download brainstorm PDFOpen editable DOCX

Privacy boundary: Leave out contact information, passwords, exact addresses, and anything you do not want displayed. A meaningful board does not require a public version of your whole life.

Success check

  • The board includes text and images.
  • The layout shows what matters most.
  • At least one choice connects who you are now to where you want to go.
  • You can explain why you chose one image, word, or color.
Word bank: curious · dependable · creative · patient · resourceful · determined · connected · independent · helpful · growing

Teacher-only guide. Keep this page unpublished and hidden from students.
Teacher guide · Extended option

Career Fair Project

Five connected steps that turn career research into a public explanation.

Core route: Plan for 7 to 10 class periods plus the Expo. This is a complete project, not five unrelated technology assignments. Research feeds the website, the website feeds the booth, and the booth gives the work a real audience.

Purpose and learning progression

Students are not pretending to choose a permanent future. They are learning how to investigate one possibility, separate current evidence from guesses, design information for a visitor, and explain that information out loud.

Research

Read career profiles, compare current sources, label pay and outlook with a source and year, and name one realistic training route.

Visual communication

Turn the research into a one-page site, poster, and handout that share a hierarchy and can be understood quickly.

Public explanation

Give a short pitch, answer questions honestly, and say where you would look when you do not know an answer.

Suggested pacing

StepStudent workSuggested timeDo not move on until
1 · ChooseThree-career shortlist and one commitment1 periodThe student can explain why the choice fits.
2 · ResearchResearch organizer and source log1 to 2 periodsEvery published fact has a source.
3 · ExplainOne public information page1 to 2 periodsThe link opens for another viewer.
4 · InvitePoster and matching handout1 to 2 periodsThe headline reads from six feet away.
5 · PresentBooth, pitch, questions, visitor round1 practice + ExpoThe student can pitch without reading the poster.

Teacher resources

Project walkthrough deckFull research deck

Website examplesPromotional-material examples

Research organizer PDFEditable organizer DOCX

How to use the decks
  • Project walkthrough: use slide 2 for the complete project map, then slides 6, 9, 12, 15, and 16 when each step begins. This is the default whole-group route.
  • Full research deck: use it as an optional planning and discussion bank. It was built for a longer CCR course, so do not teach it straight through in this flex unit.
  • Website and promotional examples: use them for critique and comparison. The current Canvas directions and rubric control the assignment if an older example shows a different requirement.

Materials and preparation

  • Career research access: Xello if available, plus the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook and CareerOneStop.
  • A website route: Google Sites or Canva, with sharing tested from an account that does not own the file.
  • A poster and handout route: digital export or physical materials, plus a printing plan.
  • Expo space, tables, visitor rotation, and a plan for students who use AAC, recorded delivery, or another teacher-approved communication route.

Formative checkpoints and likely misconceptions

  • “A high salary means it fits me.” Send students back to tasks, work setting, training, and one honest challenge.
  • “The first Google result is enough.” Require a source title, organization, URL, and checked date before the fact enters the site.
  • “The poster should contain the whole research paper.” Test it from six feet away. The site holds detail; the poster earns attention.
  • “Professional means pretending to know.” Teach the line: “I do not know yet. I would check…”

Grading and trim points

The full project remains 100 points: Steps 1 through 4 are 10 points each; the Expo is 60 points. The Expo rubric has four 15-point criteria: Content Accuracy, Visual Communication, Delivery, and Professionalism.

If time is tight: Preselect a smaller career pool, provide one common site layout, or shorten the visitor rotation. Do not quietly remove the poster, handout, or live explanation while keeping the same rubric. Change the rubric first if the demonstration of learning changes.

Optional setup · Career Fair

Build a Career Starting Pool in Xello

Use clusters and saved careers to narrow the field before Step 1.

Objective: Use career clusters and career profiles to build a focused starting pool for the Career Fair.
Demonstration of learning: Save at least one cluster and three careers, then submit screenshots and one explanation.
Access check: Use this option only if your district provides Xello and your teacher has tested the route. If Xello is unavailable, use CareerOneStop and the BLS Occupation Finder in Career Fair Step 1.

In Xello

  1. Open Xello through your district sign-in route.
  2. Review career clusters and save at least one that genuinely interests you.
  3. Open career profiles and save three careers you would be willing to investigate further.
  4. Complete the investigation or reflection prompts Xello presents when you save a career.
  5. Take one screenshot of the saved cluster and one screenshot of the three saved careers.
Reflection stem: I saved the _____ cluster. One career in it that I want to investigate is _____ because _____.

Submit

Upload both screenshots. Put the reflection sentence in the submission comments.

No Xello? Explore with CareerOneStopBLS Occupation Finder

resource.body:
Extended option · Career Fair

Build a Career Fair Experience

Research one career, design for a visitor, and explain what you found.

Topic: Career research for a public audience
Objective: Investigate one career and turn current evidence into a website, booth system, and live explanation.
Demonstration of learning: A visitor leaves your booth able to explain what the career does, how someone enters it, and one reason it may or may not fit them.

The visitor is the point

You are building for someone who does not know this career yet. Every fact, image, headline, and spoken explanation should help that visitor decide whether the career is worth a closer look.

1 · Choose

Shortlist three careers and commit to one. 10 points.

2 · Research

Collect current evidence and record where it came from. 10 points.

3 · Explain

Build one public information page. 10 points.

4 · Invite

Create a booth poster and matching handout. 10 points.

5 · Present

Run the booth, pitch, answer questions, and visit other booths. 60 points.
Keep one career across all five steps: The research you collect in Step 2 becomes the site in Step 3, the booth in Step 4, and the answers you give in Step 5.

What quality looks like

  • The research describes real tasks, work setting, training, pay, outlook, and one honest challenge.
  • Every public fact can be traced to a source.
  • The site, poster, and handout share a clear visual system.
  • The pitch sounds practiced but not memorized word for word.
  • When you do not know an answer, you name where you would look instead of guessing.

Career Fair · Step 1 · 10 points

Choose One Career to Represent

Compare three possibilities, then commit to one you are willing to investigate honestly.

Objective: Compare three careers using interests, strengths, work preferences, and current career information.
Demonstration of learning: Submit three possibilities and one sentence explaining the career you chose for the project.

Start with a real pool

If your class uses Xello, begin with saved careers, favorite clusters, or Matchmaker results. If not, use CareerOneStop or the BLS Occupation Finder. You are choosing one career to investigate, not making a permanent life decision.

Explore with CareerOneStopBLS Occupation Finder

Compare three

For each career, write:

  • the career name;
  • one reason it may fit you;
  • one thing you already know;
  • one thing you still need to investigate.
Fit check: What kind of tasks hold my attention? What do people ask me for help with? Do I want to work mostly with people, information, tools, or ideas? Could I explain this career to a visitor without pretending I already know everything?

Submit

Type your three careers and finish this sentence:

I am choosing _____ because _____. Before I represent it, I still need to learn _____.

resource.body:
Career Fair · Step 2 · 10 points

Research What the Work Is Actually Like

Collect evidence you can reuse on the site, booth, handout, and pitch.

Objective: Collect current evidence about what a career involves, how someone enters it, and what a visitor should know before considering it.
Demonstration of learning: Submit a complete organizer with a source log and no unsupported public claims.

Research what the work is actually like

Start with the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook and CareerOneStop. Xello can be another source when your district provides access. Record the page title, organization, URL, and date you checked it while you work.

BLS Occupational Outlook HandbookCareerOneStop career profiles

Research organizer PDFEditable organizer DOCX

Your organizer must answer

  • What are three real tasks?
  • Where and when does the work happen?
  • Which skills matter, and how do they connect to the tasks?
  • What is one honest challenge?
  • What education, certification, apprenticeship, military training, or on-the-job route is typical?
  • What Texas pathway or program could a student investigate?
  • What do current pay and ten-year outlook data show?
Evidence rule: If you cannot point to the source for a fact, the fact does not go on the website or booth. Label pay and outlook with the source and year.

Submit

Upload the completed organizer as a PDF, DOCX, JPG, JPEG, or PNG. Photos must show the entire page clearly.

Career Fair · Step 3 · 10 points

Build the Public Information Page

Turn the research into one page a visitor can understand without you standing beside it.

Objective: Organize career evidence into a public page that a visitor can understand quickly.
Demonstration of learning: Submit one published link that opens for a viewer outside your account.

One page, five sections

  1. Career title and hook: one sentence that gives a visitor a reason to keep reading.
  2. What the work looks like: three real tasks and the work setting.
  3. Training route: what is typically required and one Texas pathway to investigate.
  4. Pay, outlook, and honest challenge: current, labeled evidence rather than a sales pitch.
  5. Sources: at least three named pages with working links.

Make a copy of the Google Slides planning template

Watch the Google Sites tutorialYouTube fallback

The ten-second test

Open the published link on another person's screen. Give them ten seconds. If they cannot name the career and one reason it matters, fix the title, hook, and hierarchy before changing colors.

Sharing check: Test the link in a logged-out window or with someone who does not own the file. A link that only opens for you is not published.

Submit

Paste the published URL to your one-page career site.

Career Fair · Step 4 · 10 points

Design the Booth Poster and Handout

Use one visual system to attract attention and leave visitors with something useful.

Objective: Design a poster and handout that attract a visitor, communicate the same career identity, and make the key information easy to scan.
Demonstration of learning: Submit both pieces in one Canvas submission.

Two pieces, one visual system

Poster: career title, hook, three benefit or impact points, one strong image, and a link or QR code to the site.

Handout: the same title, colors, and type choices, plus the three facts a visitor should remember and your name.

Make a copy of the Google Slides templateWatch the Canva tutorial

Creative constraints

  • The poster is at least 11 × 17 inches or uses the same vertical proportion.
  • The headline reads from six feet away.
  • No block of poster text exceeds 15 words.
  • The handout fits on half a page.
  • Both pieces use the same career title, colors, and type system.
Design test: Put the poster on the floor and step back. If you cannot read the headline, the visitor will not walk closer merely because the research is good.

Submit

Upload photos or exported files for both the poster and the handout. PDF, PNG, JPG, JPEG, and PPTX are accepted.

Career Fair · Step 5 · 60 points

Run the Expo Booth

Explain the career, answer questions, and help visitors decide whether it is worth exploring.

Objective: Explain a career accurately to visitors and respond to questions using evidence.
Demonstration of learning: Run the booth, deliver a 60-second pitch, answer questions, and participate in the visitor round.

Set the booth

  • Poster upright and readable.
  • Handouts where visitors can reach them.
  • Website open and tested.
  • Research organizer nearby for questions.

Your 60-second pitch

  1. Hook: why the career matters.
  2. Work: what someone in the career actually does.
  3. Evidence: current pay and outlook.
  4. Path: the training route that gets someone there.
Pitch stem: If you like _____ and want to _____, this career may be worth exploring because _____. One thing people often misunderstand is _____.

60-point rubric

Content Accuracy · 15

Facts are specific, current, and sourced. You answer from the research rather than inventing a number.

Visual Communication · 15

Poster and handout match, read clearly, and help visitors find the important information.

Delivery · 15

The pitch is complete, understandable, and adjusted to the visitor rather than read word for word.

Professionalism · 15

You greet visitors, stay engaged, maintain the booth, and participate in the visitor round.
A strong answer when you do not know: I do not know yet. I would check the BLS profile, CareerOneStop, or the source log before giving you a number.

Turn-in

This is a live performance. Your teacher records the score from the attached rubric. No separate Canvas upload is required unless your teacher gives you an alternate presentation route.

ratings.long_description: Every fact — day in the life, education path, Texas and national pay, outlook — is correct, specific and sourced. Answers questions that go past what is on the poster.
All required facts are present, correct and sourced. Answers most visitor questions from memory.
Some facts are missing, vague or unsourced. Reads off the poster to answer questions.
Facts are mostly missing or wrong. Cannot answer basic questions about the career.
Poster and handout match, read clearly from 6 feet, and stay inside the word limits. The booth pulls visitors in on its own.
Poster and handout are both complete, matching and readable. The booth looks finished.
One piece is missing, mismatched, undersized, or too crowded to read at a distance.
Materials are missing or unreadable. The booth gives a visitor nothing to look at.
Opens with a clear pitch, holds eye contact, adjusts the explanation to each visitor, and never reads off the poster.
Delivers the full pitch clearly with eye contact and only occasional glances at notes.
Pitch is incomplete or read word for word. Little eye contact; visitors have to ask for the basics.
No pitch offered. Responds only when asked, in a few words.
Dressed for the part, greets every visitor, stays at the booth the whole session, and completes the attendee survey thoughtfully.
Dressed appropriately, greets visitors, stays at the booth, and completes the attendee survey.
Dress or attention slips. Leaves the booth unattended or rushes the survey.
Not dressed for the event, booth left unattended, survey not completed.

TEACHER GUIDE · TWO WEEKS

Circuit Systems: Paths, Control + Signals

Students learn to make electrical behavior predictable, then use a circuit to send a message another person must decode.

Time
10 class periods
Core materials
Snap Circuits kits
Final
Blind partner decode
Grade
100-point Major

What students are learning

TopicComplete paths, safe testing, series and parallel reliability, controlled outputs, and coded signals.
Student-friendly objectiveI can build, test, and explain how paths and components control what a circuit does.
Demonstration of learningA partner decodes a sound signal. The builder records the first result, revises, and tests again.

Teacher-tomorrow setup

  • ✓ Count kits and choose stable pairs before Day 1. Keep the same partners through Day 10 when possible.
  • ✓ Download the connected teacher deck and four lab packets. Each guide below names the exact slide range and leave-up screen.
  • ✓ Test one complete lamp circuit, one parallel circuit, the LED/resistor circuit, the motor circuit, and the speaker/alarm circuit.
  • ✓ Prepare only dry, teacher-approved material samples for the conductor test. Never use liquids.
  • ✓ Decide where batteries will live. Students wire first, inspect, then receive or insert batteries.
  • ✓ Choose the final evidence route: photo plus lab packet, or a short video plus lab packet.
Download the two-week teacher deckDownload all lab packets

Safety boundary

Before powerSwitch off. Build from the diagram. Check every snap and component direction.
NeverConnect one battery terminal directly to the other. A short circuit can heat parts and drain batteries.
During motor workKeep faces, hair, fingers, and loose objects clear of the fan.
After testingSwitch off and disconnect the battery pack before changing the circuit or returning the kit.

Ten-day route

Days 1-2 · Follow and test a path

Open/closed circuits, kit safety, fair conductor test, and troubleshooting.

Days 3-5 · Design for reliability

Series, parallel, failure testing, a reliability challenge, and Xello/fallback goals.

Days 6-7 · Control outputs

LED direction, resistor comparison, motor direction, and a status-and-motion system.

Days 8-10 · Send a coded signal

Morse planning, sound circuit, blind partner decode, revision, and final evidence.

Teaching routes

Whole-group routeTeach from the connected deck, pause for the modeled build or prediction, then leave the named work screen projected while pairs build and record evidence.
Independent or absence routeStudents use the Canvas Learn page, official video, and matching lab packet. They still need a teacher-approved kit session for any physical evidence.

Likely misconceptions

  • ✓ Open does not mean on. An open switch breaks the path; a closed switch completes it.
  • ✓ Brightness does not define series or parallel. Students must trace the number of available paths.
  • ✓ Reversing an LED is not proof that it is broken. Check polarity before replacing the part.
  • ✓ Sound alone is not readable code. Dot/dash duration and the quiet gaps both carry information.

Portable instruction

The Canvas Learn pages and official YouTube videos are the default student route. The connected deck supports whole-group teaching. Edpuzzle is optional and course-specific; if you use it, copy the public lesson into your own Edpuzzle account, reconnect the Canvas External Tool, keep it unpublished until Student View works, and remove any teacher setup note before students enter.

No RISE or SCORM launch is required. The lab still runs if an external package disappears.

100-point rubric

Final criterionPointsEvidence
Safe, working circuit25A dependable sound circuit demonstrated more than once.
Code accuracy + signal timing25Written Morse matches the message; dots, dashes, and letter spaces are distinct.
Partner test + revision25Exact first decode, a specific revision, and final result.
Evidence + explanation25Required circuit evidence and a clear path/switch/speaker explanation.

Support route: teacher-provided three-letter message, partially completed planner, one-letter rehearsal, and one replay. Grade the same four criteria.

If time is tight

Protect the first complete-path build, one series/parallel failure comparison, the controlled-output model, and the first-decode/revision/final-decode sequence. Reduce repeated builds and material-test rows before removing those learning moves.

Circuit Systems: Paths, Control + Signals

TEACHER GUIDE · DAYS 1-2

Complete Paths + Safe Testing

Students learn the path before they troubleshoot the parts.

Slides
1-13
Lab
Complete path + fair test
Grade
5 points

Prep

  • ✓ Parts per pair: base grid, battery holder, slide switch, lamp, connectors, and blue snap wires.
  • ✓ Prepare four to six dry materials per table: paper clip, metal spoon, coin, craft stick, rubber band, paper, or cardboard.
  • ✓ Make one incomplete sample circuit or print one troubleshooting card.
Lab 1 editable DOCXLab 1 printable PDF

Deck map

Day 1: slides 1-8. Leave slide 8 projected during the first build.

Day 2: slides 9-13. Leave slide 12 projected during the material test; use slide 13 for the exit.

Teacher moves

  1. Trace one closed path with a finger before batteries enter the circuit.
  2. Model the switch as an intentional break. Open means the path is broken; closed means the path is complete.
  3. For the material test, keep the circuit and gap unchanged. Swap one dry material only.
  4. Troubleshoot with power off: compare to diagram, check snaps, check direction, ask for another set of eyes, then power on.

Safety, Troubleshooting + watch-fors

Lamp: closed switch = on; open switch = off. Conductors: metals should complete the path. Insulators: dry wood, paper, rubber, and cardboard should not.

Do not call a dim or flickering lamp an insulator without checking the contact. The claim must match repeatable evidence. Keep power off while students compare the build to the diagram and check every snap.

If time is tight

Keep the path trace, the first lamp build, two contrasting material tests, and the troubleshooting routine. Cut the number of tested materials before cutting the explanation.

resource.body:
LEARN · DAYS 1-2

Complete Paths + Safe Testing

A circuit works when electricity has a complete path through a load and back to its source.

Objective
Trace and test a complete path
Evidence
Lab 1 + checkpoint
Kit rule
Wire first, power last

Start with the path

Power source→Conductive path→Control→Load/output→Back to source

The switch opens or closes the path. A lamp, LED, motor, or speaker is a load because it uses electrical energy to do a job.

Watch: your first Snap Circuits path

Open the video in a new tab.

Open or closed?

Open circuitThe path has a break. Current cannot travel around the full loop. The output is off.
Closed circuitThe path is complete. Current can travel through the load and return to the source. The output can turn on.

The lamp turns ___ because the path is ___.

Watch: conductors and insulators

Open the video in a new tab.

A fair test changes one material while the circuit, gap, and power source stay the same.

___ is a conductor/insulator because the lamp ___.

Word bank: path · open · closed · conductor · insulator · complete · break · output

Five safety moves

  1. Switch off and build before inserting batteries.
  2. Compare the build to the diagram before power.
  3. Never connect the battery terminals directly.
  4. Keep hands, hair, and faces away from a spinning fan.
  5. Disconnect power before changing or returning a circuit.
Circuit Systems: Paths, Control + Signals

WATCH + RESPOND · 10 POINTS

Video Check: Circuit Basics

Watch the official circuit-basics tutorial, then answer five short questions in Canvas.

Watch
5:30
Submit
Five Canvas responses
Grade
10 points

Open the video in a new tab.

Answer in the text box

  1. Name the power source, control, and load in the first build.
  2. What changes when the switch opens?
  3. Why does the lamp need a path back to the battery?
  4. What must happen before batteries are inserted?
  5. What is one connection you must never make?

A complete circuit needs ___ because ___.

Word bank: battery · switch · lamp · path · open · closed · load · short circuit

Optional Edpuzzle route

If your teacher assigns this through Edpuzzle, answer the same checks inside the player. Otherwise, use the Canvas text box below. You only complete one route.

Circuit Systems: Paths, Control + Signals

BUILD · TEST · EXPLAIN

Lab 1: Complete Path + Material Test

Build one dependable lamp circuit, then use it as a test tool instead of changing everything at once.

Days
1-2
Materials
Snap Circuits + dry samples
Grade
5 points

Get the lab packet

Open the editable labOpen the printable lab

Day 1: prove the path

  1. Identify battery, switch, lamp, and connecting path.
  2. Build with the switch off. Ask for the battery or insert it only after the circuit matches the diagram.
  3. Close the switch and record what the lamp does.
  4. Open one connection and explain why the output changes.

Day 2: run a fair material test

  1. Keep the same test gap and circuit.
  2. Test four to six dry, teacher-approved materials, one at a time.
  3. Repeat any weak or flickering result before making a claim.
  4. Troubleshoot one incomplete circuit with the power off.

___ is a conductor/insulator because the lamp ___.

Word bank: path · open · closed · conductor · insulator · complete · break · evidence

Turn it in

  • ✓ Labeled path diagram
  • ✓ Open/closed observations
  • ✓ Material-test table with evidence
  • ✓ Troubleshooting explanation

Upload the finished packet or paste the teacher-approved share link.

Circuit Systems: Paths, Control + Signals

CHECK · 4 POINTS

Checkpoint: Complete Paths + Safe Testing

Use the circuit evidence, not a guess. Retake the check after you review the missed idea.

Attempts
Unlimited
Focus
Path + safety

A closed circuit has ___. An open circuit has ___.

Teacher moves

  1. Series: identify the one route before students build. Remove one lamp and trace where the route ends.
  2. Parallel: locate the branch and return points. Remove one lamp and observe the other branch.
  3. Make students use evidence, not the memorized phrase “parallel is better.” The right circuit depends on the job.
  4. Reliability challenge: partner traces the route, removes one load, and records whether the other output stays on.

Answers + misconception

Series: one path; remove one lamp and both go out. Parallel: multiple branches; remove one lamp and the other can stay on.

Brightness can change, but brightness does not define series or parallel. Path structure does.

If time is tight

Use physical builds for series and parallel, then complete the reliability challenge as a diagram and prediction. Do not skip the failure test comparison.

Teacher moves

  3. Motor: reverse the connection and observe direction. Keep hands, hair, and faces clear of the fan.
  4. Trace the status system as user input → electrical path/process → visible or moving output.

Answers + watch-fors

An LED is directional. A resistor limits current. Reversing motor polarity changes direction. A switch is an input/control, not the output.

The water analogy can introduce resistance, but electricity is not water in a wire. Return to the circuit evidence quickly.

  2. Test the sound circuit before students encode a message.

  4. Revision must respond to evidence: timing, spacing, volume, or a loose connection.

Your brief

Choose a teacher-approved three- to five-letter message: GO, OK, YES, NO, WAIT, TURN, OPEN, or CLOSE. Translate it into Morse code and send it with short and long sounds.

During the decode: do not speak, point to the answer, mouth the word, or show the written code. Your partner may use the Morse key.

Days 8-10

  1. Build and safely test the speaker or alarm circuit.
  2. Write the message and verify every letter against the Morse key.
  3. Rehearse dots, dashes, and letter spaces.
  4. Run the first blind decode. Record the partner's exact answer.
  5. Revise timing, spacing, volume, or one weak circuit connection.
  6. Run the final decode under the same no-hint rules.
