resource.body:
SW4 · Teacher Guide

Facilitator's Guide: Machine Learning Week

Five lessons about how models learn from examples, how training choices shape results, and how to test a model instead of trusting its confidence score.

Where this week sits

The S&S places this after the introduction to AI and before the two-week AI Ethics module. Students move from defining machine learning to training, bias, classification, computer vision, and one ethical question they carry forward.

Sequence and evidence

  1. Day 1: Code.org introduction, three examples from daily life, and a journal response.
  2. Day 2: two-label Teachable Machine model, balanced and unbalanced tests, and confidence-score screenshot.
  3. Day 3: Code.org bias activity, a deliberately limited model, a failure log, and one specific data fix.
  4. Day 4: AI for Oceans classification, accuracy before and after more training data, and a real-world comparison.
  5. Day 5: computer vision, model testing, four-question synthesis, and one ethical concern for the next unit.
  6. Xello: Make Plans and upload one completed plan screenshot.

Source and account check

  • Open the Code.org How AI Works lessons and AI for Oceans from a student account before the week begins.
  • Test Teachable Machine camera access on district Chromebooks. It does not require a login, but the browser must allow the camera.
  • Day of AI now places downloadable curriculum behind teacher registration. Download or assign the exact material before class; do not send students to search the resource hub.
  • Confirm Xello access through ClassLink before the final check-in.

Materials and setup

  • One Chromebook per student or pair, with a working camera for Days 2, 3, and 5.
  • Headphones for the short videos.
  • A journal or digital note page students can photograph or export for submission.
  • Pairs for Teachable Machine testing. Students should test each other's models rather than only testing the same person and background used for training.
  • A plan for students who cannot or should not use the camera. Use teacher-provided image sets rather than requiring a personal image.

What to check

  • More confidence does not automatically mean a correct prediction.
  • A model can work for its training conditions and fail under new lighting, distance, background, or person.
  • When students propose a bias fix, require the exact data they would add or rebalance.
  • Assignment submissions need an uploaded artifact as well as the reflection comment because the five Canvas assignments accept upload or media recording, not text entry.

Current sources: Code.org How AI Works Lesson 1 · Teachable Machine · Day of AI: AI Foundations for Middle Grades · AI for Oceans

Machine Learning · Day 1 of 5

What Is Machine Learning?

Compare rules written by a person with patterns learned from examples.

  • Tool: Code.org How AI Works, Lesson 1
  • Time: one class period
  • Turn in: journal page and reflection
  • English
  • Español

English

Words for today: machine learning · training data · traditional programming

What to do

  1. Watch What Is Machine Learning?. Write what the computer learns from.
  2. Complete How AI Works, Lesson 1 with your assigned partner.
  3. In your own words, define machine learning, training data, and traditional programming.
  4. List three places you encountered machine learning in the last day. Name the app or system, what it predicted, and what examples it may have learned from.
  5. Classify a calculator, next-word prediction, a timed traffic light, and photo search as rule-based or learned from data. Explain one choice.

If you get stuck

  1. Ask whether a person could write every rule for the task.
  2. Name the prediction the system makes, not only the app.
  3. If the Code.org activity does not save, confirm that you entered through the class section.

Before you submit

  • Upload a readable photo or export of today's journal work.
  • Complete the reflection in the submission comment.

Reflection

Write 2 or 3 sentences: "Machine learning is different from traditional programming because ____. One place I see it is ____, and it may have learned from ____."

Word bank: machine learning · training data · pattern · prediction · rule

Español

Palabras de hoy: machine learning (aprendizaje automático) · training data (datos de entrenamiento) · traditional programming (programación tradicional)

Qué hacer

  1. Mira What Is Machine Learning?. Escribe de qué aprende la computadora.
  2. Completa How AI Works, Lesson 1 con el compañero asignado.
  3. Define con tus palabras aprendizaje automático, datos de entrenamiento y programación tradicional.
  4. Anota tres lugares donde encontraste aprendizaje automático durante el último día. Nombra la app o sistema, qué predijo y de qué ejemplos pudo aprender.
  5. Clasifica una calculadora, la predicción de palabras, un semáforo con temporizador y la búsqueda de fotos como sistema de reglas o sistema que aprendió de datos. Explica una decisión.

Si te atoras

  1. Pregunta si una persona podría escribir cada regla para la tarea.
  2. Nombra la predicción que hace el sistema, no solo la app.
  3. Si Code.org no guarda el trabajo, confirma que entraste por la sección de la clase.

Antes de entregar

  • Sube una foto legible o una exportación del trabajo de tu diario.
  • Completa la reflexión en el comentario.

Reflexión

Escribe 2 o 3 oraciones: "El aprendizaje automático es diferente de la programación tradicional porque ____. Un lugar donde lo veo es ____, y pudo aprender de ____."

Banco de palabras: aprendizaje automático · datos de entrenamiento · patrón · predicción · regla

Machine Learning · Day 2 of 5

Train and Test a Model

Train two labels, change the data, and record what happens to the model's predictions.

  • Tool: Google Teachable Machine
  • Time: one class period
  • Turn in: confidence screenshot, test notes, and reflection
  • English
  • Español

English

Words for today: label · confidence score · supervised learning

What to do

  1. Open Teachable Machine. Choose an image project and a standard image model.
  2. Create two labels your teacher approves. Collect at least 30 varied examples for each label, then train the model.
  3. Test both labels with a different angle, distance, background, or person. Record the prediction and confidence score for at least four tests.
  4. Train a second version with about 30 examples for one label and 5 for the other. Test both labels again and record what changed.
  5. Capture a screenshot that shows the model's labels and confidence scores.

If you get stuck

  1. Allow camera access in Chrome, or use the teacher-provided image set.
  2. If the model predicts one label every time, compare the backgrounds in the two training sets.
  3. Change one training condition at a time so you know what caused the result.

Before you submit

  • Upload the confidence-score screenshot and your short test log.
  • Complete the reflection in the submission comment.

Reflection

Write 2 or 3 sentences: "My model was most confident when ____. It became confused when ____, probably because the training data ____."

Word bank: label · confidence score · training data · balanced · unbalanced · accuracy

Español

Palabras de hoy: label (etiqueta) · confidence score (nivel de confianza) · supervised learning (aprendizaje supervisado)

Qué hacer

  1. Abre Teachable Machine. Escoge un proyecto de imágenes y el modelo estándar.
  2. Crea dos etiquetas aprobadas por tu maestro. Reúne al menos 30 ejemplos variados para cada etiqueta y entrena el modelo.
  3. Prueba las dos etiquetas con otro ángulo, distancia, fondo o persona. Anota la predicción y el nivel de confianza de al menos cuatro pruebas.
  4. Entrena una segunda versión con unos 30 ejemplos de una etiqueta y 5 de la otra. Prueba las dos de nuevo y anota qué cambió.
  5. Toma una captura que muestre las etiquetas y los niveles de confianza.

Si te atoras

  1. Permite el acceso a la cámara en Chrome o usa las imágenes que dé tu maestro.
  2. Si el modelo siempre predice la misma etiqueta, compara los fondos de los dos conjuntos de entrenamiento.
  3. Cambia una condición de entrenamiento a la vez para saber qué causó el resultado.

Antes de entregar

  • Sube la captura de los niveles de confianza y tu registro corto de pruebas.
  • Completa la reflexión en el comentario.

Reflexión

Escribe 2 o 3 oraciones: "Mi modelo tuvo más confianza cuando ____. Se confundió cuando ____, probablemente porque los datos de entrenamiento ____."

Banco de palabras: etiqueta · nivel de confianza · datos de entrenamiento · equilibrado · desequilibrado · precisión

resource.body:
Machine Learning · Day 3 of 5

Bias in Training Data

Make a model fail under conditions its training data did not represent, then propose a specific fix.

  • Tool: Code.org Lesson 5 and Teachable Machine
  • Time: one class period
  • Turn in: failure log, proposed data fix, and reflection
  • English
  • Español

English

Words for today: algorithmic bias · representation · fairness

What to do

  1. Complete the assigned parts of Code.org How AI Works, Lesson 5.
  2. Open Teachable Machine. Train a two-label model with one intentional limitation, such as one background, one lighting condition, or unequal label counts.
  3. Test the model outside that condition. Record at least four failures with the actual label, prediction, and confidence score.
  4. Name who or what the training data represents poorly. Describe one real consequence if a higher-stakes system had the same gap.
  5. Propose a fix by naming the exact examples you would add, remove, or rebalance.

If you get stuck

  1. A biased model does not have to fail every time. Look for who or what fails more often.
  2. Do not write only 'add more data.' Name the missing examples.
  3. A high confidence score can still belong to a wrong prediction.

Before you submit

  • Upload the four-test failure log and your specific data fix.
  • Complete the reflection in the submission comment.

Reflection

Write 2 or 3 sentences: "My training data did not represent ____, so the model failed when ____. I would reduce that bias by adding or changing ____."

Word bank: algorithmic bias · representation · fairness · dataset · confidence · harm

Español

Palabras de hoy: algorithmic bias (sesgo algorítmico) · representation (representación) · fairness (equidad)

Qué hacer

  1. Completa las partes asignadas de Code.org How AI Works, Lesson 5.
  2. Abre Teachable Machine. Entrena un modelo de dos etiquetas con una limitación intencional, como un solo fondo, una sola iluminación o cantidades desiguales.
  3. Prueba el modelo fuera de esa condición. Anota al menos cuatro fallas con la etiqueta real, la predicción y el nivel de confianza.
  4. Nombra a quién o qué representan mal los datos. Describe una consecuencia real si un sistema de mayor riesgo tuviera la misma falta.
  5. Propón una solución nombrando los ejemplos exactos que agregarías, quitarías o equilibrarías.

Si te atoras

  1. Un modelo con sesgo no tiene que fallar siempre. Busca quién o qué falla con más frecuencia.
  2. No escribas solamente 'agregar más datos.' Nombra los ejemplos que faltan.
  3. Un nivel de confianza alto todavía puede acompañar una predicción incorrecta.

Antes de entregar

  • Sube el registro de cuatro pruebas y tu solución específica para los datos.
  • Completa la reflexión en el comentario.

Reflexión

Escribe 2 o 3 oraciones: "Mis datos no representaron ____, así que el modelo falló cuando ____. Reduciría ese sesgo al agregar o cambiar ____."

Banco de palabras: sesgo algorítmico · representación · equidad · conjunto de datos · confianza · daño

Machine Learning · Day 4 of 5

AI for Oceans: Classification in Action

Label examples, watch the classifier change, and question who decides what a label means.

  • Tool: Code.org AI for Oceans
  • Time: one class period
  • Turn in: accuracy notes, real-world comparison, and reflection
  • English
  • Español

English

Words for today: classification · label · error

What to do

  1. Open AI for Oceans and complete the assigned trash-sorting levels.
  2. Record the model's result before adding more labeled examples. Continue training, then record the result again.
  3. Write which labels were easy to apply and which required an opinion. Explain how inconsistent labels could change the model.
  4. Compare the activity with one real use of classification, such as content moderation or medical-image review. Name what a wrong label could cause.

If you get stuck

  1. If the activity does not load, refresh once in Chrome and ask your teacher for the assigned level.
  2. A lower score is data. Record what you labeled immediately before it changed.
  3. If a label seems subjective, explain what two people might disagree about.

Before you submit

  • Upload a readable page with the before-and-after result and real-world comparison.
  • Complete the reflection in the submission comment.

Reflection

Write 2 or 3 sentences: "The model changed after I ____. This is like classification in ____ because ____."

Word bank: classification · label · training data · accuracy · error · moderation

Español

Palabras de hoy: classification (clasificación) · label (etiqueta) · error

Qué hacer

  1. Abre AI for Oceans y completa los niveles asignados de clasificación de basura.
  2. Anota el resultado del modelo antes de agregar más ejemplos etiquetados. Continúa entrenando y anota el resultado de nuevo.
  3. Escribe cuáles etiquetas fueron fáciles y cuáles necesitaron una opinión. Explica cómo las etiquetas inconsistentes podrían cambiar el modelo.
  4. Compara la actividad con un uso real de clasificación, como moderación de contenido o revisión de imágenes médicas. Nombra qué podría causar una etiqueta incorrecta.

Si te atoras

  1. Si la actividad no carga, actualiza una vez en Chrome y pregúntale a tu maestro cuál nivel debes usar.
  2. Un resultado más bajo también es información. Anota qué etiquetaste antes de que cambiara.
  3. Si una etiqueta parece subjetiva, explica en qué podrían estar en desacuerdo dos personas.

Antes de entregar

  • Sube una página legible con el resultado de antes y después y la comparación con el mundo real.
  • Completa la reflexión en el comentario.

Reflexión

Escribe 2 o 3 oraciones: "El modelo cambió después de que ____. Esto se parece a la clasificación en ____ porque ____."

Banco de palabras: clasificación · etiqueta · datos de entrenamiento · precisión · error · moderación

Machine Learning · Day 5 of 5

Computer Vision and Week Reflection

Test what a vision model recognizes, then explain what machine learning can and cannot guarantee.

  • Tool: Code.org Lesson 2 and Teachable Machine
  • Time: one class period
  • Turn in: test log, four-question synthesis, and reflection
  • English
  • Español

English

Words for today: computer vision · model · confidence score

What to do

  1. Watch Computer Vision and complete the assigned parts of How AI Works, Lesson 2.
  2. Open your Day 2 Teachable Machine model or use the model your teacher provides. Test at least six examples under new conditions.
  3. Make a hit-and-miss log with the actual label, prediction, confidence score, and what changed from training.
  4. Answer four questions: What is machine learning? How does it learn? What can go wrong? What question do you still have?
  5. Name one ethical concern the class should carry into the next module and connect it to evidence from this week.

If you get stuck

  1. If your Day 2 model is unavailable, use the teacher-provided model instead of rebuilding the whole lesson.
  2. Separate a wrong prediction from a low-confidence correct prediction.
  3. Use one specific test from this week as evidence in the ethical concern.

Before you submit

  • Upload the six-test log and four-question synthesis.
  • Complete the reflection in the submission comment.

Reflection

Write 2 or 3 sentences: "Machine learning learns by ____. It can go wrong when ____. The ethical question I am carrying forward is ____."

Word bank: computer vision · model · confidence score · classification · bias · ethics

Español

Palabras de hoy: computer vision (visión por computadora) · model (modelo) · confidence score (nivel de confianza)

Qué hacer

  1. Mira Computer Vision y completa las partes asignadas de How AI Works, Lesson 2.
  2. Abre tu modelo del Día 2 o usa el modelo que dé tu maestro. Prueba al menos seis ejemplos en condiciones nuevas.
  3. Haz un registro de aciertos y fallas con la etiqueta real, la predicción, el nivel de confianza y qué cambió desde el entrenamiento.
  4. Contesta cuatro preguntas: ¿Qué es el aprendizaje automático? ¿Cómo aprende? ¿Qué puede salir mal? ¿Qué pregunta todavía tienes?
  5. Nombra una preocupación ética para la siguiente unidad y conéctala con evidencia de esta semana.

Si te atoras

  1. Si no tienes tu modelo del Día 2, usa el modelo de tu maestro en vez de reconstruir toda la lección.
  2. Separa una predicción incorrecta de una predicción correcta con poca confianza.
  3. Usa una prueba específica de esta semana como evidencia para la preocupación ética.

Antes de entregar

  • Sube el registro de seis pruebas y las respuestas a las cuatro preguntas.
  • Completa la reflexión en el comentario.

Reflexión

Escribe 2 o 3 oraciones: "El aprendizaje automático aprende al ____. Puede salir mal cuando ____. La pregunta ética que llevo a la siguiente unidad es ____."

Banco de palabras: visión por computadora · modelo · nivel de confianza · clasificación · sesgo · ética

Machine Learning · Xello Check-in

Xello: Make Plans

Build one plan far enough to see the steps between an idea and a pathway after high school.

  • Tool: Xello through ClassLink
  • Time: about 30 minutes
  • Turn in: completed-plan screenshot and reflection
  • English
  • Español

English

Words for today: plan · pathway · steps

What to do

  1. Open Xello through ClassLink.
  2. Open Goals & Plans. Add at least one education plan for a pathway after high school and complete its steps.
  3. Open the finished plan so the pathway and steps are visible, then capture a readable screenshot.

If you get stuck

  1. Enter through ClassLink, not a personal account.
  2. A plan is not a permanent commitment. Choose one option you want to understand better.
  3. Show your teacher the screen before creating another account.

Before you submit

  • Upload the completed-plan screenshot.
  • Complete the reflection in the submission comment.

Reflection

Complete the sentence: "One pathway I want to keep open after high school is ____ because ____."

Word bank: plan · pathway · education · training · steps

Español

Palabras de hoy: plan · pathway (trayectoria) · steps (pasos)

Qué hacer

  1. Abre Xello por ClassLink.
  2. Abre Goals & Plans. Agrega al menos un plan educativo para después de la preparatoria y completa sus pasos.
  3. Abre el plan terminado para mostrar la trayectoria y los pasos. Toma una captura legible.

Si te atoras

  1. Entra por ClassLink y no con una cuenta personal.
  2. Un plan no es un compromiso permanente. Escoge una opción que quieras entender mejor.
  3. Muéstrale la pantalla a tu maestro antes de crear otra cuenta.

Antes de entregar

  • Sube la captura del plan terminado.
  • Completa la reflexión en el comentario.

Reflexión

Completa la oración: "Una trayectoria que quiero mantener abierta después de la preparatoria es ____ porque ____."

Banco de palabras: plan · trayectoria · educación · capacitación · pasos

SW4 · Teacher Guide

Facilitator's Guide: AI Ethics

Ten lessons that move from documented harms and stakeholder tradeoffs to a debate and a student-written code of ethics.

The unit contract

Days 1 through 7 build the evidence students need. Day 8 is a 100-point debate. Day 9 is a 100-point group code of ethics. Day 10 is the gallery walk and individual synthesis. The topic a group claims on Day 1 should feed its principle on Day 9.

Sequence

  1. Day 1: document one real AI ethics problem, the affected people, and two sources.
  2. Day 2: map direct and indirect stakeholders in a recommendation system, then redesign one rule and name the tradeoff.
  3. Day 3: compare helpful and harmful surveillance using consent, benefit, and the ability to opt out.
  4. Day 4: sort and verify teacher-vetted examples of real and generated content using lateral reading.
  5. Day 5: analyze at least six stakeholders in one AI decision scenario.
  6. Day 6: break a job into tasks, then decide what AI, a human, or both should do.
  7. Day 7: prepare the assigned stakeholder position for the essay-grading debate.
  8. Day 8: conduct the debate and submit evidence, opening, response, and reflection.
  9. Day 9: write at least five evidence-backed principles for creators and users.
  10. Day 10: gallery walk, defend one principle, and explain what changed in your thinking.
  11. Xello: Biases and Career Choices.

Teacher preparation that cannot wait until class

  • Register for Day of AI and download the exact units you plan to use. Current public pages describe the lessons, but the teaching materials require teacher login.
  • Build and preview the Day 4 sorting set. Include a manageable mix of real, AI-generated, altered, and genuinely uncertain examples. Keep the original sources so students can verify them.
  • Choose the Day 5 scenario. The page supports school behavior monitoring, hospital prioritization, sports, or a teacher-approved alternative.
  • Assign the five Day 7 stakeholder roles: student, teacher, parent, technology company, and government or district decision-maker.
  • Prepare a visible timer and voting method for Day 8.
  • Provide poster paper or one shared document per group for Day 9, plus sticky notes or a digital feedback method for Day 10.

Discussion and privacy boundaries

  • Discuss systems and documented cases, not classmates or their families.
  • Students may pass on personal disclosure and still complete the analysis using the supplied scenario.
  • Do not require students to upload a face, personal feed, location history, private messages, or other personal data.
  • A student represents an assigned stakeholder in the debate. The role is not a statement of the student's personal belief.
  • Require a traceable source for factual claims. A broad resource hub is a teacher starting point, not evidence by itself.

Canvas and grading checks

  • Days 1 through 7, Day 9, and Day 10 accept upload or media recording. Their directions now name an uploaded artifact so a comment alone is not mistaken for a submission.
  • Day 8 also accepts text entry, matching the option to type the opening statement.
  • Day 8 and Day 9 each have a 100-point rubric. Review both rubrics with students before Day 7.
  • The current rubrics have no zero-point rating. Their lowest selectable level is 15 points per category. Decide before assigning whether that scoring floor fits your class.

Current source set: Code.org: Our AI Code of Ethics · MIT Media Lab: AI + Ethics for Middle School · Day of AI curriculum · MIT RAISE resources

resource.body:
AI Ethics · Day 1 of 10

What Are AI Ethics?

Investigate one documented AI harm and identify the people and decisions behind it.

  • Tool: Code.org Lesson 7 and teacher-approved research
  • Time: one class period
  • Turn in: four-part research organizer, two sources, and reflection
  • English
  • Español

English

Words for today: ethics · harm · responsibility

What to do

  1. Complete the assigned introduction in Code.org How AI Works, Lesson 7. Define AI ethics in your own words.
  2. Choose one teacher-approved topic: algorithmic bias, privacy or surveillance, misinformation, AI in hiring, or another documented case.
  3. Complete four organizer sections: the AI system and decision; what went wrong; who was affected; who built, chose, or used the system.
  4. Find two traceable sources. Record the title, organization, link, and one fact from each source. Separate a source's evidence from its opinion.
  5. Claim one topic for your group's Day 9 code-of-ethics principle and save this organizer.

If you get stuck

  1. Search for the documented harm or decision, not only the technology name.
  2. If two sources disagree, record the disagreement and who published each account.
  3. Ask who lost access, money, opportunity, safety, or reputation.

Before you submit

  • Upload the completed four-part organizer with both sources.
  • Complete the reflection in the submission comment.

Reflection

Write 2 or 3 sentences: "AI ethics matters because ____. In the case I studied, ____ was affected when ____."

Word bank: ethics · harm · responsible · evidence · source · decision

Español

Palabras de hoy: ethics (ética) · harm (daño) · responsibility (responsabilidad)

Qué hacer

  1. Completa la introducción asignada en Code.org How AI Works, Lesson 7. Define ética de la IA con tus palabras.
  2. Escoge un tema aprobado: sesgo algorítmico, privacidad o vigilancia, desinformación, IA en contratación u otro caso documentado.
  3. Completa cuatro secciones: el sistema y su decisión; qué salió mal; quién fue afectado; quién construyó, escogió o usó el sistema.
  4. Busca dos fuentes que se puedan rastrear. Anota el título, la organización, el enlace y un dato de cada fuente. Separa la evidencia de la opinión.
  5. Escoge un tema para el principio que tu grupo escribirá el Día 9 y guarda este organizador.

Si te atoras

  1. Busca el daño o la decisión documentada, no solamente el nombre de la tecnología.
  2. Si dos fuentes no están de acuerdo, anota la diferencia y quién publicó cada versión.
  3. Pregunta quién perdió acceso, dinero, oportunidad, seguridad o reputación.

Antes de entregar

  • Sube el organizador de cuatro partes con las dos fuentes.
  • Completa la reflexión en el comentario.

Reflexión

Escribe 2 o 3 oraciones: "La ética de la IA importa porque ____. En el caso que estudié, ____ fue afectado cuando ____."

Banco de palabras: ética · daño · responsable · evidencia · fuente · decisión

AI Ethics · Day 2 of 10

Algorithmic Bias and Recommendation Systems

Find what a recommendation system is designed to maximize, who benefits, and who becomes less visible.

  • Tool: MIT AI + Ethics and Day of AI
  • Time: one class period
  • Turn in: stakeholder map, redesign, tradeoff, and reflection
  • English
  • Español

English

Words for today: algorithm · maximize · stakeholder

What to do

  1. Review the assigned example from MIT AI + Ethics for Middle School or the Day of AI middle-grades unit.
  2. Choose a recommendation system your teacher approves. Name what it appears to maximize, such as watch time, clicks, purchases, or completion.
  3. Map at least three direct stakeholders and three indirect stakeholders. For each one, record the likely benefit, possible harm, and amount of power.
  4. Change one rule in the recommendation system. Explain who gains, who loses attention or money, and what new problem the redesign may create.

If you get stuck

  1. Follow how the company or organization benefits to identify what the system may maximize.
  2. An indirect stakeholder may never open the app but can still be affected by its recommendations.
  3. A redesign with no tradeoff probably leaves out a stakeholder.

Before you submit

  • Upload the six-stakeholder map and redesign explanation.
  • Complete the reflection in the submission comment.

Reflection

Write 2 or 3 sentences: "The recommendation system on ____ is designed to maximize ____. That benefits ____, but it can harm ____."

Word bank: algorithm · maximize · recommendation · stakeholder · benefit · harm · tradeoff

Español

Palabras de hoy: algorithm (algoritmo) · maximize (maximizar) · stakeholder (parte interesada)

Qué hacer

  1. Revisa el ejemplo asignado de MIT AI + Ethics for Middle School o la unidad de Day of AI para grados intermedios.
  2. Escoge un sistema de recomendaciones aprobado. Nombra lo que parece maximizar, como tiempo de reproducción, clics, compras o finalización.
  3. Haz un mapa de al menos tres partes interesadas directas y tres indirectas. Para cada una, anota el beneficio, el posible daño y su poder.
  4. Cambia una regla del sistema. Explica quién gana, quién pierde atención o dinero y qué problema nuevo podría crear el rediseño.

Si te atoras

  1. Sigue la forma en que la compañía se beneficia para identificar lo que el sistema puede maximizar.
  2. Una parte interesada indirecta puede no abrir la app y todavía ser afectada.
  3. Un rediseño sin ningún costo probablemente dejó fuera a alguien.

Antes de entregar

  • Sube el mapa de seis partes interesadas y la explicación del rediseño.
  • Completa la reflexión en el comentario.

Reflexión

Escribe 2 o 3 oraciones: "El sistema de recomendaciones de ____ está diseñado para maximizar ____. Eso beneficia a ____, pero puede dañar a ____."

Banco de palabras: algoritmo · maximizar · recomendación · parte interesada · beneficio · daño · intercambio

AI Ethics · Day 3 of 10

AI, Privacy, and Surveillance

Use consent, benefit, risk, and the ability to opt out to judge one surveillance system.

  • Tool: Day of AI surveillance unit and Code.org
  • Time: one class period
  • Turn in: data list, two-sided analysis, safeguard, and reflection
  • English
  • Español

English

Words for today: surveillance · consent · digital footprint

What to do

  1. Use the teacher-assigned material from From Data to Decision. Discuss the system, not classmates or family stories. You may pass on personal disclosure.
  2. List at least three pieces of data the system collects without a person typing them in.
  3. Make two columns with at least three possible benefits and three possible harms. For each side, name who receives the benefit or carries the risk.
  4. Complete the assigned part of Code.org Digital Footprint using the supplied fictional profile or scenario.
  5. Write one safeguard that keeps a useful function while limiting collection, access, retention, or use. Explain who enforces it.

If you get stuck

  1. If both columns sound the same, change whose perspective you are using.
  2. A person may benefit from a system and still lack a real choice about being included.
  3. You may analyze the fictional scenario without sharing your own data.

Before you submit

  • Upload the data list, both columns, and safeguard.
  • Complete the reflection in the submission comment.

Reflection

Write 2 or 3 sentences: "AI surveillance may help when ____, but it may cause harm when ____. The difference is ____."

Word bank: surveillance · consent · privacy · digital footprint · safeguard · risk

Español

Palabras de hoy: surveillance (vigilancia) · consent (consentimiento) · digital footprint (huella digital)

Qué hacer

  1. Usa el material asignado de From Data to Decision. Habla del sistema, no de compañeros o familias. Puedes pasar sin compartir algo personal.
  2. Anota al menos tres datos que el sistema recopila sin que una persona los escriba.
  3. Haz dos columnas con tres posibles beneficios y tres posibles daños. En cada lado, nombra quién recibe el beneficio o carga con el riesgo.
  4. Completa la parte asignada de Code.org Digital Footprint usando el perfil o escenario ficticio.
  5. Escribe una protección que mantenga una función útil y limite la recopilación, acceso, retención o uso. Explica quién la hace cumplir.

Si te atoras

  1. Si las dos columnas parecen iguales, cambia la perspectiva de la persona.
  2. Alguien puede recibir un beneficio y todavía no tener una opción real sobre su inclusión.
  3. Puedes analizar el escenario ficticio sin compartir tus propios datos.

Antes de entregar

  • Sube la lista de datos, las dos columnas y la protección.
  • Completa la reflexión en el comentario.

Reflexión

Escribe 2 o 3 oraciones: "La vigilancia con IA puede ayudar cuando ____, pero puede causar daño cuando ____. La diferencia es ____."

Banco de palabras: vigilancia · consentimiento · privacidad · huella digital · protección · riesgo

AI Ethics · Day 4 of 10

AI and Misinformation

Use lateral reading and traceable sources instead of judging a claim by how convincing it looks.

  • Tool: teacher-vetted sorting set and Day of AI
  • Time: one class period
  • Turn in: sorting reasons, one full fact-check, and reflection
  • English
  • Español

English

Words for today: misinformation · lateral reading · source

What to do

  1. Use the examples your teacher provides with the assigned material from Truth, Tricks, and AI. Do not search for or create harmful deepfake content.
  2. Sort every example as real, AI-generated or altered, or not yet verified. Write one reason for each choice.
  3. Choose one example and open a second tab. Search the central claim, original publisher, image, or quoted phrase instead of staying on the original page.
  4. Record a verdict, the best source you found, the evidence it provides, and what remains uncertain. 'Not yet verified' is acceptable when supported.
  5. Write a three-step check you can use before sharing a surprising image, video, or claim.

If you get stuck

  1. If something looks real, stop inspecting only the image and search for its origin.
  2. A page repeating the claim is not independent confirmation if both pages cite the same source.
  3. Record uncertainty instead of replacing missing evidence with a guess.

Before you submit

  • Upload the completed sort, full fact-check, and three-step check.
  • Complete the reflection in the submission comment.

Reflection

Write 2 or 3 sentences: "I first thought ____ because ____. After checking other sources, I found ____. Before sharing, I will ____."

Word bank: misinformation · lateral reading · source · verify · evidence · claim

Español

Palabras de hoy: misinformation (desinformación) · lateral reading (lectura lateral) · source (fuente)

Qué hacer

  1. Usa los ejemplos de tu maestro con el material asignado de Truth, Tricks, and AI. No busques ni crees deepfakes dañinos.
  2. Clasifica cada ejemplo como real, generado o alterado con IA, o todavía sin verificar. Escribe una razón para cada decisión.
  3. Escoge un ejemplo y abre otra pestaña. Busca la afirmación central, el editor original, la imagen o una frase citada.
  4. Anota un veredicto, la mejor fuente, la evidencia que ofrece y lo que todavía no se sabe. 'Todavía sin verificar' se acepta cuando tiene apoyo.
  5. Escribe una revisión de tres pasos para usar antes de compartir una imagen, video o afirmación sorprendente.

Si te atoras

  1. Si algo parece real, deja de mirar solamente la imagen y busca su origen.
  2. Una página que repite la afirmación no es confirmación independiente si las dos citan la misma fuente.
  3. Anota la incertidumbre en vez de reemplazar evidencia faltante con una adivinanza.

Antes de entregar

  • Sube la clasificación, la verificación completa y la revisión de tres pasos.
  • Completa la reflexión en el comentario.

Reflexión

Escribe 2 o 3 oraciones: "Primero pensé ____ porque ____. Después de revisar otras fuentes, encontré ____. Antes de compartir, voy a ____."

Banco de palabras: desinformación · lectura lateral · fuente · verificar · evidencia · afirmación

AI Ethics · Day 5 of 10

Stakeholder Analysis

Find who benefits, who carries risk, who has power, and who is missing from an AI decision.

  • Tool: teacher-assigned AI scenario
  • Time: one class period
  • Turn in: six-stakeholder analysis, recommendation, tradeoff, and reflection
  • English
  • Español

English

Words for today: stakeholder · power · tradeoff

What to do

  1. Use the scenario your teacher assigns. Record the AI system, the decision it influences, and the people or groups affected.
  2. List at least six direct and indirect stakeholders. Include the people using the system, people judged by it, people building it, and people paying for it.
  3. For each stakeholder, record what they need, what they risk, how much power they have, and whether they can refuse the system.
  4. Recommend use, use with conditions, or do not use. Name the evidence and the tradeoff your group accepts.
  5. Present the recommendation. Be ready to answer: who pays for this tradeoff?

If you get stuck

  1. If you have fewer than six, add builders, buyers, people represented in the data, and people compared with the data.
  2. Your group may present two positions when both have evidence.
  3. If you cannot decide, name the information needed before a decision.

Before you submit

  • Upload the six-stakeholder analysis and recommendation.
  • Complete the reflection in the submission comment.

Reflection

Write 2 or 3 sentences: "In this scenario, ____ has the most power, while ____ carries the most risk, because ____."

Word bank: stakeholder · direct · indirect · power · risk · tradeoff · fairness

Español

Palabras de hoy: stakeholder (parte interesada) · power (poder) · tradeoff (intercambio)

Qué hacer

  1. Usa el escenario asignado. Anota el sistema de IA, la decisión que influye y las personas o grupos afectados.
  2. Anota al menos seis partes interesadas directas e indirectas. Incluye usuarios, personas evaluadas, personas que construyen el sistema y quienes lo pagan.
  3. Para cada parte, anota qué necesita, qué arriesga, cuánto poder tiene y si puede rechazar el sistema.
  4. Recomienda usarlo, usarlo con condiciones o no usarlo. Nombra la evidencia y el intercambio que acepta tu grupo.
  5. Presenta la recomendación. Prepárate para contestar: ¿quién paga por este intercambio?

Si te atoras

  1. Si tienes menos de seis, agrega constructores, compradores, personas representadas en los datos y personas comparadas con los datos.
  2. Tu grupo puede presentar dos posiciones cuando las dos tienen evidencia.
  3. Si no puedes decidir, nombra la información necesaria antes de decidir.

Antes de entregar

  • Sube el análisis de seis partes interesadas y la recomendación.
  • Completa la reflexión en el comentario.

Reflexión

Escribe 2 o 3 oraciones: "En este escenario, ____ tiene más poder, mientras ____ carga con más riesgo, porque ____."

Banco de palabras: parte interesada · directa · indirecta · poder · riesgo · intercambio · equidad

resource.body:
AI Ethics · Day 6 of 10

AI and Jobs: Tasks, Not Headlines

Break one job into tasks and decide where automation, human judgment, or both fit.

  • Tool: Day of AI Work in the Age of AI
  • Time: one class period
  • Turn in: six-task analysis, future-job design, ethical problem, and reflection
  • English
  • Español

English

Words for today: automation · task · judgment

What to do

  1. Use the teacher-assigned material from Work in the Age of AI. Choose one real job.
  2. Break the job into at least six tasks, including routine, communication, judgment, and responsibility tasks.
  3. Sort each task into AI could do it, a human should do it, or better together. Explain one decision from each category.
  4. Design a plausible future version of the job. Describe one workday, what the AI does, what the person does, and who is accountable for mistakes.
  5. Name one ethical problem this version of the job must handle and one safeguard.

If you get stuck

  1. A job is larger than its most visible task. Include planning, documentation, communication, and follow-up.
  2. Ask who is blamed when an automated decision causes harm.
  3. A future job needs a real user, task, and responsibility, not only a new title.

Before you submit

  • Upload the six-task analysis and future-job design.
  • Complete the reflection in the submission comment.

Reflection

Write 2 or 3 sentences: "In ____, AI could handle ____, but a human is still needed for ____ because ____."

Word bank: automation · task · job · collaboration · judgment · accountability · skill

Español

Palabras de hoy: automation (automatización) · task (tarea) · judgment (juicio)

Qué hacer

  1. Usa el material asignado de Work in the Age of AI. Escoge un trabajo real.
  2. Divide el trabajo en al menos seis tareas, incluyendo rutina, comunicación, juicio y responsabilidad.
  3. Clasifica cada tarea como IA podría hacerla, una persona debe hacerla o mejor juntos. Explica una decisión de cada categoría.
  4. Diseña una versión futura y posible del trabajo. Describe un día, lo que hace la IA, lo que hace la persona y quién responde por errores.
  5. Nombra un problema ético y una protección para esta versión del trabajo.

Si te atoras

  1. Un trabajo es más grande que su tarea más visible. Incluye planificación, documentación, comunicación y seguimiento.
  2. Pregunta quién recibe la culpa cuando una decisión automatizada causa daño.
  3. Un trabajo futuro necesita un usuario, tarea y responsabilidad reales, no solo un nombre nuevo.

Antes de entregar

  • Sube el análisis de seis tareas y el diseño del trabajo futuro.
  • Completa la reflexión en el comentario.

Reflexión

Escribe 2 o 3 oraciones: "En ____, la IA podría encargarse de ____, pero todavía se necesita una persona para ____ porque ____."

Banco de palabras: automatización · tarea · trabajo · colaboración · juicio · responsabilidad · habilidad

resource.body:
AI Ethics · Day 7 of 10

AI Ethics Debate Preparation

Represent one stakeholder with claims, evidence, a counterargument, and a clear opening statement.

  • Tool: unit evidence and teacher-provided role
  • Time: one class period
  • Turn in: completed debate-prep sheet and reflection
  • English
  • Español

English

Words for today: claim · evidence · counterargument

What to do

  1. Record the motion: Should schools use AI to grade student essays? Record your assigned stakeholder role.
  2. Write the stakeholder's position and three claims. Support every claim with evidence from a named unit day or a traceable source.
  3. Write the strongest counterargument against your position. Answer it with evidence instead of repeating the original claim.
  4. Draft a two-minute opening: position, two strongest claims, evidence, and the tradeoff your stakeholder is willing to accept.
  5. Prepare one question for another stakeholder and one full-sentence response starter.

If you get stuck

  1. You are representing a role, not announcing your personal belief.
  2. If your evidence is only an opinion, replace it with a unit activity or source you can name.
  3. You may read the opening from the prep sheet during the debate.

Before you submit

  • Upload the prep sheet with three claims, evidence, counterargument, response, opening, and question.
  • Complete the reflection in the submission comment.

Reflection

Write 2 or 3 sentences: "My strongest evidence is ____. The counterargument I still need to answer better is ____."

Word bank: claim · evidence · counterargument · rebuttal · stakeholder · position · source

Español

Palabras de hoy: claim (afirmación) · evidence (evidencia) · counterargument (contraargumento)

Qué hacer

  1. Anota la moción: ¿Deben las escuelas usar IA para calificar ensayos? Anota tu papel asignado.
  2. Escribe la posición y tres afirmaciones de tu parte interesada. Apoya cada una con evidencia de un día de la unidad o una fuente rastreable.
  3. Escribe el contraargumento más fuerte. Contéstalo con evidencia en vez de repetir la afirmación original.
  4. Prepara una apertura de dos minutos: posición, dos afirmaciones, evidencia y el intercambio que tu parte acepta.
  5. Prepara una pregunta para otra parte y un inicio de respuesta en una oración completa.

Si te atoras

  1. Representas un papel; no estás anunciando tu creencia personal.
  2. Si tu evidencia es solo una opinión, reemplázala con una actividad o fuente que puedas nombrar.
  3. Puedes leer la apertura de tu hoja durante el debate.

Antes de entregar

  • Sube la hoja con tres afirmaciones, evidencia, contraargumento, respuesta, apertura y pregunta.
  • Completa la reflexión en el comentario.

Reflexión

Escribe 2 o 3 oraciones: "Mi evidencia más fuerte es ____. El contraargumento que todavía necesito contestar mejor es ____."

Banco de palabras: afirmación · evidencia · contraargumento · refutación · parte interesada · posición · fuente

AI Ethics · Day 8 of 10

AI Ethics Debate

Use evidence to explain one stakeholder's position, answer another argument, and evaluate the tradeoffs.

  • Tool: class debate
  • Time: one class period
  • Turn in: prep sheet, opening, counterargument response, and reflection
  • English
  • Español

English

Words for today: rebuttal · position · tradeoff

What to do

  1. Review the 100-point rubric and keep your Day 7 prep sheet open.
  2. Deliver a two-minute opening with a clear position and at least two specific pieces of evidence.
  3. Listen to the other stakeholders. Record the strongest counterargument and answer it without attacking the speaker.
  4. Follow the timer and discussion norms. Vote on the strongest evidence after every group drops its assigned role.
  5. Record one argument that changed, complicated, or strengthened your thinking.

If you get stuck

  1. If you lose your place, return to the one-sentence position.
  2. Say what you know and name the evidence instead of inventing an answer.
  3. Challenge the claim, source, assumption, or tradeoff, not the person.

Before you submit

  • Upload the Day 7 prep sheet and debate notes.
  • Record, upload, or type the two-minute opening using the allowed Canvas option.
  • Complete the reflection in the submission comment and check all four rubric categories.

Reflection

Write 3 or 4 sentences: "I argued that ____. The argument that made me think hardest was ____ because ____. My response is ____."

Word bank: rebuttal · evidence · tradeoff · stakeholder · position · counterargument

Español

Palabras de hoy: rebuttal (refutación) · position (posición) · tradeoff (intercambio)

Qué hacer

  1. Revisa la rúbrica de 100 puntos y mantén abierta la hoja del Día 7.
  2. Presenta una apertura de dos minutos con una posición clara y al menos dos evidencias específicas.
  3. Escucha a las otras partes. Anota el contraargumento más fuerte y contéstalo sin atacar a la persona.
  4. Sigue el tiempo y las normas. Vota por la evidencia más fuerte después de que todos dejen sus papeles asignados.
  5. Anota un argumento que cambió, complicó o fortaleció tu forma de pensar.

Si te atoras

  1. Si pierdes tu lugar, regresa a la posición de una oración.
  2. Di lo que sabes y nombra la evidencia en vez de inventar una respuesta.
  3. Cuestiona la afirmación, fuente, suposición o intercambio, no a la persona.

Antes de entregar

  • Sube la hoja del Día 7 y tus notas del debate.
  • Graba, sube o escribe la apertura de dos minutos usando la opción permitida en Canvas.
  • Completa la reflexión en el comentario y revisa las cuatro categorías de la rúbrica.

Reflexión

Escribe 3 o 4 oraciones: "Argumenté que ____. El argumento que más me hizo pensar fue ____ porque ____. Mi respuesta es ____."

Banco de palabras: refutación · evidencia · intercambio · parte interesada · posición · contraargumento

rubric.long_description: 2 minutes, position plus evidence

ratings.long_description: You state your stakeholder's position clearly and back it with more than two pieces of evidence, each one named to a day or a source.
You state your group's position and give at least two pieces of evidence, each tied to a day or a source.
You state a position but only one piece of evidence is tied to a day or a source.
You do not finish an opening statement, or you give opinions with no evidence from the unit.

rubric.long_description: Your one minute of response

ratings.long_description: You answer the challenge that was actually made, say what the other group got right, and explain why your position still holds.
You use your minute to answer the challenge that was actually made.
You answer, but you switch to an easier question than the one you were asked.
You do not answer the counterargument, or you answer the person instead of the argument.

rubric.description: Debate norms and the class vote
rubric.long_description: How we debate here

ratings.long_description: You argue the argument every time, wait for the speaker and the timer, and your vote goes to the strongest argument even when it is not your side.
You argue the argument and not the person, stay inside the timer, and vote on the argument rather than on your friends.
You mostly follow the norms but talk over a speaker or the timer, or vote for a group instead of an argument.
You make it personal, talk over other speakers, or do not take the vote seriously.

rubric.long_description: What you turn in here

ratings.long_description: All three are here, and the reflection names a specific argument and says exactly why it made you think.
Prep sheet uploaded, 2-minute opening recorded or typed here, and the reflection posted in the comments in 3-4 sentences.
Two of the three are here, or the reflection is shorter than three sentences.
Only one of the three is here, or nothing is submitted.

resource.body:
AI Ethics · Day 9 of 10

Our AI Code of Ethics

Turn unit evidence into rules that name who must do what and how people can check whether it happened.

  • Tool: group poster or shared document
  • Time: one class period
  • Turn in: five-principle code, evidence notes, and reflection
  • English
  • Español

English

Words for today: principle · transparency · accountability

What to do

  1. Review the 100-point rubric before drafting. Return to the Day 1 topic and Days 2 through 8 evidence.
  2. Write at least five one-sentence principles covering bias, privacy, misinformation, transparency, and accountability.
  3. Each principle must name who must act, what the person or organization must do, and how someone could tell whether the rule was followed.
  4. Connect every principle to a named unit day, activity, or source. Include at least one principle for AI creators and one for AI users.
  5. Revise repeated principles, add group names, and make the final code readable for the Day 10 gallery walk.

If you get stuck

  1. If a principle only says 'be fair' or 'be responsible,' add the required action and who checks it.
  2. If you cannot connect a rule to evidence, return to the unit notes before keeping it.
  3. Merge duplicate rules and use the space for a missing category or audience.

Before you submit

  • Upload a readable image or file of the final group code and its evidence notes.
  • Complete the reflection in the submission comment and check all four rubric categories.

Reflection

Write 3 or 4 sentences: "The principle I argued hardest for is ____. The evidence from Day ____ supports it because ____."

Word bank: principle · bias · privacy · transparency · accountability · evidence · enforce

Español

Palabras de hoy: principle (principio) · transparency (transparencia) · accountability (rendición de cuentas)

Qué hacer

  1. Revisa la rúbrica de 100 puntos. Regresa al tema del Día 1 y a la evidencia de los Días 2 al 8.
  2. Escribe al menos cinco principios de una oración sobre sesgo, privacidad, desinformación, transparencia y rendición de cuentas.
  3. Cada principio debe nombrar quién actúa, qué debe hacer y cómo se puede comprobar si cumplió la regla.
  4. Conecta cada principio con un día, actividad o fuente. Incluye un principio para creadores de IA y uno para usuarios.
  5. Revisa principios repetidos, agrega los nombres del grupo y prepara un código legible para el recorrido del Día 10.

Si te atoras

  1. Si un principio solo dice 'sé justo' o 'sé responsable,' agrega la acción y quién la revisa.
  2. Si no puedes conectar la regla con evidencia, regresa a las notas antes de conservarla.
  3. Combina reglas repetidas y usa el espacio para una categoría o audiencia que falte.

Antes de entregar

  • Sube una imagen o archivo legible del código final y sus notas de evidencia.
  • Completa la reflexión en el comentario y revisa las cuatro categorías de la rúbrica.

Reflexión

Escribe 3 o 4 oraciones: "El principio que más defendí es ____. La evidencia del Día ____ lo apoya porque ____."

Banco de palabras: principio · sesgo · privacidad · transparencia · rendición de cuentas · evidencia · hacer cumplir

metadata.name: Day 9: Our AI Code of Ethics

rubric.long_description: Bias, privacy, misinformation, transparency, accountability

ratings.long_description: Your code has more than five principles and still covers bias, privacy, misinformation, transparency, and accountability.
Your code has at least five principles and covers bias, privacy, misinformation, transparency, and accountability.
You have five principles but one of the five areas is missing.
You have fewer than five principles, or two or more of the areas are missing.

rubric.long_description: One sentence saying who must do what

ratings.long_description: Every principle is one clear sentence naming who must do what, and somebody outside this class could check whether it was followed.
Each principle is one clear sentence saying who must do what, in language a 6th grader could follow.
Some principles say who must do what; others are wishes like "AI should be fair" that nobody can check.
Most principles are general statements with nobody named and nothing to check.

rubric.long_description: Name the day and the activity or source

ratings.long_description: Every principle names the day and the activity or source it came from, and the principles draw on several different days.
Every principle is tied to something you saw in this unit, with the day and the activity or source named.
Some principles name a day; others have no evidence behind them.
The code could have been written on Day 1, with no evidence from the unit attached.

rubric.long_description: Creators, users, and readers outside your group

ratings.long_description: A stranger could read it start to finish and know who each rule is for; creators and users both have rules, your group names are on it, and a poster reads clearly from six feet away.
At least one principle is for AI creators and at least one is for AI users, your group names are on it, and a poster is readable from six feet away.
All the principles point at companies, or the group names are missing, or a reader has to stand close to read it.
It was written for your group only, and a reader at tomorrow's gallery walk cannot follow it.

resource.body:
AI Ethics · Day 10 of 10

Gallery Walk and Final Reflection

Test the class codes against new questions and explain how your own position changed.

  • Tool: class gallery walk
  • Time: one class period
  • Turn in: feedback record and individual final reflection
  • English
  • Español

English

Words for today: responsibility · feedback · evidence

What to do

  1. Post or open the group code. Each group member should be ready to explain one principle and the evidence behind it.
  2. Visit every other code. Leave two specific notes on each: one strength tied to evidence and one question, missing case, or possible revision.
  3. Return to your group's code. Record one piece of feedback you would use and one principle from another group you wish your code included.
  4. Find your Day 1 answer about responsibility. Write what changed, what stayed the same, and the unit evidence that caused that result.
  5. Connect one responsibility to your own use of AI, information, or automated recommendations.

If you get stuck

  1. Feedback should name the principle or situation, not only say that the poster looks good.
  2. If your view did not change, explain what evidence now supports it more clearly.
  3. Use a named day or activity instead of writing only that the whole unit changed your mind.

Before you submit

  • Upload the feedback record and a 4- or 5-sentence final reflection, or record the reflection with Canvas.
  • The reflection must name the evidence that changed or strengthened your thinking.

Reflection

Use this frame if helpful: "I used to think ____. Now I think ____, because on Day ____ I learned ____. One responsibility I have as an AI user is ____."

Word bank: responsibility · feedback · evidence · bias · privacy · transparency · accountability

Español

Palabras de hoy: responsibility (responsabilidad) · feedback (retroalimentación) · evidence (evidencia)

Qué hacer

  1. Publica o abre el código del grupo. Cada integrante debe poder explicar un principio y su evidencia.
  2. Visita todos los otros códigos. Deja dos notas específicas en cada uno: una fortaleza basada en evidencia y una pregunta, caso faltante o revisión posible.
  3. Regresa al código de tu grupo. Anota una sugerencia que usarías y un principio de otro grupo que te gustaría incluir.
  4. Busca tu respuesta del Día 1 sobre responsabilidad. Escribe qué cambió, qué quedó igual y qué evidencia causó ese resultado.
  5. Conecta una responsabilidad con tu propio uso de IA, información o recomendaciones automáticas.

Si te atoras

  1. La retroalimentación debe nombrar el principio o la situación, no solo decir que el cartel se ve bien.
  2. Si tu opinión no cambió, explica qué evidencia ahora la apoya mejor.
  3. Usa un día o actividad con nombre en vez de decir solamente que toda la unidad cambió tu opinión.

Antes de entregar

  • Sube el registro de retroalimentación y una reflexión final de 4 o 5 oraciones, o graba la reflexión con Canvas.
  • La reflexión debe nombrar la evidencia que cambió o fortaleció tu forma de pensar.

Reflexión

Usa este marco si ayuda: "Antes pensaba ____. Ahora pienso ____, porque el Día ____ aprendí ____. Una responsabilidad que tengo como usuario de IA es ____."

Facilitator’s Guide · SW4 · College and Career Readiness

Facilitator’s Guide: Competition Pathways (CTSO)

Four browsing pages, one external link, and one graded check-in — this module is a menu, not a project.

📑 4 pages · 1 link🏆 5 points in the module📅 Dates change every year

The unit at a glance

Module itemWhat happensPoints
TSATechnology Student Association. Tabbed page: what TSA is, six popular starter events (Coding, Robotics, Video Game Design, Digital Photography, Data Science, Technical Design), the full middle-school event list, a four-step preparation path, and a TSA-vs-DI fit comparison.—
Destination ImaginationSeven challenge areas — Technical, Engineering, Scientific, Fine Arts, Improvisational, Service Learning, plus the Instant Challenge everyone does — with a preview video. Student-led teams: adults coach the process, not the solution.—
Film FestivalThe Middle School VILS Film Festival. Three categories (Animation/Motion Graphics, Documentary/News, Narrative/Story), five minutes maximum, up to three students per entry, a 200-word summary, and a six-part 180-point rubric.—
IgniteThe Ignite STEAM Competition at Verizon’s headquarters. Detailed challenges with full rubrics: Video Game Design (Ecosystem Adventure), Logo Design in GloForge, 3D Printing Mini-Sculpture, Rover Maze with a Sphero RVR, and Problem Solving (Weather the Storm). Two students per event, per school.—
TSA WebsiteExternal link to the national middle-school competition list. Opens in a new tab.—
Closing
Xello Check-in: 4-Year Course PlanStudents build a four-year high school course plan in Xello and upload a screenshot. Runs last, and it is the only graded item in the module.5

Materials + prep

  • This year’s actual dates, in your hand, before you open these pages with students. The pages are written evergreen on purpose — they say “mid-January,” “in the spring,” “ask your teacher” — so the calendar is yours to supply. Check the current TSA, Destination Imagination, Film Festival and Ignite dates each year and give students the real ones out loud.
  • The current Ignite competition packet, if you plan to enter. The page describes last cycle’s challenges in detail and they change.
  • A decision, made in advance, about which competitions your campus is actually entering. This module reads as a menu; students will pick something.
  • Xello through ClassLink for the check-in, and a sense of the high school course catalogue so you can answer questions about the four-year plan.
  • For the Film Festival: the Google Folder submission link for this year, and a plan for who films what.

Watch-fors

  • Every date on these pages is deliberately vague, and that is not an oversight. Film Festival submissions run mid-January, judging late February into early March, and the festival itself late March at Singley Academy. Ignite is a spring day at Verizon headquarters, morning to early afternoon. Confirm all of it annually — the pages will not go stale, but they also will not tell students when to show up.
  • The Ignite page says six challenges and describes five. Video Game Design, Logo Design, 3D Printing Sculpture, Rover Maze and Problem Solving are on the page in full. If the sixth matters to your students, get the current packet.
  • Ignite’s Rover Maze is a Sphero RVR event. Anyone who came through RVR Robotics is already trained for it — that is the strongest recruiting line in this module. Logo Design needs GloForge access, so check you have the machine before promising that one.
  • TSA and DI are genuinely different animals, and the TSA page says so. TSA is spec-driven: rubrics, artifacts, interviews. DI is a live performance with engineering inside the skit. Students who pick wrong usually picked on the name. Use the fit comparison at the bottom of the TSA page.
  • Links inside these pages sometimes will not open in the Canvas frame. Both the TSA and DI pages carry the same tip: right-click and open in a new tab. Say it before students start clicking.

Grading

Only one item in this module is graded: the Xello Check-in: 4-Year Course Plan, worth 5 points, submitted as a screenshot upload. The four competition pages and the TSA external link carry no points and no submission — they are there to be read and chosen from. If you want students accountable for exploring them, the check-in is the only hook currently in the gradebook.

Technology Student Association (TSA) • Competition Pathways

Competitive STEM events for makers, coders, designers, filmmakers, and problem-solvers.

  • 🧭 Overview
  • 🏁 Events
  • 🧰 Getting Ready
  • ❓ FAQ & Fit

What is TSA?

  • National STEM program with individual and team events across engineering, CS, media, and design.
  • Most events are artifact-driven (code, CAD, prototypes, videos) with clear rubrics and specs.
  • Compete at the regional and state level, with potential to go national.
Great for: builders • coders • designers Less acting • more specs & deliverables

Popular starter events

Coding

Team of 2 builds a program to solve a defined task. Languages allowed vary by prompt.

Robotics

Team designs and programs a robot to complete missions on a challenge field.

Video Game Design

Team of 2–6 builds a playable game with documentation and pitch.

Digital Photography

Individual photo portfolio around a theme with technical and artistic criteria.

Data Science & Analytics

Small team analyzes a dataset, builds visuals, and presents findings.

Technical Design

Team of 2 produces a design brief, sketches, CAD, and a portfolio.

Getting ready to compete

Pick your event

Choose one primary event. Teams form around shared interest and time commitment.

Read the rubric

Specs matter. Create a checklist from the rulebook. Prototype early; iterate weekly.

Build artifacts

Code, CAD, reports, videos, and displays. Keep files named and versioned.

Practice the pitch

Rehearse the interview or presentation. Aim for clear evidence and clean demos.

FAQ & Fit (TSA vs DI)

Is TSA like DI?

TSA leans technical with clear rubrics and artifacts; DI leans performance with skits and story builds.

  • TSA: spec-based builds, interviews, presentations
  • DI: live show with engineering/art inside the skit
Who should pick TSA?

Students who like coding, CAD, making, media production, and focused competition categories.

  • Prefer building over acting
  • Enjoy precise rules and checkpoints
  • Want individual or small-team options
Overview Browse Events How to Prepare
If a link won’t open inside Canvas, right-click → Open link in new tab.

Destination Imagination (DI) • Challenge Preview

Student-led teams build a solution to a challenge and perform it as a short show. Below: what DI is, this year’s challenge areas, and how it compares to TSA.

https://www.destinationimagination.org/challenge-experience/challenge-previews/

What is DI?

  • Team challenge chosen from categories below + a surprise Instant Challenge.
  • Make a story (skit), engineer props/tech, and perform live.
  • Student-run: you plan, build, rehearse; adults coach process, not solutions.
  • Scored on creativity, teamwork, and how well your build works on stage.
Best for students who like acting, storytelling, making/engineering, costumes, and collab.
DI preview video

Choose a Challenge Area

Technical

Build a device or mechanism that performs reliably on stage—then weave it into a story.

  • Good for: builders, coders, problem-solvers
  • Skills: prototyping, testing, storytelling

Engineering

Design and build a structure or object that meets weight/strength or task goals—then show it off in a skit.

  • Good for: tinkerers, designers, precise builders
  • Skills: materials, iteration, stagecraft

Scientific

Explain a science idea with a creative performance and a working demonstration or effect.

  • Good for: explainers, experimenters, visualizers
  • Skills: modeling, clarity, audience engagement

Fine Arts

Tell a story with bold design: sets, costumes, props, music, and visual tricks.

  • Good for: artists, performers, makers
  • Skills: design, composition, stage timing

Improvisational

Perform a skit built from surprise prompts, with almost no time to prepare.

  • Good for: actors, fast thinkers, storytellers
  • Skills: collaboration, adaptability, presence

Service Learning

Plan and complete a community project, then present the impact with evidence and a story.

  • Good for: organizers, advocates, communicators
  • Skills: research, outreach, reflection

Instant Challenge (Everyone)

5–8 minute surprise task. Build, communicate, or act—no adults helping, and a clock running.

  • Good for: quick thinkers, calm under pressure
  • Skills: planning fast, sharing roles, creativity

DI — When it’s a good fit

  • You like skits/acting and building props or effects.
  • You want one big team project + live performance.
  • You enjoy open-ended creativity over strict specs.
  • You want to blend engineering + art + story.

TSA — When it’s a better fit

  • You prefer individual or small-team events (coding, CAD, video, etc.).
  • You like clear specs/rules and judged submissions over live skits.
  • You want competitive STEM categories without performance.
  • You enjoy technical artifacts (robots, designs, software) as the focus.
Next steps: Talk with your teacher about teams and challenge picks. We’ll register once groups are set.
Tip: If a link won’t open inside Canvas, right-click → Open link in new tab.

• 🎬 Overview
  • 🎨 Best in Animation/Motion Graphics
  • 📽️ Best in Documentary/News
  • 🎭 Best in Narrative/Story
  • 📝 Judging Rubric
  • 📅 Deadlines & Guidelines

Overview

The Middle School VILS Film Festival is a film competition for middle school students. You enter in one of three categories, and every entry is scored on the same rubric.

Students can submit their original video projects in the following categories:

  • Best in Animation/Motion Graphics
  • Best in Documentary/News
  • Best in Narrative/Story

Prizes go to 1st, 2nd, and 3rd place in each category.

🎨 Best in Animation/Motion Graphics

Create an animated video using computer animation, hand-drawn animation, or motion graphics. It can be a fun story, a message, or an artistic expression.

Video Duration: Maximum of 5 minutes

Judging Criteria: Creativity, animation quality, and storytelling.

📽️ Best in Documentary/News

Make a documentary about a real-life person, event, or community issue. You can also create a news-style video covering an important topic.

Video Duration: Maximum of 5 minutes

Judging Criteria: Research, clarity, and impact.

🎭 Best in Narrative/Story

Tell a fictional story using video. This can include drama, action, comedy, horror, science fiction, or any other genre you can think of. Your video should have a clear plot, characters, and a resolution.

Video Duration: Maximum of 5 minutes

Judging Criteria: Storytelling, creativity, and acting (if applicable).

📝 Judging Rubric

Submissions will be evaluated based on the following criteria:

  • Flow & Coherency: Well-planned storyline that flows smoothly. (0-30 points)
  • Creativity: Originality and creativity in presenting the story or events. (0-30 points)
  • Technical Merit - Video: Effective use of camera angles, lighting, and editing. (0-30 points)
  • Technical Merit - Audio: Clear and appropriate use of sound effects, music, and voice clarity. (0-30 points)
  • Overall Impact: The video should evoke an appropriate response from the viewer and meet the intended category. (0-30 points)
  • Written Summary: A well-written summary that describes the video’s intent and creation process, with minimal grammatical errors. (0-30 points)

📅 Deadlines & Guidelines

Submission Deadline: Mid-January — check this year’s exact date with your teacher.

Judging Period: Late February into early March.

Film Festival Date: Late March, at Singley Academy — check this year’s exact date with your teacher.

Guidelines:

  • Videos must be original and cannot exceed 5 minutes in length.
  • Submissions should not include illegal behavior, prejudice, violence, weapons, or inappropriate content.
  • Each video should start with a title page, including the student’s name, school, and title of the video.
  • Submit your video and a 200-word summary describing the project through the provided Google Folder link.
  • Entries must include up to 3 students who worked on the project.

• 🏆 Overview
  • 🎮 Video Game Design
  • 🖌️ Logo Design

Overview

At the Ignite STEAM Competition, students from several schools compete in Science, Technology, Engineering, Art, and Math (STEAM) challenges.

Mark your calendars: The event is held at Verizon’s Headquarters in the spring, usually one day from morning to early afternoon. Ask your teacher for this year’s date and times.

The tabs above have the rules and the scoring rubric for each challenge.

Who can participate? Each school can send up to two students per event, so talk to your teacher and find a teammate, or enter as a solo competitor.

Video Game Design Challenge: Ecosystem Adventure

Overview: Middle school students are tasked with designing a video game that revolves around ecosystems. The game must have three distinct levels, each representing a different ecosystem (e.g., forest, ocean, desert, rainforest, etc.). The objective is to create a fun, educational game where the player solves an environmental problem in each ecosystem.

Key Requirements:

  • Theme: Ecosystem-based with three unique levels.
  • Problem-solving: Address environmental challenges in each level.
  • Platform: Students can use any game design platform (e.g., Scratch, Unity, Roblox).
Category Criteria Points
Creativity Game shows originality in concept, story, and design. Incorporates a unique approach to ecosystems. 10
Theme Relevance Each level accurately reflects a different ecosystem with a clear environmental problem to solve. 15
Problem-Solving Clear environmental problems are introduced, and the player is required to solve them in each level. 15
Gameplay Mechanics Game is functional, easy to navigate, and offers an appropriate level of challenge for the target age group. 10
Educational Value The game effectively teaches players about ecosystems and environmental challenges. 15
Level Design Each level is well-constructed, offering a visually distinct and engaging experience. 10
User Interface (UI) Game interface is intuitive and user-friendly. 10
Presentation Overall game presentation, including graphics, sound, and any written content, is cohesive and appealing. 10
Total Points 100

Logo Design Challenge

Overview: Students will design a 3D logo for one of three fictitious companies using GloForge. This challenge encourages branding, creativity, and design while considering the company's mission and values.

Options:

  • Lone Star Canyon State Park: Preserving the beauty of Texas Hill Country.
  • Roots & Harvest: Celebrating local food and sustainability.
  • Gulf Coast Marine Rescue: Ocean animal rescue and rehabilitation.
Category Criteria Points
Creativity & Originality Logo demonstrates an innovative and original design approach, incorporating creative use of shapes and elements. 15
Theme & Mission Alignment Logo clearly reflects the chosen company’s mission, values, and identity. 20
3D Design Execution Effective use of 3D design principles with clean and accurate detailing. 15
Symbolism & Meaning Incorporates symbols or visuals that meaningfully represent the company’s work and goals. 15
Technical Precision Well-executed technical details using GloForge, showing clean lines and smooth execution. 10
Aesthetic Appeal Visually appealing logo with balance, color, and composition appropriate for the company. 10
Functionality Logo is versatile and functional for use in various formats (print, digital, signage, etc.). 10
Total Points 100

3D Printing Mini-Sculpture Challenge: Elements of Nature

Overview: Students will create a 3D-printed mini-sculpture inspired by native Texas flora and fauna. The sculpture should capture the beauty of Texas' plant and animal life.

Key Guidelines:

  • Theme: Native Texas flora and fauna.
  • Size Restriction: Must fit within an 8-inch cube.
  • Primary Medium: 3D-printed filament, with optional post-print enhancements.
Category Criteria Points
Creativity & Originality The sculpture demonstrates a unique and creative interpretation of the chosen Texas flora or fauna. 15
Relevance to Theme The sculpture accurately represents native Texas flora and/or fauna, showcasing key details and characteristics. 20
3D Printing Precision The 3D print is clean and precise, with attention to detail and technical quality. 20
Post-Printing Alteration Effective use of additional materials or techniques to enhance the printed sculpture (if applicable). 15
Aesthetic Appeal The sculpture is visually appealing, with a harmonious and well-proportioned design. 10
Use of Technology Demonstrates proficient use of 3D printing technology and filament to achieve the design. 10
Size Compliance Sculpture adheres to the size restriction (no larger than 8 inches cubed). 10
Total Points 100

 

Rover Maze Challenge: A Drive Through Nature

Overview: Participants will code a Sphero RVR to navigate a nature-themed pathway filled with obstacles that require specific coding strategies to avoid.

Pathway Details:

  • Size: 9x12 canvas with various turns and width changes.
  • Theme: A pathway through natural obstacles.
  • Goal: Complete the path while minimizing mistakes.

 

Category Criteria Points
Distance Covered Points awarded for each checkpoint passed (indicated by a red strip of tape). 30
Teamwork Points based on the efficiency and intelligence of the navigation method. 10
Time Points awarded only if the pathway is completed. No points for unfinished pathways. 10
Obstacle Navigation Points awarded based on how well participants navigate specific obstacles. 30
Line Penalties Points deducted based on the number of line penalties incurred by crossing the boundaries of the pathway. -20
Total Points 100

Problem Solving Competition: "Weather the Storm"

Overview: In this challenge, students will explore the effects of hurricanes on specific locations and propose solutions to mitigate erosion and weathering’s impact on a bridge and a home. The competition will include a simulation using a stream table.

Key Guidelines:

  • Theme: "Weather the Storm" - Mitigating erosion caused by hurricanes.
  • Simulation: Construct a bridge and home on a stream table.
  • Presentation: Research findings and video demonstration.

 

Category Criteria Points
Research Information Detailed knowledge of topography, geography, and the pre- and post-hurricane environment for the selected location. 30
Presentation Quality The presentation is engaging, clear, and easy to understand. 10
Bridge Stability The bridge remains standing and undamaged during the stream table simulation. 20
Home Stability The home remains standing after the stream simulation. 20
Solution Effectiveness Effectiveness of the proposed solution to combat erosion and weathering on bridges and homes. 20
Total Points 100

⬡ Xello Check-in • College & Career Readiness ⬡

4-YEAR COURSE PLAN

Four years of high school, laid out on one screen.

⏱️ ~30 min
🛠️ Xello via ClassLink
💻 Your device
📤 Screenshot of my course plan
  • English
  • Español

📢 CTSO competitions run on pathways — you compete in the area you are already training in. Your course plan is where that training actually gets scheduled.

Today's words

course plan • graduation requirements • elective • pathway

1

Log in to Xello

Open ClassLink and click the Xello tile. Go through ClassLink, not a Google search — that is the only login that connects to your saved work.

2

Build your 4-year plan

Open Goals & Plans and go to your 4-year course plan. Xello shows your course history and the graduation requirements you still have to meet, then lets you place courses across all four years.

This is the longest check-in of the year: about 20 minutes of real work. No prerequisites, but open the plan you built during Machine Learning Week — your courses should point at it.

Watch the electives. That is where a CTSO pathway actually fits into a schedule.

3

Screenshot your plan

Open the plan so all four years are visible at once. Capture that screen.

• Chromebook: Ctrl + Show Windows

• Windows: Windows key + Shift + S

4

Upload the screenshot here

Attach the image to this assignment. Your work has to be readable in the picture — a blurry photo of your screen taken with a phone does not count.

💡 This one has a real deadline behind it

The plan is not final, but it is real: in the spring you submit course requests off it, and a parent or guardian approves it in Xello Family.

Courses have prerequisites of their own. A class you want as a junior often starts with something you have to pick as a freshman.

💬 Reflect

In the comments of your submission, finish this sentence:

"A high school course I put in my plan because of a CTSO pathway is ______ because ______."

✓ All four years filled in

📢 Las competencias de CTSO funcionan por trayectorias — compites en el área en la que ya te estás preparando. Tu plan de cursos es donde esa preparación de verdad se agenda.
