course plan (plan de cursos) • graduation requirements (requisitos de graduación) • elective (materia optativa) • pathway (trayectoria)

1

Entra a Xello

Abre ClassLink y haz clic en el cuadro de Xello. Entra por ClassLink, no por una búsqueda de Google — ese es el único acceso que se conecta con tu trabajo guardado.

2

Arma tu plan de 4 años

Abre Goals & Plans y ve a tu 4-year course plan. Xello te muestra tu historial de cursos y los requisitos de graduación que te faltan, y te deja acomodar los cursos en los cuatro años.

Este es el check-in más largo del año: como 20 minutos de trabajo real. No tiene requisitos previos, pero abre el plan que armaste en Machine Learning Week — tus cursos deben apuntar hacia allá.

Fíjate en las materias optativas. Ahí es donde una trayectoria de CTSO cabe de verdad en un horario.

3

Toma captura de tu plan

Abre el plan para que se vean los cuatro años a la vez. Captura esa pantalla.

• Chromebook: Ctrl + Mostrar ventanas

4

Sube la captura aquí

Adjunta la imagen a esta tarea. Tu trabajo tiene que leerse bien en la imagen — una foto borrosa de tu pantalla tomada con el celular no cuenta.

💡 Este tiene una fecha límite real detrás

El plan no es definitivo, pero sí es real: en la primavera envías tus solicitudes de cursos a partir de él, y un padre o tutor lo aprueba en Xello Family.

Los cursos tienen sus propios requisitos. Una clase que quieres en tercer año muchas veces empieza con algo que tienes que escoger en primero.

💬 Reflexiona

Four robot builds, one checkpoint, and a class of RVRs that have to be charged before any of it works.

Module itemWhat happensPoints
Drawing

Learn: Seeing with the RVRThe second interactive lesson. This one has a completely blank page in Canvas — the launch button is the whole item, and that is by design.0
Do: Seeing with RVRThe colour sensor on the underside of the robot reads a card and the LEDs change to match it. Walkthrough video on the page, worksheet through the assignment.5
Talking with RVRTwo robots pass messages over infrared, then the class builds one program together so the RVRs hold a shape the way a school of fish does. This is the biomimicry lesson and it needs more than one robot running at once.5
Closing
Xello Check-in: Volunteer Hours + Work ExperiencesStudents log one volunteer entry and one work experience with reflections, then upload a screenshot of the timeline. Runs last.5

Materials + prep

  • Sphero RVRs charged, and charged early. They do not come back from flat in a passing period. One robot per two or three students for most of the unit — but Talking with RVR needs at least two robots running at the same time, so plan that day around how many you actually have.
  • The Sphero Edu app or edu.sphero.com/code open and tested on a student device, with class code 4WDN5C confirmed still live before you teach Movement Blocks.
  • Markers and paper or butcher roll for the drawing runs, and a set of solid colour cards for the colour-sensor lesson.
  • Launch each assignment yourself once. The worksheets arrive through Google Assignments — the student’s copy is generated when they open the item from Canvas, so nothing needs distributing, but you should confirm the hand-back path works.
  • Xello through ClassLink for the closing check-in.

Watch-fors

  • The two “Learn:” items are interactive-lesson launches, not Canvas pages. They open in a new tab, and Learn: Seeing with the RVR shows an empty page in Canvas. That is normal. Say so before the first one or you will spend the period answering it.
  • Teach the core route by name: Drawing → Movement → Seeing → Talking. Biomagnification is an optional extension in Enrichment · Parked Alternates; teach it first if you choose to use it.
  • Where this sits in the AIR arc. This is Unit 2. Unit 0 (Intro to AI) is over in SW4, and Units 1 and 3 — Leaving Land and Sailing Home — are elsewhere in SW5. Unit 3’s temperature-bot lesson assumes students have done this module, so run it before Sailing Home.
  • The checkpoint is a study loop, not a gate. It carries the most points in the module (10) and allows unlimited attempts. Point students back at Learn: Drawing with RVR between tries — that is the resource it is written from.
  • Movement Blocks asks for the most and is worth nothing. It is the only lesson that sends students out to the Sphero Edu platform, it collects answers and screenshots, and it is currently set to 0 points. Give it a value if you want that work in the gradebook.

Grading

The module carries 30 points as built. Checkpoint: Drawing with RVR is 10; Do: Drawing with RVR, Do: Seeing with RVR and Talking with RVR are 5 each; the Xello check-in is 5. Learn: Drawing with RVR, Learn: Seeing with the RVR and Movement Blocks are all set to 0. The three worksheet lessons come back through Google Assignments, so the completed worksheet is what you grade.

🤖 RVR Robotics · Drawing

Learn: Drawing with RVR

Before you drive anything, see what the RVR can do with a marker attached to it.

🤖 Sphero RVR
📺 Two walkthroughs
🚀 Interactive lesson
1

Watch both walkthroughs

Watch these before you touch a robot so you know what a drawing run is supposed to look like.

2

Open the interactive lesson

📤 Turn in: Nothing here. This one is for learning — you build in Do: Drawing with RVR next.

🤖 Sphero RVR
🖊️ Drawing program
🏆 5 points

📝 Multiple choice

🤖 RVR Robotics · Movement

Movement Blocks

Drawing was about the marker. This one is about making the RVR go exactly where you tell it to.

🤖 Sphero RVR
👥 Partners allowed
📦 Answers + screenshots
1

Open the Sphero module

Go to edu.sphero.com/code and join with the class code below.

4WDN5C — enter it at edu.sphero.com/code.

2

Follow each step on the Sphero module

After each step, answer the questions and upload the required screenshot. You may work with a partner.

3

The worksheet attached to this assignment is where your answers and screenshots go.

📤 Turn in: Submit the worksheet with every question answered and every required screenshot attached.

🤖 RVR Robotics · Seeing

Do: Seeing with RVR

There is a colour sensor on the underside of the RVR. Teach the robot to react to whatever it rolls over.

🤖 Sphero RVR
🎨 Colour sensor + LEDs
🏆 5 points
1

Watch the walkthrough

This shows the colour sensor doing its job.

2

Build it

Complete the Seeing with RVR worksheet to practise using the Sphero RVR colour sensors to detect the colour around it and change its LED to match the colour card it is detecting.

🎨 What "seeing" means here

The sensor only reports the colour of the surface underneath the robot. Your program is what decides to do something about it — here, matching the LED to the card it just found.

📤 Turn in: Submit the worksheet through this assignment once the LED matches every colour card you test.

🤖 RVR Robotics · Talking

Talking with RVR

Two robots, one infrared conversation, and a pattern nobody has to steer.

🤖 Sphero RVR
📡 Infrared messaging
🏆 5 points
1

Watch the walkthrough

See what it looks like when two RVRs pass a message.

2

Build it, then build it together

Complete the Talking with RVR worksheet to learn more about IR, program your Sphero RVRs, and finally create your own program with your classmates to emulate a school of fish making patterns (biomimicry).

🐟 Biomimicry

Copying a pattern from nature to solve a design problem. A school of fish holds its shape without a leader — every fish just reacts to its neighbours. That is exactly what your robots are doing with IR.

📤 Turn in: Submit the worksheet through this assignment, including your class pattern program.

⬡ Xello Check-in • College & Career Readiness ⬡

VOLUNTEER HOURS + WORK EXPERIENCES

Work you already did, finally counted.

⏱️ ~25 min
🛠️ Xello via ClassLink
💻 Your device

  • English

📢 Half of robotics is doing a job nobody assigned you: charging the batteries, resetting the field, helping the team that is stuck. Xello has a place for exactly that kind of work.

Today's words

volunteer • community service • work experience • hours

1

Log in to Xello

Open ClassLink and click the Xello tile. Go through ClassLink, not a Google search — that is the only login that connects to your saved work.

2

Log volunteer hours

In About Me, open Experiences and add a volunteer or community service entry, including the hours you completed.

Then answer what you liked, what was challenging, and what you learned — about 7 minutes. Your 8th grade minimum is 1.

Church, a food drive, a park cleanup, helping at an elementary school, running the scoreboard — it all counts.

3

Log a work experience

Add a work experience the same way. Xello counts paid and unpaid work, so mowing lawns, babysitting, and helping at a family business all belong here.

Your 8th grade minimum is 1 work experience. Same three reflection prompts, about 7 minutes.

Screenshot both and upload

Your Xello resume in high school gets built straight out of this timeline.

BEFORE YOU PUBLISH | EDPUZZLE SETUP

Connect Edpuzzle before assigning

Use these public lesson links to add the videos to your Edpuzzle account and connect each lesson in this Canvas course:

  • Smart Solutions: micro:bit Intro: Edpuzzle lesson | original video
  • Coding Games on micro:bit: Edpuzzle lesson | original video

For each Edpuzzle assignment, choose Edit, keep Submission Type: External Tool, choose Find, then Edpuzzle. Select the matching lesson from My Content, save, and test it in Student View.

Open Edpuzzle's Canvas setup guide. If you are not using Edpuzzle, the original-video links above let you run the lesson without the integration.

⌁ Steel and Gold · Facilitator’s Guide

Coding Adventures (micro:bit)

Four block-coding lessons on real micro:bits, each one Learn → Do → Checkpoint. Everything you need to run the strand.

⏱️ ~6–8 class periods🎯 Make: four programs, ending in a game of their own🛠️ micro:bit · MakeCode blocks · Articulate RISE · EdPuzzle📝 135 points total

Run sheet

Each lesson block opens with its own Facilitator’s Guide page — that page holds the full written guide plus the presentation, worksheet and printable checkpoint for teaching the lesson live instead of sending students into the Learn lesson. This sheet is the order and the timing; the detail is one click down.

Module itemWhat happens~Time
Coding with micro:bit — four lessons in order. VilBot’s story runs through all four, and each build assumes the one before it.
Lesson 1: Intro to micro:bit and Block Coding — details, printables and the full written guide: the Lesson 1 guide page that opens this block
EdPuzzle | Smart Solutions: micro:bit IntroVideo that pauses on its own for embedded questions. The page sets the house rule: a score of 90 or higher before a student may pick up a micro:bit. 0 pts in Canvas — see grading.~20 min
Learn: Lesson 1The Learn lesson, hosted in Articulate RISE. Launches out of Canvas into the tool. 0 pts.20–30 min
Do: Lesson 1First board day, and the story setup — students meet VilBot here. They write their first block program and send it to a real micro:bit. Worksheet is linked inside the assignment — the link hands each student their own Google Doc copy. 5 pts.1 period
Checkpoint: Lesson 1Canvas quiz, 4 questions, unlimited retakes, highest score kept. 4 pts.~10 min
Lesson 2: Inputs and Outputs — details and printables: the Lesson 2 guide page
Learn: Lesson 2The Learn lesson, hosted in Articulate RISE. Launches out of Canvas into the tool. 0 pts.20–30 min
Do: Lesson 2Give the board something to react to and something to say back. Inputs and outputs paired up, then one program that uses both. Worksheet is linked inside the assignment — the link hands each student their own Google Doc copy. 5 pts.1 period
Checkpoint: Lesson 2Canvas quiz, 3 questions, unlimited retakes. 3 pts.~10 min
Lesson 3: Radio and If Statements — details and printables: the Lesson 3 guide page
Learn: Lesson 3The Learn lesson, hosted in Articulate RISE. Launches out of Canvas into the tool. 0 pts.20–30 min
Do: Lesson 3Two boards talk. Students program a micro:bit radio and help VilBot send secret messages to her sidekick Mr. Whiskers. Needs students working in pairs with two boards. Worksheet is linked inside the assignment — the link hands each student their own Google Doc copy. 5 pts.1 period
Checkpoint: Lesson 3Canvas quiz, 3 questions, unlimited retakes. 3 pts.~10 min
Lesson 4: Coding Games on the micro:bit — details and printables: the Lesson 4 guide page
EdPuzzle | Coding Games on micro:bitSecond video, and it sets up the game students build in this lesson. 0 pts in Canvas.~20 min
Learn: Lesson 4The Learn lesson, hosted in Articulate RISE. Launches out of Canvas into the tool. 0 pts.20–30 min
Do: Lesson 4Rock Paper Scissors first, then students invent a game of their own for VilBot’s cousin LilBot. The longest build in the module. Worksheet is linked inside the assignment — the link hands each student their own Google Doc copy. 100 pts.1–2 periods
Checkpoint: Lesson 4Canvas quiz, 10 questions, unlimited retakes. The biggest checkpoint in the module by a wide margin. 10 pts.~15 min

⚠️ The 90-or-above rule is not enforced by Canvas

The first EdPuzzle tells students they need 90 or higher before they may use a micro:bit, and that is the gate protecting your hardware. Both EdPuzzle items are external tool launches set to 0 points in Canvas, so the score never reaches your gradebook. Check it in the EdPuzzle dashboard before you hand out boards, or the rule is a suggestion. What sits behind the gate is all of the graded work: the four Do lessons, including Do: Lesson 4 at 100 points, the module’s Major grade.

Materials + prep

  • Physical micro:bits counted against your roster before Lesson 1, with battery packs and fresh batteries or USB data cables. A charge-only cable will not flash a board, and that failure looks exactly like broken code.
  • Lesson 3 needs two boards talking — plan the pairing before that day, not during it. Whatever grouping you set in Lesson 1, keep it, so partners are not relearning the board each lesson.
  • The four worksheets are linked inside the Do assignments as Google Docs that hand over a copy the moment a student clicks. Open all four yourself first and confirm they copy from a student account.
  • EdPuzzle roster ready before Lesson 1, and pop-ups allowed on student devices — EdPuzzle, the Learn launches and MakeCode all open outside Canvas.
  • Printables live on the lesson guide pages — presentation, worksheet and printable checkpoint for each lesson, if you would rather teach it live than send students through Articulate RISE.
  • Background reading before you teach the strand: the program’s facilitator guide for Coding Adventures (Google Doc).

Watch-fors

  • A blank Learn page is not a broken Learn page. All four Learn items are external tool launches into Articulate RISE. Their Canvas description is empty on purpose — the lesson lives inside the launch. Click through one yourself before class and do not spend an evening trying to fill a page that is meant to be empty.
  • The story is load-bearing. Do not skip Lesson 1’s setup. VilBot is introduced in Lesson 1, her sidekick Mr. Whiskers is who the Lesson 3 radio messages are sent to, and her cousin LilBot is who the Lesson 4 game is built for. Start at Lesson 3 and the names arrive with no one attached to them.
  • Check publication before class. The EdPuzzle, Learn and Do items are already published; all four checkpoint quizzes, all five guide pages and the module itself are not. Walk the list once before you open it to students, or your class finishes Lesson 1 and finds no checkpoint.
  • Lesson 4 is not a fourth ordinary lesson. Its checkpoint is 10 questions where the others are 3 or 4, and its Do is an open build after a guided one. Leave more room for it than the run sheet’s minimum, and expect the invent-your-own-game half to run into a second period.

Grading — 135 points

✓ Do: Lesson 4 is the module’s Major grade, at 100 points. The other three Do assignments are Minor grades, 5 points each (15 total). All four are graded on the finished worksheet, uploaded as a file or as a share link.

✓ Checkpoints are 4, 3, 3 and 10 points for Lessons 1 through 4, all Minor grades — one point per question, unlimited retakes, highest score kept. The Lesson 4 checkpoint is half the checkpoint points on its own.

✓ The four Learn items are 0 points — completion happens inside RISE.

✓ Both EdPuzzles are 0 points. That is deliberate here, but it does mean the 90-percent hardware gate lives in EdPuzzle and nowhere else. If you want it in the gradebook, set the points yourself.

The module is unpublished. Publish as you go, and check the quizzes.

BEFORE YOU PUBLISH | EDPUZZLE SETUP

Connect Edpuzzle before assigning

Use these public lesson links to add the videos to your Edpuzzle account and connect each lesson in this Canvas course:

  • Seasick with Empathy: Edpuzzle lesson | original video

For each Edpuzzle assignment, choose Edit, keep Submission Type: External Tool, choose Find, then Edpuzzle. Select the matching lesson from My Content, save, and test it in Student View.

Open Edpuzzle's Canvas setup guide. If you are not using Edpuzzle, the original-video links above let you run the lesson without the integration.

Facilitator’s Guide · SW5 · AIR Unit 1

Facilitator’s Guide: AIR Unit 1 — Leaving Land

Five lessons from an empathy interview to a game enemy that chases the player.

📅 5 lessons🔧 micro:bit · MakeCode Arcade🏆 25 points in the module

The unit at a glance

Module itemWhat happensPoints
Lesson 1: Seasick with Empathy
Learn: Lesson 1 Seasick with EmpathyInteractive lesson launch, opens in a new tab. Blank page in Canvas — the button is the item.0
EdPuzzle | Seasick with EmpathyThe video with questions inside the player. Run it before the activity; the activity opens by telling students they have already watched it.0
Activity: Seasick with EmpathyThe unit kickoff. Partners write five open-ended questions, interview each other, and fill an empathy map — Say, Do, Think, Feel — then write a problem statement. Answers are typed into Canvas.5
Lesson 2: micro:bit Light Meter
Learn: micro:bit Light MeterInteractive lesson launch. Blank page in Canvas.0
Do: micro:bit Light MeterThe LED screen is turned into a light sensor reading 0–255. Students build it in MakeCode, download to the micro:bit, and test it bright and covered.5
Lesson 3: Crab Cruisin’ with micro:bit
Learn: Crab Cruisin’ with micro:bitInteractive lesson launch. Blank page in Canvas.0
Do: Crab Cruisin’ with micro:bitStudents design their own game on the 5×5 screen — what the player controls, what winning is, what losing is — then hand it to a partner to playtest and fix one thing that confused them.5
Lesson 4: Code a Game in MakeCode Arcade
Learn: Lesson 4 Ocean Games in MakeCode ArcadeInteractive lesson launch. Blank page in Canvas.0
Do: Lesson 4 Ocean Games in MakeCode ArcadeOff the tiny screen and into full sprites and backgrounds at arcade.makecode.com. The Microsoft sign-in happens here and everything after it depends on that account.5
Lesson 5: AI Enemies in MakeCode Arcade
Lesson 5: AI Enemies in MakeCode ArcadeStudents reopen their Lesson 4 game from My Projects and add an enemy that reacts to the player, then tune it until it is hard but beatable. The page names the difference between rule-following game AI and a trained model.5

Materials + prep

  • A class set of micro:bits with battery packs and USB cables, tested. Lessons 2 and 3 both download code to the device; a micro:bit with a dead battery reads as broken code to a student.
  • Microsoft accounts working at arcade.makecode.com, checked on a student device before Lesson 4. Not Google, not Clever — the page says so and it is the single most common failure in this unit.
  • EdPuzzle class code tested, for Lesson 1.
  • Partners assigned for the Lesson 1 interviews. This is a talking lesson before it is a building lesson, and it sets up the whole unit.
  • Each Google Assignments worksheet opened once by you, so you know the hand-back path works. The student copy generates when they launch the item from Canvas.

Watch-fors

  • Sign in first, or Lesson 5 has nothing to open. Lesson 5 starts by opening the Lesson 4 game from My Projects. If a student built Lesson 4 signed out, that project is gone and they start over. On shared laptops, have them sign in with Remember Me turned off so the next class does not land in their account.
  • The four “Learn:” items launch an interactive lesson in a new tab and show a blank page in Canvas. Nothing is broken. Tell students once, at Lesson 1.
  • Activity: Seasick with Empathy now collects a written response in Canvas — students type the empathy map and problem statement into the submission box. It is a 5-point Minor grade, so the empathy map that opens the unit does reach the gradebook.
  • The micro:bit lessons lean on earlier units and say so. Lesson 2 refers back to Coding Adventures for inputs and outputs, Lesson 3 to the micro:bit games lesson, Lesson 4 to Video Game Design for the Arcade workflow. If a student did not take those, the lesson still stands alone — but the confidence gap is real, so pair them up.
  • Two items are currently unpublished — Learn: Lesson 1 Seasick with Empathy and the Lesson 4 heading. Publish them when you set the unit live, or Lesson 1 opens with a video students cannot reach and Lesson 4 arrives without its heading.

Grading

Five items carry points, all Minor grades at 5 points each — 25 total: Activity: Seasick with Empathy, Do: micro:bit Light Meter, Do: Crab Cruisin’, Do: Ocean Games and Lesson 5: AI Enemies. There is no Major grade in this module. Every “Learn:” launch and the EdPuzzle are set to 0. The four Do lessons submit their worksheets through Google Assignments; the Activity is typed into Canvas.

Open Edpuzzle's Canvas setup guide

No Edpuzzle? Use the original video. Review the questions in the Edpuzzle first so you can pause for them or move them into Canvas.

WATCH AND RESPOND | MIRA Y RESPONDE

Seasick with Empathy

English

  1. Open the Edpuzzle and watch the full video.
  2. The video pauses for 16 questions. Answer each one before you continue.
  3. Turn on captions and rewind before answering if you missed something.
  4. Finish inside Edpuzzle. There is no separate file to upload.

Español

  1. Abre Edpuzzle y mira el video completo.
  2. El video se detiene para 16 preguntas. Contesta cada una antes de continuar.
  3. Activa los subtítulos y regresa el video antes de contestar si se te escapó algo.
  4. Termina dentro de Edpuzzle. No hay otro archivo que subir.

⬡ AIR · Leaving Land · Lesson 1 of 5 · Activity ⬡

SEASICK WITH EMPATHY

Three weeks in someone else's house. What would you need?

📅 Lesson 1 of 5
🛠️ Interview + Empathy Map
⏱️ ~45 min
📦 Empathy map + problem statement
  • English
  • Español

📢 Pretend you and your partner swap homes and families for three weeks. Not your bed. Not your kitchen. Not your rules. How would you feel about that? What would you need just to get through it? Today your job is to find out what your partner would need — by actually asking them.

Today's words

empathy • end-user • open-ended question • empathy map • problem statement

1

Learn: why empathy belongs in AI

Watch the EdPuzzle | Seasick with Empathy and answer the questions inside it. Empathy is the first phase of design thinking, and it is where every good product starts.

2

Part 1 — Write 5 interview questions

Write 5 questions that will teach you what your partner actually needs. Make them open-ended, so your partner can tell you more than yes or no.

Think about eating, sleeping, washing clothes, and getting to school. For example:

• How do you get ready for a school day?

• How do you like to relax in the evening? TikTok? Call of Duty?

3

Part 2 — Interview your partner

Ask your questions out loud. Then do the harder part:

• Listen to the whole answer before you write anything

• Watch what they do while they answer

• Write a short note for every answer in the map below

• Ask a follow-up question that is not on your list if something surprises you

4

Part 3 — Record it on your Empathy Map

Fill in the four quadrants in this order: Say, Do, Think, Feel. The first two you can observe. The last two you have to infer.

Say

Quotes or paraphrases — write down their actual words

Think

What is important to them? What is not?

Do

Actions and non-verbals — a joke? an eyeroll? a sigh?

Feel

How would you feel if you were in their situation?

5

Part 4 — Write your problem statement

Now put it in one sentence. This is what designers write before they build anything.

Our End-User, ______ (partner's name), needs help changing ______ (some quality in their life) because they are affected by ______ (what will living in a new home for three weeks do to them?).

6

Part 5 — Tips to survive at your home

You know your partner's needs now, and you are the expert on your own house. Write the tips that would actually help them. For example:

• How to make annoying brothers and sisters go away

• Where to find a phone charger or a toothbrush

• Does someone depend on you for something?

• What can you do for fun?

• Where the snacks are, and what is off limits

🎥 Need the directions again?

Your teacher has the Seasick with Empathy activity video queued up in class. If you were out, start with the EdPuzzle below — it covers the same empathy ideas — then catch the activity video with your teacher.

▶ EdPuzzle | Seasick with Empathy

🔍 OPEN-ENDED, NOT YES OR NO

A yes-or-no question ends the conversation. An open-ended question keeps it going.

• Closed: "Do you like breakfast?" → Open: "Walk me through your morning."

• Closed: "Do you have chores?" → Open: "What are you responsible for at home?"

• Closed: "Do you take the bus?" → Open: "How do you get to school?"

If your partner answered in one word, the question was closed. Rewrite it.

💬 Reflect

Write your answer, then post it in the comments of this assignment in 2-3 sentences:

"If I lived at my partner's house for three weeks, the hardest thing for me would be ______. The most important thing my partner would need at my house is ______, because ______."

Word Bank

empathy • end-user • needs • observe • open-ended • Say • Think • Do • Feel • problem statement

✅ By the end of this activity:

✓ Completed the empathy EdPuzzle

✓ Wrote 5 open-ended interview questions

✓ Interviewed my partner and took notes on every answer

✓ Filled in all four quadrants of my Empathy Map

✓ Wrote a problem statement for my end-user

✓ Wrote survival tips for my partner about my home

📢 Imagina que tú y tu compañero intercambian casa y familia por tres semanas. No es tu cama. No es tu cocina. No son tus reglas. ¿Cómo te sentirías? ¿Qué necesitarías nada más para sobrevivirlo? Hoy tu trabajo es averiguar qué necesitaría tu compañero, preguntándoselo de verdad.

Palabras de hoy

empathy (empatía) • end-user (usuario final) • open-ended question (pregunta abierta) • empathy map (mapa de empatía) • problem statement (planteamiento del problema)

1

Learn: por qué la empatía va en la IA

Mira el EdPuzzle | Seasick with Empathy y contesta las preguntas que trae. La empatía es la primera fase del design thinking, y es donde empieza todo buen producto.

2

Parte 1 — Escribe 5 preguntas de entrevista

Escribe 5 preguntas que te enseñen qué necesita tu compañero de verdad. Hazlas abiertas, para que tu compañero te pueda contar más que un sí o un no.

Piensa en comer, dormir, lavar la ropa y llegar a la escuela. Por ejemplo:

• ¿Cómo te alistas para un día de escuela?

• ¿Cómo te gusta relajarte en la noche? ¿TikTok? ¿Call of Duty?

3

Parte 2 — Entrevista a tu compañero

Haz tus preguntas en voz alta. Luego viene lo más difícil:

• Escucha toda la respuesta antes de escribir nada

• Fíjate en lo que hace mientras contesta

• Escribe una nota corta por cada respuesta en el mapa de abajo

• Haz una pregunta de seguimiento que no esté en tu lista si algo te sorprende

4

Parte 3 — Anótalo en tu Mapa de Empatía

Llena los cuatro cuadrantes en este orden: Say, Do, Think, Feel. Los primeros dos los puedes observar. Los últimos dos los tienes que deducir.

Say (Dice)

Citas o paráfrasis: anota sus palabras tal como las dijo

Think (Piensa)

¿Qué es importante para él o ella? ¿Qué no lo es?

Do (Hace)

Acciones y gestos: ¿una broma? ¿voltea los ojos? ¿suspira?

Feel (Siente)

¿Cómo te sentirías tú en su situación?

5

Parte 4 — Escribe tu planteamiento del problema

Ahora resúmelo en una oración. Esto es lo que los diseñadores escriben antes de construir nada.

Nuestro usuario final, ______ (nombre de tu compañero), necesita ayuda para cambiar ______ (algo de su vida) porque le afecta ______ (¿qué le va a provocar vivir tres semanas en una casa nueva?).

6

Parte 5 — Tips para sobrevivir en tu casa

Ya conoces las necesidades de tu compañero, y tú eres el experto en tu propia casa. Escribe los tips que de verdad le servirían. Por ejemplo:

• Cómo hacer que los hermanos molestos se vayan

• Dónde encontrar un cargador o un cepillo de dientes

• ¿Alguien depende de ti para algo?

• ¿Qué se puede hacer para divertirse?

• Dónde están los snacks y qué no se vale tocar

🎥 ¿Necesitas las instrucciones otra vez?

Tu maestra tiene listo el video de la actividad Seasick with Empathy en clase. Si faltaste, empieza con el EdPuzzle de abajo, que cubre las mismas ideas de empatía, y luego ve el video de la actividad con tu maestra.

▶ EdPuzzle | Seasick with Empathy

🔍 ABIERTAS, NO DE SÍ O NO

Una pregunta de sí o no acaba la conversación. Una pregunta abierta la mantiene viva.

• Cerrada: "¿Te gusta desayunar?" → Abierta: "Cuéntame cómo es tu mañana."

• Cerrada: "¿Tienes quehaceres?" → Abierta: "¿De qué eres responsable en tu casa?"

• Cerrada: "¿Te vas en camión?" → Abierta: "¿Cómo llegas a la escuela?"

Si tu compañero contestó con una sola palabra, la pregunta era cerrada. Vuelve a escribirla.

💬 Reflexiona

Escribe tu respuesta y luego publícala en los comentarios de esta tarea, en 2-3 oraciones en inglés:

(Si yo viviera en casa de mi compañero por tres semanas, lo más difícil para mí sería ______. Lo más importante que mi compañero necesitaría en mi casa es ______, porque ______.)

"If I lived at my partner's house for three weeks, the hardest thing for me would be ______. The most important thing my partner would need at my house is ______, because ______."

Word Bank / Banco de Palabras

empathy (empatía) • end-user (usuario final) • needs (necesidades) • observe (observar) • open-ended (abierta) • Say (dice) • Think (piensa) • Do (hace) • Feel (siente) • problem statement (planteamiento del problema)

✅ Al final de esta actividad:

✓ Completé el EdPuzzle de empatía

✓ Escribí 5 preguntas de entrevista abiertas

✓ Entrevisté a mi compañero y tomé notas de cada respuesta

✓ Llené los cuatro cuadrantes de mi Mapa de Empatía

✓ Escribí un planteamiento del problema para mi usuario final

✓ Escribí tips de supervivencia sobre mi casa para mi compañero

⬡ AIR · Leaving Land · Lesson 2 of 5 ⬡

MICRO:BIT LIGHT METER

Turn the LED screen into a sensor that reads the light around you.

  • English
  • Español

📢 The New Horizon has left land. Below deck there are no windows, so how does the crew know whether it is bright day or full dark outside? Your micro:bit can answer that, because the same LED screen that shows pictures can also read the light falling on it.

1

Open your worksheet

Click the assignment link on this page to open your own copy of the worksheet in Google. It has the build steps and the questions you will answer.

2

Build the light meter

Follow the worksheet to build your light meter in MakeCode, then download it to your micro:bit.

3

Test it in two places

Hold it under the classroom lights, then cup your hand over the screen. Watch the number change. If it does not change, check that you are reading light level and not something else.

4

Answer and turn in

Answer every question on the worksheet and turn it in here.

Do not see a worksheet when you open this assignment? Ask your teacher for it before you start.

🔦 You have done half of this already

In Coding Adventures you wired inputs to outputs: press button A, show a picture. The light sensor is just another input.

The only new part is what comes back. A button gives you pressed or not pressed. The light sensor gives you a number from 0 to 255, so your code has to decide how dark is dark enough.

✅ By the end of this lesson:

✓ Built my light meter and downloaded it to the micro:bit

✓ Tested it in bright light and with the screen covered

✓ Answered every question and turned in my worksheet

📢 El New Horizon ya salió de tierra. Abajo, en la bodega, no hay ventanas, entonces ¿cómo sabe la tripulación si afuera es de día o ya es de noche? Tu micro:bit te lo puede decir, porque la misma pantalla de LEDs que muestra dibujos también puede leer la luz que le cae encima.

1

Abre tu hoja de trabajo

Haz clic en el enlace de la tarea en esta página para abrir tu propia copia de la hoja de trabajo en Google. Ahí vienen los pasos y las preguntas que vas a contestar.

2

Construye el medidor de luz

Sigue la hoja de trabajo para armar tu medidor de luz en MakeCode y descárgalo a tu micro:bit.

3

Pruébalo en dos lugares

Ponlo debajo de las luces del salón y luego tapa la pantalla con la mano. Fíjate cómo cambia el número. Si no cambia, revisa que estés leyendo light level y no otra cosa.

4

Contesta y entrega

Contesta todas las preguntas de la hoja de trabajo y entrégala aquí.

¿No ves ninguna hoja de trabajo al abrir esta tarea? Pídesela a tu maestra antes de empezar.

🔦 Ya hiciste la mitad de esto

En Coding Adventures conectaste entradas con salidas: aprietas el botón A y sale un dibujo. El sensor de luz es otra entrada más.

Lo único nuevo es lo que regresa. Un botón te dice apretado o no apretado. El sensor de luz te da un número del 0 al 255, así que tu código tiene que decidir qué tan oscuro cuenta como oscuro.

✅ Al final de esta lección:

✓ Construí mi medidor de luz y lo descargué al micro:bit

✓ Lo probé con mucha luz y con la pantalla tapada

✓ Contesté todas las preguntas y entregué mi hoja de trabajo

⬡ AIR · Leaving Land · Lesson 3 of 5 ⬡

CRAB CRUISIN' WITH MICRO:BIT

Design a micro:bit game of your own, then hand it to somebody else to play.

  • English
  • Español

📢 You have made the micro:bit sense things and signal things. Now you make it play. Crab Cruisin' is your game, on a screen five LEDs wide, and the hardest part is not the code. It is deciding what makes the game fun.

1

Open your worksheet

Click the assignment link on this page to open your copy of the worksheet in Google. It walks you through planning the game before you write any code.

2

Plan before you code

On the worksheet, decide three things: what the player controls, what counts as winning, and what counts as losing. A game with no way to lose is not a game.

3

Build it and download it

Build your game in MakeCode and download it to your micro:bit. Test it yourself first.

4

Playtest with a partner

Hand it to somebody who has never seen it and say nothing. Watch where they get confused. Fix one thing they struggled with, then finish the worksheet and turn it in here.

Do not see a worksheet when you open this assignment? Ask your teacher for it before you start.

🎮 This is your second micro:bit game

Coding Adventures Lesson 4 was Coding Games on the micro:bit. Same editor, same download step, same tiny screen.

What is different here is that nobody is handing you the design. The tutorial told you what to build last time. This time it is yours.

✅ By the end of this lesson:

✓ Planned my game before I coded it

✓ Built it and downloaded it to my micro:bit

✓ Had a partner playtest it and fixed one thing that confused them

✓ Turned in my worksheet

📢 Ya hiciste que el micro:bit detectara cosas y avisara cosas. Ahora vas a hacer que juegue. Crab Cruisin' es tu juego, en una pantalla de cinco LEDs de ancho, y lo más difícil no es el código. Es decidir qué hace que el juego sea divertido.

1

Abre tu hoja de trabajo

Haz clic en el enlace de la tarea en esta página para abrir tu copia de la hoja de trabajo en Google. Ahí te guía para planear el juego antes de escribir código.

2

Planea antes de programar

En la hoja de trabajo decide tres cosas: qué controla el jugador, qué cuenta como ganar y qué cuenta como perder. Un juego donde no se puede perder no es un juego.

3

Constrúyelo y descárgalo

Arma tu juego en MakeCode y descárgalo a tu micro:bit. Pruébalo tú primero.

4

Pruébalo con un compañero

Dáselo a alguien que nunca lo ha visto y no le digas nada. Fíjate dónde se confunde. Arregla una cosa que se le dificultó, termina la hoja de trabajo y entrégala aquí.

¿No ves ninguna hoja de trabajo al abrir esta tarea? Pídesela a tu maestra antes de empezar.

🎮 Este es tu segundo juego en micro:bit

La Lección 4 de Coding Adventures fue Coding Games on the micro:bit. El mismo editor, el mismo paso de descarga, la misma pantallita.

Lo que cambia aquí es que nadie te está dando el diseño. La otra vez el tutorial te dijo qué construir. Esta vez es tuyo.

✅ Al final de esta lección:

✓ Planeé mi juego antes de programarlo

✓ Lo construí y lo descargué a mi micro:bit

✓ Un compañero lo probó y arreglé una cosa que lo confundió

✓ Entregué mi hoja de trabajo

⬡ AIR · Leaving Land · Lesson 4 of 5 ⬡

OCEAN GAMES IN MAKECODE ARCADE

Leave the five-by-five screen behind and build a real arcade game.

  • English
  • Español

📢 Twenty-five LEDs make a very small ocean. MakeCode Arcade gives you a full screen, real sprites and real backgrounds, so the game you build here can actually look like the sea it is set in.

1

Sign in first

Go to arcade.makecode.com and sign in with Microsoft. Not Google, not Clever. If you skip this step your game will not save.

2

Open your worksheet

Click the assignment link on this page to open your copy of the worksheet in Google, and follow its steps to build your ocean game.

3

Test, fix, finish

Play your own game all the way through at least once. Fix whatever breaks, then finish the worksheet and turn it in here.

Do not see a worksheet when you open this assignment? Ask your teacher for it before you start.

🕹️ You have used Arcade before

In Video Game Design you finished the skillmap tutorials and then remixed one of your own games. The Microsoft sign-in, My Projects, sprites, sharing a link: all of it works exactly the same way here.

The ocean is the new part. Everything else you already know.

✅ By the end of this lesson:

✓ Signed in to MakeCode Arcade with Microsoft so my work saves

✓ Built my ocean game and played it all the way through

✓ Fixed what broke and turned in my worksheet

📢 Veinticinco LEDs son un océano bien chiquito. MakeCode Arcade te da una pantalla completa, sprites de verdad y fondos de verdad, así que el juego que hagas aquí sí puede verse como el mar donde pasa.

1

Primero inicia sesión

Entra a arcade.makecode.com e inicia sesión con Microsoft. No con Google, no con Clever. Si te saltas este paso, tu juego no se va a guardar.

2

Abre tu hoja de trabajo

Haz clic en el enlace de la tarea en esta página para abrir tu copia de la hoja de trabajo en Google y sigue sus pasos para construir tu juego del océano.

3

Prueba, arregla, termina

Juega tu propio juego completo por lo menos una vez. Arregla lo que se descomponga, termina la hoja de trabajo y entrégala aquí.

¿No ves ninguna hoja de trabajo al abrir esta tarea? Pídesela a tu maestra antes de empezar.

🕹️ Ya usaste Arcade antes

En Video Game Design terminaste los tutoriales del skillmap y luego hiciste un remix de uno de tus juegos. El inicio de sesión con Microsoft, My Projects, los sprites, compartir el enlace: todo funciona igualito aquí.

Lo nuevo es el océano. Lo demás ya te lo sabes.

✅ Al final de esta lección:

✓ Inicié sesión en MakeCode Arcade con Microsoft para que se guarde mi trabajo

✓ Construí mi juego del océano y lo jugué completo

✓ Arreglé lo que se descompuso y entregué mi hoja de trabajo

Lesson 5: AI Enemies in MakeCode Arcade

resource.body:
⬡ AIR · Leaving Land · Lesson 5 of 5 ⬡

AI ENEMIES IN MAKECODE ARCADE

Give something in your game a mind of its own.

  • English
  • Español

📢 An enemy that sits still is scenery. An enemy that comes after you is a threat. The difference is a short list of rules the computer checks over and over, many times a second, and that is where your game runs into AI.

1

Open your game

Go to arcade.makecode.com, sign in with Microsoft, and open your ocean game from My Projects.

2

Open your worksheet

Click the assignment link on this page to open your copy of the worksheet in Google, and follow its steps to add an enemy that reacts to the player.

3

Tune the difficulty

Playtest until the enemy is hard but beatable. Too fast and nobody wants to play. Too slow and nobody has to try. Then finish the worksheet and turn it in here.

Do not see a worksheet when you open this assignment? Ask your teacher for it before you start.

🧠 Is that really AI?

You have met this idea twice already. In Intro to AI you wrote algorithms for HorizonBot, step-by-step rules a machine follows exactly. In Machine Learning Week you trained a model to sort things it had never seen.

Your enemy is the first kind. It is not thinking about you. It is checking a rule you wrote, over and over, very fast. Most of what people call game AI is exactly that, and knowing the difference is the whole point.

✅ By the end of this lesson:

✓ Added an enemy that reacts to the player

✓ Playtested until it was hard but beatable

✓ Turned in my worksheet

📢 Un enemigo que se queda quieto es decoración. Un enemigo que te persigue es una amenaza. La diferencia es una listita de reglas que la computadora revisa una y otra vez, muchas veces por segundo, y ahí es donde tu juego se topa con la IA.

1

Abre tu juego

Entra a arcade.makecode.com, inicia sesión con Microsoft y abre tu juego del océano desde My Projects.

2

Abre tu hoja de trabajo

Haz clic en el enlace de la tarea en esta página para abrir tu copia de la hoja de trabajo en Google y sigue sus pasos para agregar un enemigo que reaccione al jugador.

3

Ajusta la dificultad

Prueba el juego hasta que el enemigo esté difícil pero vencible. Si va muy rápido, nadie quiere jugar. Si va muy lento, nadie tiene que esforzarse. Luego termina la hoja de trabajo y entrégala aquí.

¿No ves ninguna hoja de trabajo al abrir esta tarea? Pídesela a tu maestra antes de empezar.

🧠 ¿Eso de verdad es IA?

Ya te topaste con esta idea dos veces. En Intro to AI escribiste algoritmos para HorizonBot, reglas paso a paso que la máquina sigue tal cual. En Machine Learning Week entrenaste un modelo para clasificar cosas que nunca había visto.

Tu enemigo es del primer tipo. No está pensando en ti. Está revisando una regla que tú escribiste, una y otra vez, muy rápido. Casi todo lo que la gente llama IA de videojuegos es exactamente eso, y saber la diferencia es justo de lo que se trata.

✅ Al final de esta lección:

✓ Agregué un enemigo que reacciona al jugador

✓ Probé el juego hasta que quedó difícil pero vencible

✓ Entregué mi hoja de trabajo

⛵ Sailing Home · Lesson 1 of 2

Conflicting Viewpoints

Two articles, same ocean, opposite conclusions. Work out what each one is actually claiming.

🧭 AEIOU organiser
🏆 5 points
1

It sets up what you are reading for.

2

Read both articles

Read them in either order, but read both before you decide anything.

Both readings

📄 Ocean Plastic Does Not Lead to Marine Life Population Decline

📄 Plastic Pollution Affects Sea Life Throughout the Ocean

3

Capture what each text says

Complete the AEIOU graphic organiser in the Lesson 1 worksheet to help you capture important information from each text.

⚖️ Both can be careful and still disagree

Two sources can each be accurate and still reach opposite conclusions, because they choose different evidence to put in front of you. Note what each article leaves out — that gap is usually the argument.

📤 Turn in: Submit your completed AEIOU organiser through this assignment.

⛵ Sailing Home · Lesson 2 of 2

RVR + micro:bit Temperature Bot

Mount a micro:bit on the RVR and send it out to take the temperature for you.

🏆 100 points
1

Watch the walkthrough

This shows the wiring and the code side by side.

2

Build the temperature bot

Complete the Lesson 2 worksheet to create a temperature sensor bot with the RVR + micro:bit.

🌡️ Sensor first, decision second

The micro:bit only reports a number. Your code is what decides which numbers count as too hot or too cold, and what the robot does about it. Change the threshold and you change the robot’s behaviour without touching the sensor.

resource.body:
🚨 Rescue Steel · Facilitator’s Guide

Save the Day with Smart Electronics

Two required micro:bit wiring lessons, then one extension lesson your class picks. Everything you need to run it.

⏱️ ~5–7 class periods🎯 Make: traffic light · possession arrow · one extension build🛠️ micro:bit + expansion board · Articulate RISE📝 26 or 120 points on the path you run

Run sheet

Each lesson block opens with its own Facilitator’s Guide page — that page holds the full written guide plus the presentation, worksheets and printable checkpoint for teaching the lesson live instead of sending students into the Learn module. This sheet is the order and the timing; the detail is one click down.

Module itemWhat happens~Time
Advanced micro:bit Circuits — Lessons 1 and 2 run in order, then the class picks ONE extension lesson
Lesson 1: Wiring LEDs with micro:bit Expansion Board — details, printables and the full written guide: the Lesson 1 guide page that opens this block
Learn: Lesson 1The Learn module, hosted in Articulate RISE. Launches out of Canvas into the tool. 0 pts.20–30 min
Do: Lesson 1First wiring day. Students seat the micro:bit in the expansion board, wire the LED modules, then program a working traffic light with realistic timing. Worksheet linked inside the assignment. 5 pts.1–2 periods
Checkpoint: Lesson 1Canvas quiz, 4 questions, unlimited retakes, highest score kept. 4 pts.~10 min
Lesson 2: Wiring and Programming Inputs — details and printables: the Lesson 2 guide page
Learn: Lesson 2The Learn module, hosted in Articulate RISE. Launches out of Canvas into the tool. 0 pts.20–30 min
Do: Lesson 2Wire the button module, prove the board is reading it, then build a basketball possession arrow that flips on a press. The debounce problem is the lesson. 5 pts.1 period
Checkpoint: Lesson 2Canvas quiz, 3 questions, unlimited retakes. 3 pts.~10 min
🔀 Extension: pick ONE of Lessons 3–4. This is a fork, not a sequence. Decide before Lesson 2 ends which one your class runs — the two Do assignments both tell students they do one or the other, and the kit you have on hand usually decides it for you.
Lesson 3: Servo Motors — extension option A. Details and printables: the Lesson 3 guide page
Learn: Lesson 3The Learn module, hosted in Articulate RISE. Launches out of Canvas into the tool. 0 pts.20–30 min
Do: Lesson 3Wire and test a servo, then let the micro:bit light sensor drive it — a sunshade for VilBot that opens and closes on its own. 5 pts.1–2 periods
Checkpoint: Lesson 3Canvas quiz, 4 questions, unlimited retakes. 4 pts.~10 min
Lesson 4: Advanced Inputs and Outputs — extension option B. Details and printables: the Lesson 4 guide page
Learn: Lesson 4The Learn module, hosted in Articulate RISE. Launches out of Canvas into the tool. 0 pts.20–30 min
Do: Lesson 4Buzzer, neopixel and touch module tested one at a time, then an open-ended build: a prototype educational toy for Lil Vil. The most open-ended work in the module. 100 pts.1–2 periods
Checkpoint: Lesson 4Canvas quiz, 3 questions, unlimited retakes. 3 pts.~10 min

🔀 Pick the extension before you start Lesson 3

Lessons 3 and 4 are alternatives. Servo motors (Lesson 3) needs servos on hand; the toy prototype (Lesson 4) needs buzzers, neopixels and touch modules and takes the loosest rein. Whichever you choose, the other block stays in the module unpublished — leave it that way rather than deleting it, so next year’s teacher still has the choice. The two do not weigh the same in the gradebook either: Lesson 4’s Do is the module’s 100-point Major grade, while Lesson 3’s Do is a 5-point Minor.

Materials + prep

  • Know which expansion kit you have before day one. Every Do assignment links two worksheets — one for the standard expansion board and one for the Kitronik kit. They are not interchangeable; the pin numbers differ. Open the pair for Lesson 1 and decide which one your class uses.
  • micro:bits, expansion boards and jumper wires counted against your roster before Lesson 1. Kit counts decide whether students work solo or in pairs, and that grouping should hold across all the lessons so partners are not relearning the board each time.
  • Power for every board: battery packs with fresh batteries, or USB cables long enough to reach. Students are told to cut power before rewiring, which only works if power is easy to cut.
  • Modules for the lessons you actually run: LED modules (Lesson 1), a button module (Lesson 2), servos (Lesson 3) or buzzer, neopixel and touch modules (Lesson 4).
  • Printables live on the lesson guide pages — presentation, worksheet, Kitronik worksheet and printable checkpoint for each lesson, if you would rather teach it live.
  • Background reading before you teach the module: the program’s facilitator guide for Save the Day with Smart Electronics (Google Doc).

Watch-fors

  • A blank Learn page is not a broken Learn page. All four Learn items are external tool launches into Articulate RISE. Their Canvas description is empty on purpose — the lesson lives inside the launch. Click through one yourself before class, allow pop-ups on student devices, and do not spend an evening trying to fill a page that is meant to be empty.
  • Lesson 1’s student worksheet link opens the teacher guide. Known issue, flagged and not silently repointed: the link labelled Worksheet: Lesson 1 in both the Do assignment and the Lesson 1 guide page resolves to the same Drive file as the facilitator guide above it. No separate Lesson 1 student worksheet exists anywhere in the course. The Kitronik worksheet is the real Lesson 1 student worksheet — send students to that one, or print it.
  • Lesson 4 has no printable checkpoint. Lessons 1, 2 and 3 each have one on their guide page; Lesson 4 does not, because none was produced. The Canvas quiz is the checkpoint for that lesson. Nothing is missing from your copy.
  • Wiring, not code, is what stalls Lesson 1. Budget the front of the period for seating boards and checking connections, and hold the class until every table has something that lights. When a light never comes on, the pin number in the code and the pin on the board disagree far more often than the wire is bad.

Grading — 26 or 120 points, depending on your extension

✓ Do: Lesson 4 is a Major grade, at 100 points. The other three Do assignments are Minor grades, 5 points each. All four are graded on the finished worksheet, uploaded as a file or as a share link.

✓ Checkpoints are 4, 3, 4 and 3 points for Lessons 1, 2, 3 and 4, all Minor grades — one point per question, unlimited retakes, highest score kept.

✓ The four Learn items are 0 points. Completion happens inside RISE, so track it there or in the Do work that follows.

✓ Lessons 1 and 2 come to 17 points, all Minor. Add Lesson 3 and the total is 26, still all Minor. Add Lesson 4 instead and it is 120, because that Do is the Major grade. Nobody runs both, so 129 is not a real total.

Every item and the module are unpublished. Publish as you go.

Open the Lesson 1 worksheet

Open Worksheet: Lesson 1 Wiring LEDs with micro:bit Expansion Board and put your name on your copy.

Using the Kitronik expansion kit instead? Use this one: Worksheet: Lesson 1 Wiring LEDs with micro:bit Expansion Board (Kitronik kit)

Wire the LED modules

Seat the micro:bit in the expansion board, then connect each LED module to the pin the worksheet names.

Program the traffic light

Unplug the battery or the USB cable before you move a module. Rewiring a live board is the fastest way to kill a component.

Inputs let the board react to a person instead of just running on its own.

Build the basketball possession arrow

One press flips the arrow to the other team.

Show it to someone who has never seen it and see whether they can tell which team has the ball.

🔘 One press should mean one change

A button held down a beat too long can register as several presses, and your arrow flips twice.

Fix it in the code, not with your finger: wait for the press to end before you let the next one count.

Open Worksheet: Lesson 3 Servo Motors and put your name on your copy.

Using the Kitronik expansion kit instead? Use this one: Worksheet: Lesson 3 Servo Motors (Kitronik kit)

2

Wire and test the servo

Match the three servo wires to the right pins — signal, power, ground — before you run anything.

Send it to a few set angles and watch that it stops where you told it to.

3

Let the light sensor drive it

Read the micro:bit light sensor, then decide the level at which the sunshade should open and the level at which it should close.

Test it under real classroom light, not just with your hand over the sensor.

⚙️ A servo holds an angle, it does not spin

Tell it 0, 90, or 180 and it travels there and stays. That is what makes it good for a shade and bad for a wheel.

If it buzzes and shakes at rest, you are asking for an angle past its range. Pull the number back.
