◈ Virtual Reality • Lesson 3 of 3 ◈

📚 VR Stories: ELAR Novel Project 🎬

Build 3 VR Scenes from a Novel You Read in ELAR

📋 At a Glance

⏱️ Time: 5 class periods
🎯 Make: 3 VR Scenes
📱 Tool: Delightex
📤 Submit: Worksheet + Link
  • English
  • Español

📍 5 class periods

🎯

Final Project Overview

⏱️ 10 min

Create a VR story with 3 scenes from any novel or short story you've read this year in ELAR. Examples: A Long Walk to Water, The Outsiders, Lord of the Flies.

📖 New Words:
VR Story = A virtual reality experience that tells a story through 3D scenes
CoBlocks = Code blocks that make objects move, talk, and change scenes
🔗 Access Delightex:

🚀 Open Delightex

ask your teacher for your class link.

Sign in with Microsoft using @stu.irvingisd.net

✅ Each Scene Must Have:
  • At least 6 or 7 Objects (characters, items, props)
  • At least 2 animated objects
  • At least 1 moving on a path
  • Speech bubbles or dialogue for characters
  • 360 image OR environment background
  • Background sound
📅

Project Timeline

📍 Day 1: Ideate & Storyboard - Complete your planning worksheet
📍 Days 2-4: Build Your Scenes - Create all 3 scenes in Delightex
📍 Day 5: Showcase & Feedback - Present and get peer feedback
🎥

Watch the Tutorial

⏱️ 20 min

Learn how to create VR stories by watching this "Hansel and Gretel" example:

🌟

Example Project

⏱️ 5 min

Open this example and look at how each scene is built:

🏆

Level Up!

Extra Credit
🥉 Bronze: Add a title screen with your name and book title
🥈 Silver: Create 4+ scenes instead of 3
🥇 Gold: Add clickable objects that trigger events or narration
📝

Step-by-Step Written Instructions

⏱️ 5 class periods

Prefer reading? The written steps are below.

Click here for detailed steps

1️⃣

Day 1: Ideate & Storyboard

⏱️ 1 class period

Plan your VR story BEFORE you start building.

📝 Complete Your Storyboard Worksheet:

  • Write the name of your novel
  • Choose 3 important scenes/chapters
  • Draw each scene with the objects you'll use
  • Label what's happening in each scene
🧠 Think About: What makes this scene important? What objects and characters need to be there? What's the setting/environment?
2️⃣

Days 2-4: Build Your Scenes

⏱️ 3 class periods

Create all 3 scenes in Delightex using your storyboard as a guide.

✅ Each Scene Checklist:

  • 6+ objects (characters, items, props)
  • 2+ animated objects (use CoBlocks)
  • 1+ object moving on a path
  • 360 image or environment background
  • Background sound that fits the mood
💡 Tip: Use CoBlocks to make characters talk, show emotions, and automatically switch between scenes.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Forgetting to add scene transitions! Make sure players can move from Scene 1 → 2 → 3.
3️⃣

Day 5: Showcase & Feedback

⏱️ 1 class period

Share your VR story and get feedback from classmates.

🎉 Showcase Day:

  • Present your VR story to classmates
  • Explain which novel scenes you chose and why
  • Give and receive peer feedback
  • Submit your final Delightex link.
📤

Share Your Project

⏱️ 3 min

📤 How to share:

  1. Click Share in Delightex
  2. Select Share link
  3. Copy the link
  4. Paste in your worksheet and submit.

🌟 Submit your storyboard worksheet + Delightex link! 🚀

📍 5 períodos de clase

🎯

Resumen del Proyecto Final

⏱️ 10 min

Crea una historia de VR con 3 escenas de cualquier novela o cuento que hayas leído este año en ELAR. Ejemplos: A Long Walk to Water, The Outsiders, Lord of the Flies.

📖 Palabras Nuevas:
Historia de VR = Una experiencia de realidad virtual que cuenta una historia a través de escenas 3D
CoBlocks = Bloques de código que hacen que los objetos se muevan, hablen y cambien de escena
🔗 Acceder a Delightex:

🚀 Abrir Delightex

pregúntale a tu maestro/a por el enlace de tu clase.

Inicia sesión con Microsoft usando @stu.irvingisd.net

✅ Cada Escena Debe Tener:
  • 6+ Objetos (personajes, artículos, accesorios)
  • Al menos 2 objetos animados
  • Al menos 1 moviéndose en un camino
  • Burbujas de diálogo para los personajes
  • Imagen 360 O entorno de fondo
  • Sonido de fondo
📅

Cronograma del Proyecto

📍 Día 1: Idear y Guión Gráfico - Completa tu hoja de planificación
📍 Días 2-4: Construye Tus Escenas - Crea las 3 escenas en Delightex
📍 Día 5: Presentación y Retroalimentación - Presenta y recibe comentarios
🎥

Mira el Tutorial

⏱️ 20 min

Aprende a crear historias de VR viendo este ejemplo de "Hansel y Gretel":

🌟

Proyecto de Ejemplo

⏱️ 5 min

Abre este ejemplo y mira cómo está hecha cada escena:

🏆

¡Sube de Nivel!

Crédito Extra
🥉 Bronce: Agregar una pantalla de título con tu nombre y el título del libro
🥈 Plata: Crear 4+ escenas en vez de 3
🥇 Oro: Agregar objetos clicables que activen eventos o narración
📝

Instrucciones Escritas Paso a Paso

⏱️ 5 períodos

¿Prefieres leer? Los pasos escritos están abajo.

Haz clic aquí para ver los pasos detallados

1️⃣

Día 1: Idear y Guión Gráfico

⏱️ 1 período

Planifica tu historia de VR ANTES de empezar a construir.

📝 Completa Tu Hoja de Guión Gráfico:

  • Escribe el nombre de tu novela
  • Elige 3 escenas/capítulos importantes
  • Dibuja cada escena con los objetos que usarás
  • Etiqueta lo que está pasando en cada escena
🧠 Piensa en: ¿Qué hace importante esta escena? ¿Qué objetos y personajes deben estar ahí? ¿Cuál es el escenario/entorno?
2️⃣

Días 2-4: Construye Tus Escenas

⏱️ 3 períodos

Crea las 3 escenas en Delightex usando tu guión gráfico como guía.

✅ Lista de Verificación por Escena:

  • 6+ objetos (personajes, artículos, accesorios)
  • 2+ objetos animados (usa CoBlocks)
  • 1+ objeto moviéndose en un camino
  • Imagen 360 o entorno de fondo
  • Sonido de fondo que coincida con el ambiente
💡 Consejo: Usa CoBlocks para hacer que los personajes hablen, muestren emociones y cambien automáticamente entre escenas.
⚠️ Error Común: ¡Olvidar agregar transiciones de escena! Asegúrate de que los jugadores puedan moverse de Escena 1 → 2 → 3.
3️⃣

Día 5: Presentación y Retroalimentación

⏱️ 1 período

Comparte tu historia de VR y recibe comentarios de tus compañeros.

🎉 Día de Presentación:

  • Presenta tu historia de VR a tus compañeros
  • Explica qué escenas de la novela elegiste y por qué
  • Da y recibe retroalimentación
  • Envía tu enlace final de Delightex.
📤

Comparte Tu Proyecto

⏱️ 3 min

📤 Cómo compartir:

  1. Haz clic en Share en Delightex
  2. Selecciona Share link
  3. Copia el enlace
  4. Pégalo en tu hoja de trabajo y envía.

🌟 ¡Envía tu hoja de guión gráfico + enlace de Delightex! 🚀

BEFORE YOU PUBLISH | EDPUZZLE SETUP

Connect Edpuzzle before assigning

Use these public lesson links to add the videos to your Edpuzzle account and connect each lesson in this Canvas course:

  • The Art of Logo Design: Edpuzzle lesson | original video

For each Edpuzzle assignment, choose Edit, keep Submission Type: External Tool, choose Find, then Edpuzzle. Select the matching lesson from My Content, save, and test it in Student View.

Open Edpuzzle's Canvas setup guide. If you are not using Edpuzzle, the original-video links above let you run the lesson without the integration.

FACILITATOR’S GUIDE · SW6

Facilitator’s Guide: Pitching and Presenting

Everything you need to run this unit.

⏱ ~5 class periods🎭 Make: a personal logo and a personal brand video💻 Adobe Express · Canva · EdPuzzle

A note on the look: the two student lessons in this module wear their own orange and pink. This guide wears the career-brand slate that runs across every college and career readiness item, because that is the thread this unit belongs to. Same unit, two voices — the student pages are the loud one on purpose.

The unit at a glance

Module itemWhat happens~Time
Pitching and Presenting — two lessons, one personal brand
EdPuzzle | The Art of Logo DesignRuns first. Lesson 1 opens by telling students they have already watched it. This assignment has no description in Canvas — the page is the video and nothing else, so set it up out loud.~20 min
Lesson 1: Personal Logo and Brand in Adobe ExpressTwo periods in Adobe Express. The logo needs their name, one icon that represents them, and no more than three colors. Worksheet plus the share link come back through Google Docs.2 periods
Lesson 2: Personal Brand VideoTwo periods. Seven or more slides, the logo from Lesson 1, meaningful images, music they chose, and ten “I am…” statements from the brainstorm. Adobe Express or Canva, their choice.2 periods

Materials + prep

  • Adobe Express through ClassLink, signed in with the school account, tested before Lesson 1. Canva is the alternative for Lesson 2 only.
  • EdPuzzle class code, tested.
  • Both Google Docs worksheets opened and checked yourself — each lesson turns in from that tab, so confirm the hand-back path works before you assign it.
  • Headphones for Lesson 2. Every student is auditioning background music at the same time.
  • The student example videos linked in Lesson 2 — open one as a class before they start building.

Watch-fors

  • The EdPuzzle carries the setup and has no text on its page. Lesson 1 refers back to it as something already done. Play it as a class, or at minimum say what it is for, because the Canvas page itself says nothing.
  • This brand looks backward as much as forward. The Career Fair Expo is already behind them — they researched a career, built a booth and pitched it. Point at that: this is the same skill turned on themselves. It then goes forward into the Capstone presentation and into the ePortfolio in Closing Week, which asks for this exact logo by name.
  • The default music is the tell. Lesson 2 flags it directly: students leave whatever track the template came with. Make changing the music a check you actually do, not a line on a checklist.
  • Hold the three-color rule in Lesson 1. Name, one icon, three colors maximum. It is the whole design lesson, and it is the first thing to go when a student discovers the sticker library.

Grading

Lesson 2: Personal Brand Video is the unit’s Major grade, at 100 points. Lesson 1: Personal Logo and Brand is a Minor grade worth 5 points, and the EdPuzzle is set to 0 — 105 points in the module. Both lessons submit through Google Docs, so the worksheet with the share link pasted in is what you grade.

  3. Select the matching video from My Content. Set skipping and caption options, choose Assign, then Select.
  4. Save and test the assignment in Student View. Then remove this teacher box before students see the page.

Pitch Yourself with Images, Music & Your Logo

  • English

📍 Lesson 2 of 2 · 2 class periods

🎯

Project Overview

⏱️ 10 min

Last lesson you made a logo. Now you'll create a video that expands your personal brand using images, videos, music, and your logo.

📖 New Words:
Personal Brand Video = A short video that shows who you are and what you care about.
🔗 Access Your Tool:

🚀 Open Launchpad

Choose Adobe Express or Canva from Launchpad

✅ Your Video Must Have:

  • Your logo from Lesson 1

Extra Credit

Step-by-Step Written Instructions

⏱️ 90 min total

1️⃣

Watch: Personal Brand Example

⏱️ 5 min

Watch Brittany's personal brand video to see what elements to include:

🔍 Notice: Words that describe her, interests & hobbies, accomplishments, goals, meaningful pictures & video clips

⬢ FACILITATOR’S GUIDE · SW6 ⬢

Facilitator’s Guide: Tech for Good Capstone

Everything you need to run the last project of the year.

📅 2 weeks · ~10 class days✅ 1 project chosen from 6 options🌐 Topic: a cause the student cares about

The unit at a glance

Module itemWhat happens~Time
Tech for Good Capstone — two weeks, student-chosen project, student-chosen topic
Tech for Good CapstoneThe project itself. Students pick one of six builds — MakeCode Arcade game, ThingLink 360 tour, TinkerCAD 3D print, Adobe Express or Canva campaign, Delightex AR experience, or Piskel pixel animation — copy the matching portfolio Google Doc, and work through it. Days 1–2 research, 3–4 plan, 5–8 build, 9 polish, 10 reflect and submit.~10 days
Capstone Research HelperUsed during the project, not before it. Send students here on Days 1–2. It holds the source rules, the general-purpose starting sites, and curated links for each of the eight suggested topics.Days 1–2
Closing
Xello Check-in: Scholarship ProfileComplete the Scholarship profile in Goals & Plans, filter matches by grade, screenshot and upload. Runs last, and it reads off every Xello check-in they have done this year.~20 min

Materials + prep

  • Decide which of the six options you can actually support before you show students the menu. The 3D print option needs printer time and a queue; the AR option needs Delightex and cubes; the ThingLink option needs accounts. It is fair to take an option off the table — it is not fair to take it off on Day 6.
  • Tool access confirmed for whatever you keep: MakeCode Arcade, ThingLink, TinkerCAD plus a working 3D printer, Adobe Express and Canva, Delightex, Piskel.
  • The portfolio Google Doc copy links, one per option, tested. That doc is the student’s instructions and the graded artifact at once.
  • Newsela and Britannica School logins working before Day 1 — the Research Helper leans on them.
  • Xello through ClassLink for the check-in.
  • Presentation or booth space for Day 10, plus the time to use it. Book it in week one.

Watch-fors

  • This is the last piece of a thread that started in Week 0. The project body says so: what students build here is the final addition to the portfolio they opened in Starting our Portfolio and grew in Portfolio Part 2. Open the capstone by walking that thread backward with them, so the two weeks read as an ending rather than one more assignment.
  • Day 10 echoes the Career Fair Expo. Students already know how to stand at a booth and pitch, because they did it in SW2. Run the showcase the same way and say that out loud — it is the second time, not the first.
  • Approve topics and projects by end of Day 2. A student still deciding on Day 4 will not finish, and the 3D print option in particular has to be in the printer queue with days to spare.
  • The Research Helper exists because of the AI Overview problem. It rules out chatbots, Google’s AI summary box and Wikipedia as sources, and shows students how to mine Wikipedia’s reference list instead. Read those rules with the class rather than linking past them — that page is doing real work.

Grading

Tech for Good Capstone is the unit’s Major grade, at 100 points. The portfolio Google Doc comes back through Google Docs and holds all five parts plus the reflection, so that doc is what you grade. The Xello Check-in: Scholarship Profile is a Minor grade worth 5 points, submitted as a screenshot — 105 points in the module. The Capstone Research Helper is a page and is not graded.

TECH FOR GOOD CAPSTONE

🔍 Research Helper

Find real facts. Cite real sources. Fill out Part 2 of your portfolio.

Encuentra datos reales. Cita fuentes reales. Completa la Parte 2 de tu portafolio.

← Back to Tech for Good Capstone · Volver al Capstone

🚨 Research Rules / Reglas de Investigación

✅ YES – These count as sources

• News sites (Newsela, PBS, CNN10)

• Government sites (.gov – CDC, EPA, USDA)

• Organizations (Nat Geo, Feeding America, etc.)

• Encyclopedias (Britannica, not Wikipedia)

• Educational sites (.edu, .org)

❌ NO – These do NOT count

• “Google” (Google is a search engine, not a source)

• ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini, or any AI chatbot

• Google AI Overview (the box at the top of search)

• Wikipedia (use it to FIND sources, not as one)

• Random blogs, TikTok, YouTube comments

💡 “But I Found It on Google...”

When you Google something, you might see an AI Overview at the top. That box is written by AI – it pulls info from real websites but sometimes gets things wrong. Don’t copy from it. Don’t cite it.

What to do instead: Scroll past the AI box. Click on the actual articles below it. Read THOSE. That’s your real source.

Wikipedia trick: Wikipedia itself isn’t a source, but it can help. Scroll to the bottom of any Wikipedia page and look at the References section. Those links ARE real sources. Click them.

Cuando buscas en Google, el cuadro de “AI Overview” arriba NO es una fuente. Baja y haz clic en los artículos reales. Wikipedia tampoco es fuente, pero sus referencias al final sí lo son.

📚 Start Here – Works for ANY Topic

These sites have articles on almost every topic. Search your topic here first. / Estos sitios tienen artículos sobre casi todos los temas.

Newsela

News articles at YOUR reading level. Log in with your school account.

PBS LearningMedia

Videos and articles from PBS. Free, no login needed.

Britannica School

Encyclopedia with middle school level articles. Use school login.

Nat Geo Kids

Science and environment articles. Free.

DoSomething.org

🎯 Links for YOUR Topic

🍞 Food Insecurity in Our Community

🛡 Cyberbullying & Digital Citizenship
Click to expand

Click any link to open it in a new tab.

• StopBullying.gov – What Is Cyberbullying?

🤖 AI & What It Means for Your Future
Click to expand

✨ I Picked My Own Topic / Elegí mi propio tema
Click to expand

If your topic isn’t on the list above, here’s how to find good sources:

Step 1: Search your topic on Newsela or Britannica School first. They’ll give you the most readable articles.

Step 2: Try DoSomething.org – search for “11 Facts About [your topic]”. They cover a lot.

Step 3: If you need to Google it, add the word “facts” or “statistics” to your search. Example: “water pollution facts for students”

Step 4: Look for .gov, .org, or .edu in the URL. Those are usually trustworthy.

Si tu tema no está arriba: busca en Newsela o Britannica primero. Luego prueba DoSomething.org. Si usas Google, agrega “facts” o “statistics” a tu búsqueda y busca sitios .gov, .org, o .edu.

✍ How to Write Your Source in the Portfolio Doc

You don’t need fancy citations. Just write the website name and URL. That’s it.

Example / Ejemplo:

Source: CDC – Children’s Mental Health

URL: https://www.cdc.gov/children-mental-health/data-research/index.html

No necesitas citas formales. Solo escribe el nombre del sitio web y la dirección URL.

FACILITATOR’S GUIDE · SW6

Facilitator’s Guide: Closing Week

Two items, one week, and the year gets packaged into a single link.

⏱ ~2 class periods🌐 Make: one published ePortfolio page💻 Adobe Express · Canvas survey

The unit at a glance

Module itemWhat happens~Time
Closing Week — run the portfolio first, the survey last
Create an ePortfolioOne published Adobe Express web page holding the year: a title with their name and a meaningful image, a short introduction, a photo or link and a description for every project, and their personal logo from Pitching and Presenting. They submit the published share link.1–2 periods
Student: Post-SurveyThe twin of the Pre-Survey from Week 0. Not for a grade — it exists to measure what changed across the year. Run it in class, in the last minutes of the final period.~10 min

Materials + prep

  • Adobe Express through ClassLink, signed in, tested.
  • Their work, gathered before they start building. The portfolio doc from Week 0, Portfolio Part 2, the Tech for Good Capstone, and their personal logo from Lesson 1: Personal Logo and Brand. A student hunting for files is a student not building a page.
  • The student ePortfolio examples linked in step 1 — open one together before they start.
  • The Post-Survey link confirmed working on a student device, not just yours.

Watch-fors

  • The tutorial video says Adobe Spark. Spark is Adobe Express now. The assignment already warns about it: where the video says Spark, choose Webpage from the Get Started templates. Say it before you press play or you will answer it fifteen times.
  • Submission is a published URL, not a file. Students have to publish the page and paste the share link. An unpublished draft link opens for them and for nobody else — check one submission early in the period and you will catch the pattern before the whole class repeats it.
  • The survey is not graded, and it still needs to be done. Give it real class time at the end rather than assigning it as homework on the last day, or the response rate collapses.

Grading

Create an ePortfolio is the module’s Major grade, at 100 points, submitted as a website URL — that link is what you review. Student: Post-Survey is 0 points, ungraded by design, and says so to students.

🎬 Tutorials

📽️ Stop Motion Storytelling Project

In this 6-day project you write, direct, animate and edit your own film. Using Stop Motion Studio, you’ll make a short animated film—between 30 to 60 seconds long—that tells a story with characters and props you build yourself. You start by planning the plot and finish with the film uploaded.

You turn in the plot diagram and the storyboard along the way, then upload the finished film as an .mp4 or .mov.

🗂️ Step-by-Step Breakdown

  1. Brainstorm & Plan: Choose your genre and think through your characters and conflict.
  2. Plot Diagram: Map your story structure using exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, and resolution.
  3. Storyboard: Sketch or describe 6–12 key scenes from your film.
  4. Set Design & Filming: Build your sets, animate your story using Stop Motion Studio, and capture each shot carefully.
  5. Final Edits & Reflection: Add sound or titles and reflect on what you learned.

You will have approximately 6–7 class periods to complete your final video.

📊 Rubric (40 Points)

Criteria 4 - Exemplary 3 - Proficient 2 - Developing 1 - Incomplete
Plot Diagram & Structure Strong arc; creative conflict/resolution Clear plot with some detail Basic or rushed structure Missing key parts
Storyboard All scenes visualized clearly Most scenes planned Some scenes unclear No storyboard submitted
Technical Quality Smooth, well-lit, stable shots Minor issues with quality Choppy or poorly lit Very poor or incomplete video
Creativity Unique ideas and style Some creative choices Standard or copied Unoriginal or unclear
Effort Consistent and focused effort Mostly focused Rushed or incomplete Little to no effort
Reflection Thoughtful and insightful Answers all prompts Minimal or vague Missing

📥 Assignments & Uploads

  • Plot Diagram & Storyboard: Submit to the assigned Canvas pages before filming begins.
  • Final Stop Motion Video: Export and upload your 30–60 second film (.mp4 or .mov)
  • Optional Voiceovers or Credits: Add in Stop Motion Studio or iMovie

🧠 Reflection Questions

Submit your answers in the discussion post or text entry field:

  • 🎬 What part of the process did you enjoy most?
  • ⚙️ What was the biggest technical challenge?
  • 🔁 If you could redo one thing, what would it be?
  • 💡 What advice would you give to a student doing this next?

TEACHER SETUP | REMOVE THIS BOX AFTER TESTING

Reconnect this Edpuzzle before you publish it

The imported player belongs to the source Canvas class. It will not open as a working assignment for your students.

  1. Open the reusable Edpuzzle video: Intro to Stop Motion Process and copy it to My Content if needed.

  3. Select the matching video from My Content. Set skipping and caption options, choose Assign, then Select.
  4. Save and test the assignment in Student View. Then remove this teacher box before students see the page.

Open Edpuzzle's Canvas setup guide

No Edpuzzle? Use the original video. Review the questions in the Edpuzzle first so you can pause for them or move them into Canvas.

WATCH AND RESPOND | MIRA Y RESPONDE

resource.body:
📘 Day 1: Brainstorm & Story Planning

Today you come up with your story idea. Choose your characters, your setting, and your conflict. This is what your script and your animation are built on.

Instructions:

  • Pick a story genre (funny, drama, sci-fi, fantasy, etc.)
  • Create a basic outline of:
    • Main character
    • Setting (where and when?)
    • Conflict (what's the problem?)
    • Resolution (how will it end?)
  • Submit your plan as a paragraph, list, or mind map

Checkpoint (5 pts):

  • ☐ Has a clear main character
  • ☐ Includes setting and conflict
  • ☐ Uploaded on time

📊 Day 2: Plot Diagram Your Story

Before you write your script, plan your story with the 5 parts of a plot diagram.

Instructions:

  • Exposition: Who is the main character? Where are they?
  • Rising Action: What problem or challenge begins to form?
  • Climax: What’s the most intense or exciting moment?
  • Falling Action: How is the conflict starting to get resolved?
  • Resolution: How does the story end?

You can submit your plot diagram in any of these ways:

  • Draw it on paper and upload a picture
  • Use a Google Slides or Docs template
  • Type it directly in the text box

Checkpoint (5 pts):

  • ☐ Includes all 5 plot parts
  • ☐ Conflict is clear and makes sense
  • ☐ Story has a beginning, middle, and end

🎨 Day 3: Storyboard Your Scenes

Create a simple storyboard showing how each part of your story will be animated.

Instructions:

  • Sketch or describe 6–12 scenes
  • Write what’s happening in each scene
  • Include character actions, props, and movement

Checkpoint (5 pts):

  • ☐ At least 6 scenes are planned
  • ☐ Follows the script in order
  • ☐ Notes are clear about what happens

• Set, Prop & Character Design
  • Filming
  • Voiceovers & Effects

Set, Prop & Character Design 🧱

Build your characters and scenes using clay, paper, recycled items, or toys. Cardboard backdrops, LEGO and markers all work.

  • Try to reuse and recycle—boxes, fabric scraps, and bottle caps make great props.
  • Test your setup: Can your characters stand and be moved slightly without falling?
  • Make sure your background won’t distract from the action.

Example Images:

 

Filming 🎥

Open Stop Motion Studio and capture your story one photo at a time.

  • Use a tripod or books to keep your camera steady.
  • Take 8–12 photos for every second of animation.
  • Tap gently to avoid moving your setup accidentally.

Try to keep your lighting consistent. Use lamps or natural light and avoid casting shadows.

Watch this example for inspiration:

Cardboard Stop-Motion Example

Voiceovers & Sound Effects 🎙️

Add voice acting and sound effects to your film.

  • Write a script for each character—then practice reading with emotion.
  • Record in a quiet space; keep your mouth near the mic without bumping it.
  • Re-record as needed if there’s background noise or mistakes.

Sound FX ideas:

  • Rustling leaves = crumpling paper
  • Thunder = shaking a cookie sheet
  • Footsteps = tapping your fingers on a table

You may also add background music using royalty-free sites or soundtracks built into iMovie or Stop Motion Studio Pro.

Example: "We designed a smart watch that tells a football player if he may have a concussion by using the motion sensor to detect hard hits"

Then, provide feedback to three other students using "I like..." and "I wonder..." statements.

rubric.long_description: Name, symbol, colors

ratings.long_description: Your logo carries the product name and a symbol somebody could recognize again, in two or more colors chosen for what the product does.
Your logo has the name of your product, a memorable symbol, and at least two colors that represent the product.
The logo is made but the product name or the symbol is missing, or it uses one color.
No logo was made for the product.

rubric.description: Pitch video: your product and your user
rubric.long_description: Name, user, SDG, problem, solution

ratings.long_description: All five are in the video, and a viewer who knows nothing about your project can say who it is for and what problem it solves.
Your video gives the product name and logo, who your end user is with their empathy map, the SDG your product addresses, your problem statement, and how the product solves it.
The video covers the product but skips the end user, the SDG, or the problem statement.
There is no pitch video, or it names the product and stops there.

rubric.description: Pitch video: how you built it
rubric.long_description: Process, budget, feedback changes

ratings.long_description: The video shows the prototype changing over time, with the feedback that caused each change and the budget it had to fit.
Your video shows the prototyping process with pictures or video, says how the prototype met the budget and the other requirements, and says what you changed after user feedback.
The video shows the finished prototype but not the process, the budget, or the feedback changes.
The video says nothing about how the prototype was built or changed.

rubric.long_description: Worksheet, links, and project files

ratings.long_description: Everything is in the worksheet, and the reflection answers name specific changes you made and specific problems you solved.

Your worksheet has the share link to your video, the share link to your MakeCode project, all four reflection questions answered, and your artifacts: empathy map, feedback capture grid, sketches, and budget.
The worksheet is turned in but a share link does not open, or artifacts or reflection answers are missing.
No worksheet is submitted.

resource.body:
🏠 Design Your Dream Room: Step 1 - Introduction and Research 🏠

🌟 Intro To Project 🌟

Begin by watching the introduction video. Jot down your initial ideas and discuss them with a partner.

🔍 Step 1: Research and Brainstorm 🔍

Use a digital notebook or paper to brainstorm items for your dream room. Sketch your ideas and search online for reference images. Keep in mind the room type (Bedroom, Entertainment Room, Backyard, etc.) and what you would put in it.

  • Think about furniture, decorations, and functionality.
  • Consider the measurements of your items to keep everything proportional in your design.

Create a digital or paper “style board” to organize your ideas and images.

Submit your style board with reference images and item dimensions on Google Slides or another platform. Share and submit the link in this Canvas module.

📚 Materials Needed 📚

  • Computer with internet access
  • Digital notebook or paper sketchbook
  • Pencil or pen

🎯 Learning Outcomes 🎯

  • Develop an organized system for documenting design ideas.
  • Create models based on real-world measurements and proportions.

🏠 Design Your Dream Room in Tinkercad: Understanding Scale 🏠

🌟 What is Scaling? 🌟

Imagine using a magical shrink ray to make a life-sized room fit into your computer screen! That's what scaling does. It shrinks everything down proportionally, so we can create a mini-version of something big, like a room, and work on it in Tinkercad.

🔍 Step 1: Convert Room Dimensions 📏

Let's turn the size of a real room into a tiny model that fits in Tinkercad. We'll use a room size of 31ft x 21ft x 8ft as an example. We'll convert these dimensions from feet to meters, then to millimeters, and finally scale them down to fit a 1:100 scale model.

✏️ Conversion Process Explained ✏️

Dimension Feet to Meters Meters to Millimeters Scaled Measurement (1:100)
Length (31ft) 31 x 0.305 = 9.455m 9.455 x 1000 = 9455mm 9455 / 100 = 94.55mm
Width (21ft) 21 x 0.305 = 6.405m 6.405 x 1000 = 6405mm 6405 / 100 = 64.05mm
Height (8ft) 8 x 0.305 = 2.44m 2.44 x 1000 = 2440mm 2440 / 100 = 24.4mm

Feet to Meters: We start by converting feet to meters because Tinkercad doesn't use feet. 1 foot is approximately 0.305 meters. So, if your room is 31 feet long, in meters, it's 31 times 0.305.

Meters to Millimeters: Next, we change meters to millimeters because Tinkercad uses millimeters. There are 1000 millimeters in a meter. So, our room's length in meters gets multiplied by 1000.

Scale Down: Finally, we shrink our measurements for Tinkercad. To make our room 100 times smaller (1:100 scale), we divide the millimeter measurement by 100. This makes our model the perfect mini-size for designing in Tinkercad!

 

 

📋 Worksheet Activity: Scale Down Your Furniture 📋

Download the provided worksheet. Choose 5 pieces of furniture from your Style Board. Convert their real-life measurements to millimeters, then scale them down to 1:100.

🛋️ Example: Converting Furniture Measurements 🛋️

Let's practice with an example. Suppose you have a couch that is 72 inches long. Here's how we scale it down:

  • Convert inches to meters: 72 inches = 72 x 0.0254 = 1.83 meters.
  • Convert meters to millimeters: 1.83 meters = 1.83 x 1000 = 1830 mm.
  • Scale down to 1:100: 1830 mm x 0.01 = 18.3 mm.

Your Tinkercad couch will be 18.3 mm long. You will need to do this process for the Length, Width, and Height of each furniture piece.

Measurement Conversion Cheat Sheet

Conversion Formula
Feet to Meters 1 foot = 0.305 meters
Inches to Meters 1 inch = 0.0254 meters
Meters to Millimeters 1 meter = 1000 millimeters
Scaling Down (1:100) Length (mm) / 100 = Scaled Length (mm)
Feet to Millimeters (Direct Conversion) Length (ft) × 0.305 × 1000 = Length (mm)
Inches to Millimeters (Direct Conversion) Length (in) × 0.0254 × 1000 = Length (mm)

Example Calculations:

  • Example 1 (Feet to mm, then Scale): A couch is 6 feet long. 6 ft × 0.305 m/ft = 1.83 m, 1.83 m × 1000 mm/m = 1830 mm, then scaled: 1830 mm / 100 = 18.3 mm.
  • Example 2 (Inches to mm, then Scale): A table is 48 inches wide. 48 in × 0.0254 m/in = 1.2192 m, 1.2192 m × 1000 mm/m = 1219.2 mm, then scaled: 1219.2 mm / 100 = 12.192 mm.

🏠 Dream Room: Determine Scale 🏠

👩‍💻 Start with the 'Room Scale Template' in Tinkercad 👨‍💻

Begin your design journey in Tinkercad by finding the "Room Scale Template." Here's how:

  1. Go to the TinkerCAD activity titled "Design your Dream Room".
  2. Locate the template "Room Scale Template".
  3. Select "Copy and Tinker" to start working on your design.

🎥 Learning to Work with Boxes 🎥

Watch this instructional video to learn how to work with boxes in Tinkercad. These skills will be essential for creating the structure of your room:

🛋️ Working with Furniture 🛋️

This video will show you how to create furniture like sofas for your room. Jot down notes to apply these techniques in your Tinkercad design:

🔨 Create Room Objects 🔨

Review this Tips for Creating Room Objects.pdf for ideas and inspiration. This guide offers various images and tips for building different objects in Tinkercad.

🌟 Bringing Your Design to Life 🌟

After watching the example room video, you're ready to start creating your room and its contents. Remember, the video is for reference; express your unique ideas creatively in Tinkercad!

Your teacher will provide instructions on how to share your Tinkercad file once your design is complete.

 

The Extrusion Tool

 

🌐 Downloading 3D Files for Tinkercad 🌐

Expand your Tinkercad project with cool 3D models! Here's how you can download them:

  1. Visit free3d.com to explore a variety of free 3D files.
  2. Choose a model you like. Remember, it must be in .stl or .obj format.
  3. Ensure the file size is under 25MB to be compatible with Tinkercad.
  4. Click to download. The file will usually download as a zip file.
  5. After downloading, double-click the zip file to open it.
  6. Drag the .stl or .obj file into your Downloads folder.

Now you're ready to import these files into your Tinkercad project and get creative!

📏 Tinkercad Dream Room Project Rubric 📐

Learning Outcomes 4: Advanced/Mastery 3: Proficient 2: Satisfactory 1: Needs Improvement Student Score
Used technology or a sketchbook to develop an organized system for drawing ideas and documenting progress.  (StyleBoard Presentation) Consistently and effectively used Mostly used with minor lapses Used but not consistently Rarely or ineffectively used  
Developed proportional models based on real measurements. (2 Objects Properly Scaled in TinkerCAD) Models are accurately proportional Mostly accurate proportions Some issues with proportions Inaccurate proportions  
Converted feet/inches to millimeters. (Conversion Sheet) Accurate conversion Minor inaccuracies in conversion Some errors in conversion Incorrect conversion  
Chose an appropriate scale to create room on a Tinkercad workplane. (Used Template) Appropriately scaled Mostly appropriate scaling Some scaling issues Incorrect scale  
Created a 3D room and accessories that are easily identifiable.  Highly detailed and identifiable Generally identifiable with some detail Basic identification with limited detail Lacks identifiable features  
Designed a 3D room that can be 3D printed. (Flat Foundation, Avoid Overhangs) Printable without issues Mostly printable with minor adjustments needed Printable with significant adjustments Not printable

🌈 Vision Board Assignment Submission Guidelines 🌈

Versión en Español aquí

🌟 General Objectives 🌟

TEKS Section 127.2 (4)(D): Apply core academic skills to meet personal growth and goal-setting.

Aim: Students will learn the importance of self-reflection and its role in personal, academic, and career goals.

Materials Needed: Laptop/Tablet, Pencil, Paper, art supplies for vision board.

📝 Preliminary Steps 📝

  • Self-Reflection Time: Use the camera on your device to look at yourself and reflect on what you see. This is more than skin-deep—go beyond the physical.
  • The Mirror of Self-Reflection: Complete Part A of your worksheet based on your reflections.

🎨 Vision Board Creation 🎨

Criteria: Create a vision board using art supplies, magazines, scissors, glue, and poster board or cardboard. You may also opt for digital platforms like Google Slides, Vectr, or Canva.

Elements to Include:

  • Images that represent your goals, dreams, and aspirations.
  • Text that resonates with your objectives.
  • Personal touches like drawings or mementos.

🔥 Requirements 🔥

  • 🎨 Create one vision board.
  • ✒️ Must include text.
  • 🖼️ Must include images.
  • 🌟 Add personal touches like drawings or mementos.

🌟 Final Touches 🌟

Make sure your vision board aligns with the essence of your self-reflection and future goals. If you choose a digital platform, make sure to download your vision board as a PDF or image file.

📄 Project Submission 📄

Platform: Submit your completed vision board through Canvas.

File Types: Acceptable file types include PDF, JPG, PNG, or a shared link to your digital vision board.

Deadline: [Insert Deadline Here]

🎓 Proyecto de Feria de Carreras: Pasos 1 y 2 🎓

Versión en Inglés aquí

🌟 Curso de Preparación Universitaria y de Carrera para Octavo Grado 🌟

La investigación de carreras implica recopilar información sobre una carrera específica, como las funciones laborales, la educación requerida, el salario y el entorno laboral.

🔍 Paso 1: Elección de una Carrera 🔍

Exploración de tus Intereses

Identifica tus pasiones y hobbies. Considera tus habilidades y fortalezas.

XELLO - Explora Carreras

XELLO es una plataforma en línea que ayuda a los estudiantes a explorar diferentes carreras. Proporciona información detallada sobre varios trabajos, incluida la educación requerida, habilidades y expectativas salariales.

Otros Sitios Web Recomendados para la Investigación

Además de XELLO, otros sitios web pueden ayudarte en la investigación de tu carrera:

  • CareerOneStop: Información sobre exploración de carreras, programas de formación y herramientas de búsqueda de empleo.
  • Bureau of Labor Statistics: Datos sobre perspectivas laborales, salarios y educación.
  • O*NET En línea: Información completa sobre habilidades, capacidades y actividades laborales.

Entrega en Canvas - Elige una Carrera y Explica por Qué

Después de tu investigación, elige una carrera que te interese y explica por qué. Envía tu respuesta en Canvas, proporcionando razones y ejemplos específicos.

📋 Paso 2: Hoja de Planificación para la Investigación de Carreras 📋

Para organizar tu investigación de carreras, utiliza la Hoja de Planificación para la Investigación de Carreras. Esto te guiará en el proceso de investigación y te asegurará de recopilar toda la información necesaria.

Crearás un sitio web centrado en la carrera de tu elección. Xello será tu recurso principal. Aquí hay algunos otros sitios web para comenzar tu investigación:

  • CA Career Zone: Para elecciones iniciales de carrera.
  • My Next Move: Resúmenes rápidos, videos y enlaces.
  • CareerOneStop: Descripciones detalladas, videos, gráficos y tablas.
  • Salary.com: Información detallada sobre el salario del trabajo.

Utiliza la Hoja de Planificación para prepararte para las otras partes del proyecto. Esto debería incluir:

  • Mejores Ubicaciones
  • Perspectivas laborales para los próximos 5 años
  • Beneficios de esta carrera
  • Desafíos de esta carrera
  • Enlaces a videos/fuentes/referencias
  • Cualquier otra nota sobre esta carrera

📖 Instructions

Follow each step below to learn how to create VR stories and movies using CoSpaces, then recreate three scenes from the novel your are reading in ELAR

FINAL PROJECT: ELAR NOVEL IN VR

Create a VR story with:

  • 3 different scenes, each representing a significant chapter in the ELAR novel you are reading.
  • Each scene must include:
    • >= 6 Objects
    • At least two animated
    • At least one moving on a path
    • A 360 image or Environment
    • Background Sound

🎥 Video Tutorial

Follow the video tutorial below to learn how to create "Hansel and Gretel" in CoSpaces. Pause and rewind the video if you get stuck!

Storytelling in CoSpaces

Having trouble viewing the video? Click here

If you aren't sure how certain chapters of this CoSpace were programmed, click on this share link and then select "remix" to copy this project into your own CoSpaces. Then, you can look inside at all the details for yourself!

🎬 Activity: Create your own CoSpaces VR Story!

For this activity, you will create your own VR story in CoSpaces by representing 3 scenes/chapters in one of your current ELAR novels including, The Giver, Refugee, and The Outsiders.

Your CoSpaces story should:

  • Have at least three different scenes.
  • Use CoBlocks to move characters, add speech/thoughts, and change scenes automatically.
  • Each scene must include:
    • >= 6 Objects
    • At least two animated
    • At least one moving on a path
    • A 360 image or Environment
    • Background Sound

Think About:

  • Brief Description of the Scene: What happens in this scene? Why is it important?
  • Key Objects: What objects need to be included? Why are these objects important to the scene?
  • Background Environment/360 Image: What is the setting? What kind of background or 360 image will you use? (e.g., forest, cityscape, classroom) Why did you choose this environment?
  • Characters and Expressions: What are their emotions or expressions? How will you show these in the VR space?
  • Animations and Path Movements: What path movements will characters or objects take? (e.g., walking, running, flying)

Example:

⛵ Sailing Home · Lesson 3 of 3

AI Ethics Debate

Last stop in the arc: decide what you actually think, and be able to defend it out loud.

💬 Nearpod debate
🏆 5 points
📦 Upload or link
1

Join the Nearpod and work through it with your class

Everything you need is in the Nearpod below — follow along and answer as it goes.

2

Take a position and say why

When you pick a side, name the evidence behind it. "I think" is a start; "I think, because" is an argument.

⚖️ A debate is not an argument

You are not trying to win by talking louder. You are trying to make the strongest version of your own case — and to answer the strongest version of theirs, not the weakest one.

📤 Turn in: Submit your debate notes as a file upload, or paste a link to your document.

TEACHER SETUP | REMOVE THIS BOX AFTER TESTING

Reconnect this Edpuzzle before you publish it

The imported player belongs to the source Canvas class. It will not open as a working assignment for your students.

  1. Open the reusable Edpuzzle video: The Making of a Young Entrepreneur and copy it to My Content if needed.
  2. Edit this Canvas assignment. Keep Submission Type: External Tool, choose Find, then Edpuzzle.
  3. Select the matching video from My Content. Set skipping and caption options, choose Assign, then Select.
  4. Save and test the assignment in Student View. Then remove this teacher box before students see the page.

Open Edpuzzle's Canvas setup guide

No Edpuzzle? Use the original video. Review the questions in the Edpuzzle first so you can pause for them or move them into Canvas.

The Making of a Young Entrepreneur

Gabrielle Jordan Williams built her own business while she was still a kid, and in this TEDx talk she explains how she did it. Watch for what she does when something does not go her way.

Instructions: Play the video below and answer the questions as they come up. The video opens in a new tab. Bring her ideas with you into Lesson 4, where you design your own hero's brand and logo.
